The gap that matters is at the top dose: Foundayo's reported ceiling is $349, the Wegovy pill's $299. The gap that matters more is whether your insurance covers either one, because $25 beats both. Wegovy pill price online walks the semaglutide side in full.

sections.heading: Do insurance and Medicare cover Foundayo and the Wegovy pill?
sections.body: Both drugs sit inside the same two programmes. Commercial insurance. Each manufacturer offers a savings card for commercially insured patients whose plan covers the drug - Lilly's bringing Foundayo to $25 a month, Novo Nordisk's reported to bring the Wegovy pill to as low as $25 - and neither card is available on Medicare, Medicaid or other government plans. Coverage itself is the hurdle: plans still vary widely on weight-management GLP-1s, and our insurance guide explains how to check before you choose. Medicare. The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge, a CMS pilot running July 1, 2026 through December 31, 2027, covers the Wegovy pill and injection, the Zepbound KwikPen and Foundayo at a flat $50 copay that does not rise with the dose. If you are on Medicare, that single question - am I eligible for the Bridge - matters more than anything else on this page; GLP-1s after 65 covers what to ask your Part D plan.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of Foundayo and the Wegovy pill?
sections.body: The same family as every GLP-1: mostly gastrointestinal, mostly early, mostly during dose increases. In OASIS 4, gastrointestinal adverse events occurred in 74% of people on the Wegovy pill against 42% on placebo, led by nausea and diarrhoea. In ATTAIN-1, gastrointestinal events were also the most frequent with Foundayo and were typically mild to moderate. Neither trial reported a safety signal outside the known class profile, which carries the standard GLP-1 warnings around thyroid C-cell tumours in rodents, pancreatitis and gallbladder disease. Dose and how gradually you step up matter more than which pill you take, and a clinician who manages the titration is the single biggest factor in tolerating either - our semaglutide side-effects guide covers what helps.

sections.heading: How fast do Foundayo and the Wegovy pill work?
sections.body: Neither trial reported a head-to-head speed comparison, so the honest answer comes from how each pill is dosed and how long each trial ran. Both start low and step up: the Wegovy pill from a 1.5 mg starting tablet to the 25 mg maintenance dose over the first months, Foundayo across six tablet strengths from 0.8 mg to 17.2 mg, with at least 30 days on each step so the gut can adapt. Appetite effects are usually noticed within the first weeks at the starting doses; measurable weight loss builds as the dose rises and keeps accumulating for months. The headline results are end-of-trial numbers, measured at week 64 for the Wegovy pill (OASIS 4) and week 72 for Foundayo (ATTAIN-1), roughly 15 and 17 months in. A 12-week result on either pill is therefore not the trial figure; it is an early point on a curve that was still falling through the first year in both studies. The practical reading: give either pill a full titration plus several months at the maintenance dose before judging it, and expect the first months to be as much about tolerability as about weight. Our guide to how long semaglutide takes to work gives the week-by-week picture for the molecule in the Wegovy pill.

sections.heading: What is the 25 mg dose, and what does '2.5 mg' mean?
sections.body: Three different numbers get mixed up in searches about these pills. 25 mg is the Wegovy pill's maintenance dose: one 25 mg semaglutide tablet a day, reached after the 1.5 mg starting steps. It is far higher than the injection's dose because only a small fraction of an oral peptide is absorbed. 2.4 mg is the weekly maintenance dose of the Wegovy injection. 2.5 mg has nothing to do with either pill: it is the starting dose of Zepbound and Mounjaro (tirzepatide), a different injectable molecule. Foundayo's doses are 0.8 mg to 17.2 mg once daily across six tablet strengths. The 17.2 mg top strength is the one behind the 11.1% figure in ATTAIN-1. The 6, 12 and 36 mg numbers you may see online were doses of the investigational formulation used in the trials; the FDA label presents those results as equivalent approved doses. If you are comparing "Wegovy 25 mg vs Foundayo", the fair pairing is the Wegovy pill at 25 mg against Foundayo at its 17.2 mg top strength, the highest approved dose of each product.

sections.heading: Do Foundayo and the Wegovy pill work for adults without diabetes?
sections.body: Yes, and that is exactly who the headline trials studied. OASIS 4 (Wegovy pill) and ATTAIN-1 (Foundayo) both enrolled adults with obesity, or overweight with at least one weight-related condition, and both excluded people with diabetes, so the 13.6% and 11.1% figures are results in people without diabetes. Each drug has separate trials in type 2 diabetes, and as with every GLP-1, average weight loss in those populations is smaller; a diabetes trial figure should never be set against a non-diabetes one. For someone without diabetes deciding between the two pills, the numbers in the table above are the right ones to use, with the standing caveat that they come from two different trials of different sizes (307 participants versus 3,127) and different lengths.

sections.heading: What do the FDA labels say that the marketing does not?
sections.body: Both labels carry the GLP-1 class warnings, and they matter more than the brand differences. Each has a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumours seen in rodents, and each is contraindicated for anyone with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2. Both warn about pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, dehydration-related kidney injury, low blood sugar when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas, and use in pregnancy. Where they differ: the Wegovy pill's label is built around absorption, with the instruction to take it on an empty stomach with a small amount of plain water and to wait at least 30 minutes before food, drink or other oral medicines, and its approval covers reducing cardiovascular risk as well as weight management, as the injection's does. Foundayo's label has no food, water or timing instructions, and its approval is for chronic weight management. Neither label is a reason to self-select: a prescriber reads your history against these lists, which is the point of the prescription.

sections.heading: Which pill is more cost-effective?
sections.body: Price per month is close; price per year and price per unit of result are where the two separate, and only one of those is a fair calculation. Per year, self-pay, as reported: Foundayo at $149 to $349 a month by dose is $1,788 to $4,188; the Wegovy pill at the reported $149 to $299 tiers is $1,788 to $3,588; through ro, the Wegovy pill's $149 first month then $299 comes to $3,438 for the medication plus the membership ($39 the first month, then $74 to $149, so $853 to $1,678 more). With commercial coverage both are $25 a month, $300 a year, and on Medicare's Bridge both are $50 a month, $600 a year, which is why coverage decides this question before anything else. Per percentage point of weight lost is the calculation to resist: dividing a price by a trial average mixes two different studies, two different durations and your own unknown response, and no clinician would choose that way. What the numbers do support: at the maintenance dose, Foundayo's reported ceiling is $50 a month ($600 a year) higher than the Wegovy pill's, while the Wegovy pill's published trial result is 2.4 percentage points larger. Whether that trade is worth it turns on whether you can keep the empty-stomach routine, which is the one factor that decides whether you get the Wegovy pill's result at all.

sections.heading: Besides cost, what else is different?
sections.body:
Six things, in rough order of how much they matter day to day.
  • The routine. Empty stomach, a little water and a 30-minute wait every morning for the Wegovy pill; any time, with or without food, for Foundayo.
  • Other morning medicines. The Wegovy pill's wait applies to other oral medicines too, which matters if you take thyroid medication, blood-pressure tablets or anything else on waking. Foundayo has no such rule.
  • The molecule. The Wegovy pill is a peptide, the same semaglutide as the injection, formulated to survive the stomach. Foundayo is a small molecule, orforglipron, which is why it needs no absorption rules.
  • The dose ladder. 1.5 mg to 25 mg for the Wegovy pill; 0.8 mg to 17.2 mg for Foundayo. Both are stepped up by a clinician.
  • The evidence base. OASIS 4 enrolled 307 people for 64 weeks; ATTAIN-1 enrolled 3,127 for 72 weeks. Foundayo's trial is larger; the Wegovy pill's result is higher. Neither is head to head.
  • Where you can get it. The Wegovy pill through ro is the telehealth route we have verified; Foundayo through LillyDirect at Lilly's published self-pay tiers, with telehealth availability stated by Lilly but no provider price we could verify yet.
Everything else, including the side-effect profile and the warnings, is shared.

sections.heading: Are there real patient reviews of Foundayo and the Wegovy pill yet?
sections.body: Not in any form we can verify, and we do not quote what we cannot verify. Customer review sites rate providers, not medicines: a review of a telehealth service such as ro, which sells the Wegovy pill, says nothing about the pill itself. Forum and social posts about both pills exist, but they are unverified, often from people a few weeks in, and frequently about the injections. Until a verified review record exists, the trial reports above, which recorded the experience of 3,434 people over 15 to 17 months, are the best patient evidence there is; they are also the source of the side-effect rates in the section below. We will add a verified review record here when one exists.

sections.heading: Can you switch from a weekly injection to one of the pills?
sections.body: Yes, under a prescriber, and there is now trial evidence for one direction. Lilly's ATTAIN-MAINTAIN trial (topline results announced December 18, 2025; full publication pending) took people who had lost weight on Wegovy or Zepbound injections and switched them to daily orforglipron, the molecule in Foundayo, or to placebo for a year. Those switched from Wegovy held their weight almost exactly; those switched from Zepbound regained about 5 kg of a much larger loss; the placebo groups had regained roughly 9 kg within six months. These are company-reported figures. There is no equivalent published switch trial for the Wegovy pill, although moving from the semaglutide injection to the semaglutide pill keeps the same molecule. Either switch is a prescriber's decision, usually with a new titration. Our guide to stopping GLP-1s and keeping the weight off covers the maintenance evidence in full.

sections.heading: Is the Wegovy pill the same as Rybelsus, and is Foundayo a version of Wegovy?
sections.body: The Wegovy pill and Rybelsus are both oral semaglutide from Novo Nordisk, but they are not interchangeable: Rybelsus is approved for type 2 diabetes at 3 mg, 7 mg and 14 mg, while the Wegovy pill is approved for weight management at 25 mg. Foundayo is not a version of Wegovy at all; it is a different molecule, orforglipron, from a different company, Eli Lilly, that acts on the same GLP-1 receptor. The only things the two pills share are the receptor and the once-daily tablet form.

sections.heading: Which should you choose, Foundayo or the Wegovy pill?
sections.body: Work down the list. Your insurance covers one and not the other: take the covered one; at $25 a month the difference between them is a rounding error. You are on Medicare: both are in the Bridge at $50, so choose on routine and results, not price. You want the larger trial result: the Wegovy pill, on the published figures, with the caveat that the trials are not directly comparable. You cannot or will not keep an empty-stomach, 30-minute-wait routine every morning: Foundayo, which has no timing rules at all. You are paying cash and want a verified telehealth route today: the Wegovy pill through ro is the route we have checked; for Foundayo, LillyDirect's published self-pay price is the reference. You are needle-averse but price-led: read what $100-$200 a month gets you first, because the compounded injections at $41-$199 sit well below either pill at cash prices. Whatever you pick, the prescriber decides on your history, not on a table.

sections.heading: The bottom line
sections.body: Foundayo and the Wegovy pill are the two FDA-approved GLP-1 pills for weight management, and they split cleanly: the Wegovy pill has the larger published trial result (13.6% vs 11.1%, different trials) and Foundayo has the simpler routine (no food or water timing). On price they overlap - $149 at the starting dose from either manufacturer as reported, $25 with commercial coverage, $50 on Medicare's pilot - with Foundayo's reported top-dose price $50 higher. ro's $149-then-$299-plus-membership is the one telehealth price here we have verified. Both are prescription medicines; a licensed clinician decides whether either is appropriate for you. This article is general information, not medical advice.

sections.heading: What starting on embody tirzepatide looks like

The short answerYes. ro is one of the longest-established telehealth companies in the US, its weight-loss program runs through licensed providers who review a medical intake and can decline you, and medication ships from ro's own in-house pharmacy. What "legit" does not settle is whether its pricing model suits you: ro bills a membership and the medication separately, and that bill is the thing to understand before you sign up.

This audit uses the same three tests we apply to every provider in our GLP-1 provider guide: is there a real clinical gate, do the published prices survive contact with the checkout, and what do patients report when you read the critical posts first.

sections.heading: How ro's weight-loss process actually works
sections.body:
You complete an online medical assessment. A qualified provider reviews it and decides whether treatment is appropriate. If prescribed, medication is dispensed by ro's integrated pharmacy and delivered to your home, with dose adjustments handled by the provider over time.

Two things make ro structurally different from the compounded-first providers in our ranking. First, ro's published weight-loss pricing centers on brand-name medication - the Wegovy pill and pen and the Zepbound KwikPen - rather than a flat compounded plan. Second, insurance can apply to the medication. If your plan covers a GLP-1, ro's route can cost far less than any cash price on this site; if it does not, you pay ro's cash rates plus the membership.

Results and service draw little criticism; the membership-plus-medication cost is the thing people leave over. Single posts are anecdotes; we quote them because the same theme repeats.

sections.heading: What 'GLP-1 weight loss online' actually means in 2026
sections.body:
The short answerThere are three legal ways to get a GLP-1 online in 2026, each needing a prescription from a licensed clinician: brand-name pens or pills through a prescriber, compounded semaglutide or tirzepatide from a state-licensed 503A pharmacy through a telehealth provider, or brand-name through your own insurance with a telehealth prescriber. Verified cash prices run from $41 a month for compounded semaglutide and $71 for tirzepatide, checked October 28, 2026, while brand-name pens bought online start around $1,249. In the pivotal trials semaglutide 2.4 mg produced 14.9% mean weight loss at 68 weeks and tirzepatide up to 20.9% at 72 weeks, and most of it returns within a year of stopping.

Five years ago, getting a GLP-1 medication for weight loss meant an endocrinologist, an insurance fight and a pharmacy that might or might not have it in stock. In 2026 the same prescription can be written after an online intake, filled by a mail-order pharmacy and delivered in a cold pack to your door, at a cash price that in some cases is lower than a copay. That convenience created an industry - and a lot of confusion about what, exactly, you are buying.

This guide is the long version. It is written for someone who has decided they want to find out whether a GLP-1 is right for them and wants to understand the whole path before spending money: how the drugs work, which molecule to consider, what is legal, who qualifies, what it costs at every provider we have verified, how the process runs from intake to first injection, how to pick a provider, what the first twelve weeks feel like, what results the trials actually showed, and where the traps are. Each section stands alone, so skip to what you need; the shorter guides linked throughout go deeper on single questions.

The three routes, in one paragraph each

Route one: brand-name through a telehealth prescriber. Wegovy (semaglutide) and Zepbound (tirzepatide) are the FDA-approved injectable pens for chronic weight management. The Wegovy pill (oral semaglutide 25 mg) and Foundayo (orforglipron) joined them as approved daily tablets. A telehealth provider such as ro can prescribe them, bill your insurance where it applies, or sell them cash. This is the only route where the product itself has been through FDA review.

Route two: compounded semaglutide or tirzepatide through a telehealth provider. A state-licensed compounding pharmacy prepares the same active ingredient under a clinician's patient-specific prescription. It is not an FDA-approved product, which is the trade-off behind prices that start at $49 a month instead of four figures. Most of the providers on this site - embody, welludr, altRx, Eden, Medvi, TrimRx, DirectMeds and others - work this way.

Route three: brand-name through your own insurance. If your plan covers Wegovy or Zepbound for weight loss, a telehealth prescriber can run the prior authorization and send the prescription to a retail or mail pharmacy like any other. Coverage applies to the medication, not to how you saw the clinician. Our insurance guide covers what plans typically require.

What all three have in common: a licensed clinician reviews your health history and decides whether to prescribe. There is no legal route to a GLP-1 without that step, and any website offering one without it is selling something you should not inject.

How to read the prices in this guide

Every provider price quoted here was checked on the provider's own site on October 16, 2026 and is carried with the condition that goes with it - a 12-month plan, a first-month promotion, a flat rate at every dose. Prices change; the providers' pages are the only live source, and our price-change log records every change we have caught since we started tracking. Manufacturer and third-party figures are cited with their date and are not verified by us. Where we could not verify something, we say so rather than estimate.

sections.heading: How GLP-1 medications work, and what the trials showed
sections.body:
GLP-1 stands for glucagon-like peptide-1, a hormone your gut releases within minutes of eating. It tells the pancreas to release insulin, slows the rate at which your stomach empties, and signals the brain that food has arrived. Natural GLP-1 breaks down within a couple of minutes. The medications are engineered versions of the hormone that resist that breakdown, so a once-weekly injection keeps the "you have eaten" signal switched on for days. The result most people notice first is not willpower but the absence of the usual hunger: smaller portions feel like enough, and the mental noise around food goes quiet. The physiology is covered in plain language in our guide to how GLP-1 medications work.

Semaglutide and tirzepatide are not the same drug

Semaglutide acts on the GLP-1 receptor only. Tirzepatide acts on two receptors - GLP-1 and GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide) - which is why it is sometimes described as a "dual agonist" and why, in its trials, it produced larger average weight loss. Both are given as a once-weekly injection under the skin, and both are started at a low dose and stepped up over months to limit stomach side effects.

The numbers from the pivotal trials

These are the two studies every serious claim about these drugs traces back to. Both were randomized, double-blind and placebo-controlled in adults with obesity (or overweight with a weight-related condition) without diabetes, on top of lifestyle advice.

TrialDrug and doseLengthMean weight changePlacebo
STEP 1 (NEJM, March 18, 2021)Semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly68 weeks-14.9%-2.4%
SURMOUNT-1 (NEJM, July 21, 2022)Tirzepatide 5 mg weekly72 weeks-15.0%-3.1%
SURMOUNT-1Tirzepatide 10 mg weekly72 weeks-19.5%-3.1%
SURMOUNT-1Tirzepatide 15 mg weekly72 weeks-20.9%-3.1%

Sources: Wilding et al., Once-Weekly Semaglutide in Adults with Overweight or Obesity, New England Journal of Medicine, March 18, 2021; Jastreboff et al., Tirzepatide Once Weekly for the Treatment of Obesity, New England Journal of Medicine, July 21, 2022. The SURMOUNT-1 figures above are the treatment-regimen estimand; the paper's efficacy estimand, which assumes everyone stayed on treatment, reports up to 22.5% at 15 mg, the figure most marketing quotes.

Three things those numbers do not say. First, they are averages: in STEP 1 about a third of participants lost 20% or more and some lost very little, and nothing in an intake form predicts which group you will be in. Second, they were measured at the full maintenance dose after a long titration, so they describe month fifteen, not month two. Third, they include the lifestyle counseling everyone in the trial received, which is more than most telehealth programs provide. Treat the trial figures as a ceiling that a well-run, fully-dosed course can approach, not a promise for a $49 plan.

What happens when you stop

The least-advertised result is the one that should shape how you budget. In the STEP 1 extension, participants who stopped semaglutide and the lifestyle program regained about two-thirds of the weight they had lost within a year (Wilding et al., Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, published April 19, 2022). These are maintenance medications in the way blood-pressure medication is: they work while you take them. Our guide to what happens when you stop covers tapering and maintenance strategies clinicians use.

Why the pills matter now

Until late 2025 "GLP-1 for weight loss" meant an injection. The Wegovy pill - oral semaglutide at 25 mg - was FDA-approved in December 2025 as the first oral GLP-1 for chronic weight management, and Foundayo (orforglipron, Eli Lilly) followed on April 1, 2026. Both are brand-name, prescription-only and priced like brand-name products, but they remove the needle, which for many people was the reason not to start. The difference in routine is practical: the Wegovy pill is taken on an empty stomach with a sip of water and a 30-minute wait before eating, while Foundayo has no food or water restriction. Our Foundayo vs Wegovy pill comparison sets out the trial results and prices side by side, and GLP-1 pills vs injections explains why the compounded "pills" and "drops" sold by some programs are a different category entirely.

sections.heading: Semaglutide or tirzepatide: how to choose the molecule
sections.body:
The first fork in the road is the molecule, because it changes the price by roughly $40 to $100 a month at the same provider and changes what the evidence says you can expect. There is no universal right answer. Here is how the two compare on the things that decide it.

FactorSemaglutideTirzepatide
Brand namesOzempic (diabetes), Wegovy (weight), Wegovy pillMounjaro (diabetes), Zepbound (weight)
ReceptorsGLP-1GLP-1 and GIP
Pivotal-trial weight loss-14.9% at 68 weeks (STEP 1)-15.0% to -20.9% by dose at 72 weeks (SURMOUNT-1)
Verified compounded price range$41-$199/month$71-$299/month
Cheapest verified compounded price$41/month, welludr, 12-month plan$71/month, welludr, 12-month plan
Cheapest no-commitment price$49/month, embody$99/month, embody
Oral optionWegovy pill (approved December 2025)None; Foundayo is a different molecule
Years on the US marketSince 2017 (Ozempic), 2021 (Wegovy)Since 2022 (Mounjaro), 2023 (Zepbound)

When semaglutide is the sensible first choice

It is cheaper everywhere we track by a margin that adds up to $480 to $1,200 over a year. It has the longer safety record, with more years of real-world use. The trial result - about 15% mean weight loss - is a large number by any historical standard; for a 220-pound person it is 33 pounds. And it has an oral form if injections are the obstacle. For a first course where you do not yet know how your body responds, starting on the lower-cost molecule and switching only if you plateau is the sequence most clinicians describe.

When tirzepatide earns its price

The trial gap is real: at the top dose, tirzepatide's average loss was about six percentage points greater than semaglutide's in its own trial, and the proportion of participants reaching 20% or more was substantially higher. If your goal is large (say, 60 pounds or more), if you have already been on semaglutide and stalled, or if a clinician judges that the dual mechanism suits your metabolic picture, the extra cost buys a measurably larger expected result. Our tirzepatide vs semaglutide guide walks through the head-to-head evidence, and best tirzepatide online lists every verified tirzepatide price.

Side effects are similar, not identical

Both labels list the same leading adverse events - nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, constipation, abdominal pain, reduced appetite - clustered around dose increases. Both carry the same boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumors observed in rodents, and both are contraindicated for people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2. Tirzepatide's label adds a specific note that it can reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives for four weeks after starting and after each dose increase. There is no reliable way to predict which molecule you will tolerate better; if one causes persistent side effects a clinician may slow the titration or switch you. The labels are summarized on MedlinePlus for semaglutide and tirzepatide.

The honest answer to "which is better"

Tirzepatide produced more weight loss in trials. Semaglutide costs less, has been used longer and comes as a pill. Which is "better" depends on the size of your goal, your budget over a year rather than a month, and how you respond - which nobody can know in advance. What we can say with confidence is that either, taken as prescribed at a maintenance dose for a year, has produced results in controlled trials that no previous weight-loss medication came close to.

sections.heading: Brand-name, compounded, or pills: what is legal and what you are actually buying
sections.body:
This is the section to read twice, because it is where most of the money and most of the risk sits. "GLP-1 online" covers four different products that are sold with similar language and very different legal standing.

Brand-name pens and pills: FDA-approved, priced accordingly

Wegovy was approved for chronic weight management on June 4, 2021 (FDA press announcement) and Zepbound on November 8, 2023 (FDA press announcement). Each dose is a factory-made, sealed pen whose contents were tested in the trials above and whose manufacturing is inspected by the FDA. The Wegovy pill and Foundayo carry the same status. The cash prices online reflect that: on the providers we have verified, brand-name Zepbound is $1,249 a month at altRx and $1,599 at welludr; Ozempic is $1,399 at welludr; ro sells Zepbound KwikPens from $299 the first month then $399-$449, and the Wegovy pill at $149 the first month then $299, in each case plus its membership. Our Zepbound price guide and Wegovy pill price guide keep these current and explain the manufacturers' own direct-pay programs, whose prices we report from dated third-party sources but have not verified ourselves.

Compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide: legal under conditions, not FDA-approved

Compounding is the practice of a licensed pharmacist preparing a medication for an individual patient under a prescription. US federal law allows it under two frameworks, both described on the FDA's human drug compounding page. Section 503A covers state-licensed pharmacies compounding for a specific patient on a specific prescription; this is the route almost every telehealth GLP-1 program uses, which is why "503A pharmacy" appears so often on provider sites. Section 503B covers registered outsourcing facilities that can produce larger batches under tighter federal oversight.

The reason compounded GLP-1s exploded in 2023 and 2024 is that both semaglutide and tirzepatide were on the FDA's drug shortage list, and the law allows compounding of a drug in shortage with fewer restrictions. That window has closed. The FDA declared the tirzepatide shortage resolved on December 19, 2024, and the semaglutide shortage resolved on February 21, 2025, with enforcement grace periods that ended in the spring of 2025 (FDA statement on compounder policies). What remains legal is what was always legal: a 503A pharmacy may compound for an individual patient when a prescriber documents a clinical need that the approved product does not meet - a different dose, a different formulation, an added ingredient, an inability to tolerate an excipient. Mass-producing copies of the approved drug is not permitted. Enforcement is ongoing and the rules continue to evolve; the practical consequence for you is that the prescription should be patient-specific and the pharmacy should be named.

The FDA's own summary of the risks is worth reading in full: FDA's Concerns with Unapproved GLP-1 Drugs Used for Weight Loss. The agency's points, in short: compounded products are not reviewed for safety, effectiveness or quality before they are sold; it has received reports of adverse events including dosing errors from vials that require the patient to measure a dose; some products have been found to contain salt forms of semaglutide (semaglutide sodium, semaglutide acetate) that are not the active ingredient in the approved drugs; and products sold without a prescription or from unlicensed sources may be counterfeit.

None of that means compounded GLP-1 is a scam. It means the quality lives in the pharmacy, not in a brand, and that you are trusting the telehealth provider's choice of pharmacy. The providers on this site name theirs, and that is the first thing we check. Our guide to compounded vs brand-name semaglutide and the 503A vs 503B explainer go deeper, including the "28-day rule" on beyond-use dating that determines how much medication a pharmacy can ship at once.

Compounded "pills," "drops" and "gum": a different thing again

Some programs sell compounded oral semaglutide as tablets, sublingual drops or troches. These are not the FDA-approved Wegovy pill, which is a specific formulation designed to survive the stomach; they are compounded preparations with no trial data of their own, and oral absorption of a peptide is poor without the formulation work the approved pill went through. If you want a pill, the two approved options exist. If a program's "pill" is compounded, understand that you are buying an unstudied product, not a cheaper Wegovy pill. Our weight-loss pills guide separates the categories.

The one-sentence test

If a product is described as "FDA-approved" and it is compounded, the description is false - the FDA said so in a June 2026 warning letter to altRx's parent company over marketing that suggested approval, as we note in our altRx review. If a product requires no prescription, it is not a legal GLP-1 in the United States. Everything else is a question of price, pharmacy and terms, which the rest of this guide is about.

sections.heading: Do you qualify? Eligibility, disqualifiers and what the intake asks
sections.body:
The online intake is not a formality. A licensed clinician - a physician, nurse practitioner or physician assistant, depending on the provider and your state - reviews it and can decline. Knowing the criteria in advance saves you a declined application and, at providers without a refund-if-declined policy, the fee.

The label criteria

Wegovy and Zepbound are indicated for adults with a body mass index of 30 or more, or 27 or more with at least one weight-related condition such as type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol or obstructive sleep apnea. Telehealth providers prescribing compounded versions generally apply the same thresholds. BMI is weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared; at 5'6" the 27 threshold is about 167 pounds and the 30 threshold about 186 pounds. Our guide to who qualifies has a full table by height.

Disqualifiers every provider screens for

  • A personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma, or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (the boxed warning on both labels).
  • A history of pancreatitis.
  • Severe gastrointestinal disease, including gastroparesis, since the drugs slow stomach emptying.
  • Pregnancy, planning a pregnancy, or breastfeeding. The labels advise stopping at least two months before a planned pregnancy.
  • Type 1 diabetes, and insulin or sulfonylurea use without diabetes supervision, because of hypoglycemia risk.
  • Current or recent eating disorder, at most providers.
  • Age under 18 for the compounded programs (Wegovy itself is approved from age 12 under specialist care).

Interactions and conditions to declare

Because GLP-1s slow stomach emptying, they can change how quickly oral medications are absorbed; the clinician needs your full medication list, including thyroid hormone, anticoagulants and oral contraceptives (the tirzepatide label specifically advises a backup method for four weeks after starting and after each increase). Kidney disease, diabetic retinopathy, gallbladder disease and a history of depression or suicidal thoughts are not automatic disqualifiers but will be asked about and may change the recommendation. Honesty here protects you: the same answers that might get you declined are the ones that would make the medication dangerous.

What the intake looks like in practice

Expect 10 to 25 minutes of questions: height, weight and sometimes a photo for BMI verification; medical history; medications; weight-loss history; goals; and at some providers a short video or phone consultation. Many providers ask for recent lab work and will order it if you have none; some accept an attestation. A government ID is required, because the prescription is written in your name. Then the clinician reviews - typically within one to three days, at embody usually within 24 hours - and either prescribes, asks follow-up questions, or declines. If you do not qualify for a GLP-1, several providers offer alternatives such as metformin or bupropion-naltrexone; our alternatives guide covers them.

If you are declined

Check the refund terms before you apply, not after. embody refunds the unused portion, less services rendered, if a clinician does not approve you. Others vary, and some charge a consultation fee that is not refundable. The terms are on each provider's review page under pricing.

The cheapest GLP-1 page keeps this table live and the provider comparison adds refund terms.

The price you keep paying

Four pricing mechanics decide what month four costs, and the headline price hides all of them.

  • Promotional rates. altRx's $89 is a promotion against a regular $199, and Medvi's $99 is a starting price with no regular price listed in our index; SHED takes 20% off the first month only. A promotion that lasts three months on a $199 plan means year one costs about $2,100, not $1,068.
  • Commitment plans. welludr's $41 and $71 require a 12-month plan (billed monthly, not prepaid); HealthRx's longer plans cost less per month than its $125 and $199 monthly plan, but it does not show the tiers, and Sprout's $99 and $149 come on a 12-month plan billed upfront ($1,188 and $1,788). The discount is real - welludr's committed rate is roughly half a month-to-month equivalent - and so is the exposure if you stop early.
  • Dose-tied pricing. Some programs elsewhere charge more at higher doses. Every provider in the table above publishes one price per medication at every dose, which is one reason they are in the table; always confirm on the plan page.
  • Separate fees. ro bills membership and medication separately; some providers bill an initial consultation; labs may be extra. Add every line.

Year one, worked

Twelve months of compounded semaglutide, medication and program only, at verified rates: welludr's 12-month plan is 12 times $41, or $492. embody month to month is 12 times $49, or $588. altRx at the promo rate for the whole year would be $1,068, and at the regular rate $2,388 - the gap between those two numbers is the question to ask altRx before you start. DirectMeds' $249 sublingual semaglutide is $2,988. SHED is roughly $2,348. Tirzepatide adds between $480 (welludr) and $1,200 (SHED) to each of those. Our guide to what you will really pay, month one to year one works every provider through, and before you prepay is the checklist for the commitment plans.

Brand-name cash and insurance

Cash brand-name through the providers we verify runs from $1,249 a month (Zepbound at altRx) upward, with ro's pen prices lower because its pricing assumes a membership and, often, insurance. With commercial insurance that covers Wegovy or Zepbound, the manufacturers' savings offers are reported to bring the copay down sharply, and Medicare's GLP-1 Bridge pilot is reported to charge a flat $50 a month through December 2027 - both figures from dated third-party sources we have not verified, and both detailed in GLP-1 with insurance and GLP-1 after 65. Insurance rarely covers compounded medication at all; the compounded prices above are cash prices by design. HSA and FSA funds generally can be used; Medvi and SHED state HSA/FSA eligibility explicitly.

What $100 to $200 a month buys

At the low end you get the medication, the clinician review and shipping, with messaging support and dose adjustments through a portal. As the price rises you add things like unlimited check-ins (TrimRx), a dietitian and coaching built into the price (Medvi), a money-back results guarantee (SHED's 5%-in-120-days), overnight delivery (HealthRx) or a brand-name shelf alongside compounded (altRx, Sprout, welludr). Whether those are worth it depends on whether you would use them; the medication itself is the same molecule from a licensed pharmacy at $41 and at $199. Our guide to what $100 to $200 a month gets you itemizes it.

sections.heading: The process, step by step: from intake to your first injection
sections.body:
Here is the whole path in order, with the timing we have verified at the providers we track. The sequence is the same everywhere; the days vary.

Day 0: choose a provider and complete the intake

Fifteen to twenty-five minutes online. Height, weight, photo, medical history, medications, goals, ID. Some providers charge at this point; some charge on approval. Check which - it decides whether a decline costs you money.

Days 1-3: clinician review

A licensed clinician reviews your intake, sometimes with a short video or phone consultation, and sometimes with a request for labs. embody's review is usually within 24 hours; most others quote one to three days. The clinician decides the molecule, the starting dose and the titration plan, and sends a patient-specific prescription to the pharmacy. If something in your history needs clarifying, you will get a message, and answering quickly keeps the clock moving.

Days 2-8: pharmacy fills and ships

The compounding pharmacy prepares your prescription and ships it in an insulated cold pack with ice. Verified delivery windows: DirectMeds ships in 1-2 days; embody publishes free expedited delivery with no timeline guaranteed; TrimRx offers free tracked delivery that is often next-day; HealthRx ships overnight cold-chain; Sprout ships within 2 days of the prescription; welludr quotes 3-5 business days; altRx 5-7 days. Our provider comparison sets each provider's published shipping promise side by side.

Delivery day: check the package

Refrigerate the medication on arrival. Check that the vial or pen is labeled with your name, the drug, the strength, the pharmacy's name and a beyond-use date. A compounded product that arrives unlabeled or without a pharmacy name is a reason to stop and contact the provider. Most compounded semaglutide arrives as a multi-dose vial with syringes; you draw the prescribed units yourself, which is where the FDA's dosing-error reports come from, so read the instructions twice and use the provider's video or nurse line for the first dose.

First injection

Once weekly, same day each week, under the skin of the abdomen, thigh or upper arm, rotating sites. The needle is short and fine; most people describe it as less than a flu shot. Inject at a time when you can eat lightly afterward, because the first dose is when nausea is most likely. Keep a simple log: date, dose, how you felt. It makes the check-ins useful.

Weeks 1-4 and onward: check-ins and dose steps

Your clinician will schedule check-ins - messaging at most providers, unlimited at TrimRx, video at Medvi - and step the dose up roughly every four weeks if you are tolerating it. Refills ship on the plan cadence; welludr ships every 4 weeks. Price does not change with dose at any provider in our table. If side effects are more than mild, message before the next dose rather than pushing through; holding at a dose for an extra month is routine. Our first-month guide and side-effects guide cover what is normal and what is not.

Realistic calendar

From clicking "start" to a first injection, expect four to ten days at the fast providers and one to two weeks elsewhere. From first injection to your maintenance dose, expect four to five months. From first injection to the trial-level result, a year or more. Anyone promising a faster timeline is selling the ad, not the medicine.

sections.heading: How to choose a provider: the twelve checks we run
sections.body:
We rank providers on this site, but the ranking is our judgment on our criteria, and your priorities may differ. These are the checks behind the ranking, in the order they matter, so you can run them yourself on any provider - including ones we do not list. The full method is on our how to choose a GLP-1 provider page.

  1. Is the pharmacy named, and is it state-licensed? A provider that will not say which pharmacy compounds its medication is asking you to trust an anonymous manufacturer. Look for a named 503A pharmacy (or 503B facility) and check its license on the state board of pharmacy site.
  2. Does a licensed US clinician review your intake and write a patient-specific prescription? The provider should say who prescribes (physician, NP, PA) and in which states it operates. "Doctor-approved" is marketing; "a licensed provider in your state will review your intake" is the standard.
  3. Is the medication described honestly? If the word "FDA-approved" appears next to a compounded product, walk away. If "semaglutide" is sold as a "pill" or "drops," understand it is compounded and unstudied.
  4. What is the price at your maintenance dose, after any promotion? Find the regular rate and the promo length on the plan page, not the ad.
  5. What are you committing to? Month to month, a 12-month plan billed monthly, or a prepaid year are three different financial exposures. Prepaying is only sensible once you know you tolerate the medication.
  6. What happens if a clinician declines you, or you stop early? Read the refund and cancellation terms. embody's partial refund if not approved (unused portion less services rendered) is the clearest we have found.
  7. What is included? Clinician visits, messaging, dose adjustments, shipping, labs, supplies - included or billed separately?
  8. How is it shipped and how fast? Cold-chain packaging is non-negotiable for an injectable peptide. Published delivery windows range from next-day to a week.
  9. What do customers say, and what do they complain about? Read the newest community posts rather than a headline number, look at what people complain about, and look at whether and how the company responds. Our provider comparison covers how to reach each provider.
  10. Is the company real? A physical address, a phone number, named leadership, and a LegitScript certification (embody carries one) are all signals that someone is accountable.
  11. Does the program fit how you want to be cared for? Some people want a pharmacy with a portal and nothing else; some want a dietitian and weekly calls. Paying for coaching you will not use is the most common way to overspend.
  12. Does the plan let you change? Switching molecule, pausing for travel or illness, adjusting dose - the terms should allow it without penalty.

What we deliberately do not score

Weight-loss results. A provider cannot make the medication work better; the molecule and the dose do that, and response varies by person. Any provider advertising its customers' average results is advertising a self-selected sample. We also do not score "doctor quality," because we cannot verify it; we score whether a licensed clinician is in the loop and reachable.

Our ranking, and why it is not the whole answer

Our ranking of weight-loss providers puts embody first for the combination of the lowest no-commitment price, free expedited delivery, a LegitScript certification and a partial refund if declined (unused portion less services rendered), with altRx and Eden behind it and welludr fourth on the strength of the lowest committed price. Reasonable people could order those differently. If your single priority is the lowest monthly cost and you are confident you will stay a year, welludr's $41 is the answer. If you want to try one month and walk away, embody's $49 is. If you want brand-name alongside compounded and a flat price with Buy Now, Pay Later, altRx is. Our matching quiz turns those priorities into a recommendation in a minute.
