sections.heading: Dosing and the first twelve weeks: what to expect, week by week
sections.body:
Both drugs are started low and raised in steps so your stomach can adapt. The schedules below are the approved labels for Wegovy and Zepbound; compounded programs follow the same logic, usually with the same milligram steps for tirzepatide and the same or finer steps for semaglutide, because vials let a clinician prescribe in-between doses.

Semaglutide (Wegovy label)

WeeksWeekly dose
1-40.25 mg
5-80.5 mg
9-121 mg
13-161.7 mg
17 onward2.4 mg (maintenance)

Tirzepatide (Zepbound label)

WeeksWeekly dose
1-42.5 mg
5-85 mg
Every 4 weeks after+2.5 mg steps to 7.5, 10, 12.5 mg
Maintenance5, 10 or 15 mg, as tolerated

The step-ups are "if tolerated." Holding at a dose for an extra month because of nausea is normal and does not mean the medication is failing. Clinicians also stop short of the top dose when a lower one is working; the labels allow 1.7 mg semaglutide and 5 or 10 mg tirzepatide as maintenance.

Weeks 1-2: the starting dose

Appetite usually drops within days; many people describe forgetting to eat lunch. Mild nausea, feeling full quickly, burping or reflux are common, especially one to three days after the injection. Some fatigue. Weight change in these weeks is mostly water and smaller portions, and the scale can move two to five pounds or not at all.

Weeks 3-8: first increases

Each step-up brings a few days where the side effects return before settling. Constipation becomes more common than nausea for many people; fiber, water and movement handle most of it. Food aversions can appear - fatty, fried and very sweet foods are the usual culprits, and eating them anyway is the usual cause of the worst nausea. The weight loss becomes consistent, typically one to two pounds a week.

Weeks 9-12: the middle doses

Most people are now losing at a steady rate and have learned which foods and portion sizes keep the side effects quiet. Protein becomes important because appetite suppression makes it easy to under-eat it, and muscle loss is the cost of losing weight too fast without it. Our guide to what to eat on GLP-1 medication is built around that. Injection-site reactions, hair shedding in the months after rapid loss, and "Ozempic face" - the gaunt look from losing facial fat quickly - are the second-tier effects people ask about; the latter two are consequences of fast weight loss, not of the drug specifically, and are covered in Ozempic and hair loss and Ozempic face.

What to do about side effects

  • Eat smaller meals, slowly, and stop at the first signal of fullness; the signal arrives earlier now.
  • Avoid high-fat and fried food on injection day and the day after.
  • Stay hydrated; constipation and headaches are usually fluid.
  • Inject in the evening if nausea is worst in the hours after the dose, so you sleep through it.
  • Tell your clinician before the next dose if you are vomiting, cannot keep fluids down, or have side effects that last more than a few days; the right response is usually to hold the dose, not push through.

When to seek care immediately

Severe, persistent abdominal pain, with or without vomiting, that may radiate to the back can be pancreatitis; severe pain in the upper right abdomen, fever or yellowing skin can be gallbladder disease; a lump or swelling in the neck, trouble swallowing or persistent hoarseness are the thyroid symptoms the boxed warning describes; sudden vision changes in someone with diabetes need an eye exam. These are rare, and they are why a licensed clinician is in the loop. Our side-effects guide and first month on weight-loss medication cover them in depth.

sections.heading: Results: what the timeline looks like, and when to switch, hold or stop
sections.body:
The trial curves have a shape worth knowing before you start, because it tells you when to be patient and when to ask questions.

Months 1-2

Modest loss on the starting doses - the trials show a few percent of body weight by week eight. This is the window where people quit because "it isn't working." It is working; the dose is low by design.

Months 3-6

The steepest part of the curve. By the time the dose reaches the middle of the schedule, loss of one to two pounds a week is typical, and by six months the STEP 1 curve is past 10% of starting weight. Our guide to how long semaglutide takes to work maps the curve month by month.

Months 6-12

Continued loss at a slower rate as the maintenance dose takes hold. In STEP 1, the 68-week average of 14.9% was reached with most of the loss done by about month twelve; in SURMOUNT-1 the curves were still falling at 72 weeks at the higher doses.

Plateaus

Everyone plateaus. The honest options when you do, in order: confirm you are actually at a maintenance dose and have been for at least eight weeks; review protein, sleep and alcohol, which blunt results more than anything else; ask about a dose increase if you are below the top dose; and only then consider switching molecule. Weight-loss plateau: what to do walks through each.

Switching

Switching from semaglutide to tirzepatide after a plateau is common and clinically routine; the clinician restarts tirzepatide at a low dose rather than at an equivalent one. Switching providers is simpler than it sounds: a new provider runs its own intake and writes a new prescription, and most will continue the dose you are on if you can document it. Our switching guide has the sequence, and the head-to-head pages - embody vs welludr, welludr vs embody vs TrimRx - compare the terms that matter when you move.

Maintenance and stopping

The extension data above are the clearest statement we can make: when the medication stops, appetite returns and most of the weight follows within a year. Maintenance strategies clinicians use include staying on the maintenance dose indefinitely, stepping down to the lowest effective dose, or spacing injections out, all under supervision; what the evidence does not support is a short course as a reset. Budget for the long run, which is why the year-one math and the commitment terms above matter more than the first-month price.

What results you should not expect

Anyone's "I lost 50 pounds in 3 months" is one person's story at one dose with one starting weight. The trial averages are the only numbers that describe what a population of people like you experienced, and they describe a year, not a season. A provider's job is to prescribe and support safely; a provider cannot make you a faster responder, and one that implies it can is marketing. Our statistics page collects the trial results and the dated price index in one place.

sections.heading: Safety online: red flags, counterfeits and how to protect yourself
sections.body:
The legitimate market described in this guide sits next to an illegitimate one that uses the same words. The FDA's concern page cited above describes products sold without prescriptions, products containing the wrong form of the molecule, and dosing errors from unlabeled vials. These are the signs that separate the two.

Walk away if

  • No prescription is required, or the "consultation" is a checkbox.
  • The site will not name the pharmacy, or the pharmacy is outside the United States.
  • A compounded product is described as FDA-approved.
  • The medication is sold as "research chemicals," "for research use only," or in pre-filled pens of unknown origin.
  • Payment is by cryptocurrency, wire transfer or gift card only.
  • The price is dramatically below the verified range in this guide - below about $49 a month for semaglutide, there is no legitimate margin left.
  • There is no physical address, no phone number and no named company.

Verify, in five minutes

  • Look up the pharmacy on its state board of pharmacy license lookup.
  • Check the telehealth company on LegitScript's certification lookup; embody is certified, and certification is a meaningful signal.
  • Find the refund policy and the cancellation policy on the site itself, not in a review.
  • Confirm the molecule: "semaglutide" or "tirzepatide" base, not "semaglutide sodium" or "semaglutide acetate," which the FDA has flagged as not the approved active ingredient.

Handling and storage

Refrigerate at 36-46°F (2-8°C). Compounded vials carry a beyond-use date, typically 28 days once in use and sometimes from the date of compounding; the 28-day rule explainer covers why. Do not freeze. Use a new needle each time, never share, and dispose of sharps in a container, not the trash. If a vial looks cloudy or discolored, do not use it.

Interactions and alcohol

Tell every clinician you see that you are on a GLP-1 - including before any procedure under sedation, because slowed stomach emptying raises aspiration risk, and anesthesiologists commonly ask you to pause the medication a week before. Alcohol is not contraindicated but hits harder on a near-empty stomach, and many people lose the taste for it. Our guide to GLP-1 and mental health covers mood effects, which the labels ask prescribers to monitor.

Telehealth across state lines

A provider can only prescribe in states where its clinicians are licensed, and most list the states they serve. If you move, tell the provider; the prescription may need to be rewritten by a clinician licensed in your new state.

sections.heading: Insurance, HSA/FSA and Medicare: the practical version
sections.body:
Three sentences cover most situations, then the detail. Insurance sometimes covers brand-name Wegovy or Zepbound for weight loss, almost never covers compounded, and always requires a prescription either way. HSA and FSA funds can generally pay for prescribed treatment, compounded included. Medicare's position has moved in 2026 and depends on the program.

Commercial insurance

Coverage for weight loss is plan-specific: many plans cover GLP-1s for type 2 diabetes and far fewer for weight management alone, and the formulary is the only real answer. Expect prior authorization with BMI thresholds, documented comorbidities and sometimes step therapy. A telehealth prescriber can run that process as well as an in-person one, and ro is built around it. When coverage comes through, the manufacturers' savings offers are reported to bring the monthly copay down to a small fraction of the list price; we report those figures from dated sources and have not verified them. The insurance guide and what to do if you lose coverage are the detailed versions.

HSA and FSA

A prescribed medication is generally an eligible expense, including compounded medication from a licensed pharmacy, and several providers state HSA/FSA eligibility outright (Medvi, SHED). Keep the itemized receipt that shows the prescription. Membership fees and coaching may not be eligible; check with your plan administrator.

Medicare

Medicare Part D has historically excluded drugs used for weight loss. The GLP-1 Bridge pilot is reported to charge a flat $50 a month for the approved medications through December 2027; that figure comes from dated third-party sources, and our GLP-1 after 65 guide explains the eligibility conditions and what to confirm with your plan.

When paying cash is the better deal anyway

With a high deductible, a brand-name pen at four figures a month can cost you more out of pocket before the deductible than a year of compounded semaglutide at $41 to $99 a month. Run both numbers against your deductible and your plan's coinsurance before assuming coverage is the cheaper path; weight-loss medication without insurance works the comparison.

sections.heading: Which route fits you: four readers, four answers
sections.body:
The sections above give you the facts. This one turns them into decisions by walking four common situations through the same questions - molecule, route, provider, budget - using only the verified terms. Find the reader closest to you.

Reader one: "I want the lowest possible monthly cost and I am in this for a year"

Molecule: semaglutide, because the price gap to tirzepatide is $40 a month at the cheapest provider and $100 or more elsewhere. Route: compounded. Provider: welludr at $41 a month on the 12-month plan, billed monthly, the same price at every dose, shipped every four weeks in 3-5 business days. The year costs $492. The two things to accept: a longer shipping window than the fastest providers, and a plan you are committing to for twelve months - read the cancellation terms before you sign, and consider a month at embody first if you have never taken a GLP-1 and do not know how you tolerate it. HealthRx's monthly plan ($125 after a $39 first month, overnight shipping) is another option, at about three times the price for faster delivery.

Reader two: "I want to try it for a month or two with no strings"

Molecule: either; the no-commitment price gap is $50 a month (embody $49 vs $99). Route: compounded. Provider: embody - month to month, cancel anytime, $49 semaglutide or $99 tirzepatide, free expedited cold-chain delivery (no timeline guaranteed), LegitScript-certified, clinician review usually within 24 hours, and a partial refund if you are not approved (unused portion less services rendered). Alternatives with the same no-commitment logic: Eden at $99/$129 flat with 24/7 human support, altRx at $89/$149 on promotion with Buy Now, Pay Later, and DirectMeds at $249 for sublingual semaglutide with 1-2 day shipping. If you stay past month three, revisit reader one's math: embody's year is $588 against welludr's $492.

Reader three: "I want the FDA-approved product, and I may have insurance"

Molecule: whichever your plan covers; many formularies cover one and not the other. Route: brand-name through a prescriber that bills your insurance. Provider: ro, whose membership ($39 the first month, then $74-$149 a month) is separate from the medication so that coverage applies to the pen or pill, and which runs prior authorization. Cash fallback if coverage is denied: ro's Zepbound from $299 the first month then $399-$449, or the Wegovy pill from $149 then $299; or altRx's flat $1,249 Zepbound if you want the compounded shelf alongside. Check the manufacturers' savings offers through your plan before paying cash; the insurance guide lists what to ask.

Reader four: "I will not inject"

Two approved pills exist: the Wegovy pill (oral semaglutide 25 mg, approved December 2025) and Foundayo (orforglipron, approved April 1, 2026). Both are brand-name and priced as such - ro sells the Wegovy pill at $149 the first month then $299 plus membership; Foundayo lists $149 to $349 a month self-pay by dose through LillyDirect, a manufacturer figure we have not verified. The compounded "pills," "drops" and "troches" some programs sell are not these products. If the injection itself is the only barrier, it is also worth knowing that the needle is short and fine, the dose is weekly, and most people who were nervous describe the first one as a non-event; the first-month guide describes it. The Foundayo vs Wegovy pill comparison is the page for this reader.

Readers in between

Want coaching and a dietitian bundled in: Medvi at $99 on promotion, all-inclusive, HSA/FSA accepted. Want a results guarantee: SHED's 5%-in-120-days money-back promise at $199. Want unlimited clinician contact and custom dosing: TrimRx, with plans from $179. Want overnight delivery: HealthRx at $125 after a $39 first month. The matching quiz runs these trade-offs in under a minute.

sections.heading: GLP-1 by situation: women, over 40, over 65, menopause, athletes
sections.body:
The trials enrolled a broad adult population, and the labels do not distinguish by sex or age above 18. But the questions people search are specific, and some situations change the practical advice.

Women

Roughly three-quarters of STEP 1 participants were women, so the headline results describe women more than men. Two label points matter: both drugs should be stopped at least two months before a planned pregnancy, and tirzepatide can reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives for four weeks after starting and after each dose increase, so a backup method is advised in those windows. PCOS is a common reason for weight gain that responds to GLP-1s, and some clinicians prescribe for it specifically; it is a conversation for the intake. Our guide to GLP-1 weight loss for women covers cycle effects, fertility timing and body-composition considerations.

Menopause and perimenopause

Weight gain around menopause has a hormonal driver that diet alone addresses poorly, and GLP-1s are increasingly prescribed alongside or instead of hormone therapy. The trade-off to understand is muscle and bone: rapid weight loss in the years when both are already declining raises the stakes on protein intake and resistance training. Menopause weight gain explains the physiology, and our sister vertical covers hormone therapy providers for readers weighing both.

Over 40

Metabolic rate falls and lean mass is harder to keep, which argues for the same two things - protein and strength work - and for patience with the titration rather than racing to the top dose. Blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar are also more likely to be the "weight-related condition" that qualifies someone with a BMI of 27 to 29. GLP-1 weight loss over 40 is the dedicated guide.

Over 65

The labels have no upper age limit, and older adults were included in the trials. The practical issues are polypharmacy - more medications to check for absorption effects - kidney function, the risk that appetite suppression tips into under-nutrition, and Medicare's rules, which historically excluded weight-loss drugs from Part D and have moved in 2026 through the GLP-1 Bridge pilot described above. GLP-1 after 65 covers all four.

Athletes and people who lift

The concern is lean mass. Any large weight loss includes some muscle; the research on GLP-1s suggests the proportion is similar to diet-induced loss, which means it is manageable with the same tools - a protein target of roughly 1.2 to 1.6 grams per kilogram of goal body weight, progressive resistance training three times a week, and a slower titration if performance is dropping. Reduced appetite makes hitting a protein target genuinely hard, which is why it needs to be planned rather than hoped for. Exercise while on GLP-1 medication has a program.

People with type 2 diabetes

Ozempic and Mounjaro are the diabetes-indicated brands, and insurance coverage is far more common for that indication. If you have diabetes, the conversation is with your prescriber about which indication to pursue, because it changes the brand, the coverage and the monitoring - insulin and sulfonylureas raise hypoglycemia risk when combined with a GLP-1. Mounjaro vs Ozempic and Ozempic vs Wegovy untangle the names.

Emotional eating

Many people report that the medication quiets "food noise" - the constant background pull toward eating that has nothing to do with hunger. That is real and is one of the most consistent things people on the medication describe. It is not the same as treating the reasons behind emotional eating, and the months on the medication are a good time to work on those, because the drug lowers the volume enough to hear yourself think. Emotional eating and weight loss is written for exactly that window.

sections.heading: Making the medication work: food, movement, sleep and the mistakes to avoid
sections.body:
The medication does the hard part - appetite - but the trial participants also had lifestyle counseling, and a handful of avoidable mistakes account for many disappointing results. This section is the short course.

Protein first, every meal

Appetite suppression makes it easy to eat 900 calories a day of whatever is convenient, and the cost is muscle. A simple rule that survives contact with a GLP-1: protein first on the plate, 25 to 40 grams per meal, before anything else. Greek yogurt, eggs, fish, poultry, tofu, legumes, protein shakes if whole food is too much. What to eat on GLP-1 medication has meal patterns that keep side effects quiet.

Fiber and fluids for the gut

Constipation is the most persistent complaint after the first weeks. Twenty-five grams of fiber a day from vegetables, fruit, oats and legumes, two to three liters of water, and a daily walk resolve most of it; a stool softener is the next step, and the clinician the one after that.

Strength training over cardio

Cardio is good for you; resistance training is what preserves the muscle that weight loss would otherwise take. Two or three sessions a week of compound movements - squats, hinges, pushes, pulls - at any level is the recommendation that matters most. Exercise on GLP-1 medication has beginner and intermediate programs.

Sleep and alcohol

Short sleep raises hunger hormones enough to blunt the medication's effect, and alcohol is empty calories that also hit harder on a nearly empty stomach. Neither needs to be perfect; both are the first places to look when a plateau arrives early.

The seven mistakes to avoid

  1. Prepaying a year before knowing you tolerate the medication. The $49 plan is the right plan for month four, not necessarily for month one. A month at a no-commitment provider first is cheap insurance.
  2. Comparing first-month prices. altRx's $89 and Medvi's $99 are promotions against $199; SHED's discount is month one only. Compare the regular rate.
  3. Not reading the shipping window. A 5-7 day window is not a delay; it is the published terms. A reviewer expecting 1-2 day delivery from a provider that promises 3-5 business days is the most common avoidable complaint we read.
  4. Doubling up after a missed dose. The Wegovy label says to take a missed dose within 5 days and otherwise skip it; the Zepbound label says within 4 days. Never take two doses to catch up.
  5. Pushing through serious nausea to stay on schedule. Holding a dose for a month is routine and costs nothing; vomiting for a week costs you the month anyway.
  6. Ignoring the beyond-use date on a compounded vial. Typically 28 days once in use. Medication past it is not necessarily dangerous but is not reliably potent.
  7. Stopping cold at goal weight. The extension data say most of the weight returns within a year. Plan the maintenance conversation before you reach the goal, not after.

The names, untangled

Ozempic and Wegovy are the same molecule (semaglutide) in different doses with different approvals: Ozempic for type 2 diabetes, Wegovy for weight management. Mounjaro and Zepbound are the same molecule (tirzepatide) with the same split. "Compounded Ozempic" does not exist as a product; it means compounded semaglutide. Rybelsus is an older oral semaglutide for diabetes; the Wegovy pill is the weight-management oral. Foundayo is a different molecule (orforglipron) from a different company. Zepbound vs Wegovy vs Ozempic is the three-way explainer.

Glossary

  • 503A pharmacy: a state-licensed pharmacy compounding for an individual patient on a prescription; the usual source for telehealth GLP-1s.
  • 503B outsourcing facility: an FDA-registered facility that can compound larger batches under federal oversight.
  • Beyond-use date (BUD): the date after which a compounded preparation should not be used; commonly 28 days from first use for vials.
  • Titration: the schedule of stepping the dose up over months to limit side effects.
  • Maintenance dose: the dose you stay on once titration is complete; the trial results are measured here.
  • Units: the markings on an insulin-style syringe used to draw a compounded dose from a vial; your prescription converts milligrams to units for your vial's concentration, and the provider should confirm it in writing.
  • Prior authorization (PA): the insurer's approval process for a brand-name GLP-1, usually requiring BMI and comorbidity documentation.
  • LegitScript: an independent certification for online pharmacies and telehealth companies that verifies licensing and practices; embody carries it.
  • Treatment-regimen vs efficacy estimand: two ways trials report results - what happened to everyone randomized, versus what happened to those who stayed on treatment. The second number is always larger and is the one marketing quotes.

sections.heading: Reading a compounded prescription: the label, the vial and the units
sections.body:
Brand-name pens hide the pharmacology behind a click-and-inject device. Compounded medication usually arrives as a small glass vial and a bag of insulin syringes, and the one skill it asks of you is reading what you have been sent. Five things to check on the day it arrives.

The label

A legitimately compounded prescription is labeled with your name, the prescriber's name, the pharmacy's name and address, the drug name and concentration (for example, "semaglutide 2.5 mg/mL"), the total volume, the directions, the date compounded and a beyond-use date. A vial without a pharmacy name, or with "for research use only," has not come through the route this guide describes, regardless of what the website said.

The concentration and the units

Compounded semaglutide is dispensed at various concentrations, and your weekly dose in milligrams has to be converted into units on an insulin syringe at your vial's concentration. The provider should give you that conversion in writing - "draw 10 units for 0.25 mg" - and it changes when the concentration changes, which can happen between refills. This conversion is where the dosing errors the FDA describes happen: a patient reading units from an old instruction with a new vial, or confusing milligrams with milliliters. If anything about the number on the syringe does not match the number on the instruction, do not inject until the provider confirms.

The molecule

The active ingredient in the approved drugs is the semaglutide or tirzepatide base. The FDA has flagged compounded products made with salt forms - semaglutide sodium and semaglutide acetate - as not the same active ingredient and not eligible for compounding under the law. The label should say "semaglutide," not a salt name. If the provider's pharmacy will not confirm which form it uses, that is an answer in itself.

The additives

Some compounded formulations add vitamin B12, NAD+ or other ingredients. There is no trial evidence that any of them improves weight loss; the usual stated rationale is to reduce nausea or to provide a documented clinical difference from the approved product. They are not harmful at the doses used, but they are not why the medication works, and a program whose marketing leans on them is selling the garnish. welludr lists a GLP-1 plus NAD+/B12 microdose among its options; it is a choice, not a requirement.

The beyond-use date and storage

A compounded vial typically carries a beyond-use date of 28 days from first puncture, and the pharmacy's own stability data may allow longer unopened. Keep it refrigerated, out of the door shelf where temperature swings, and let it reach room temperature for a few minutes before injecting to reduce stinging. If the medication arrives warm because a cold pack failed in transit, photograph it and contact the provider before using it; the legitimate providers replace it.

Vials versus pens

Brand-name products come in pre-filled, pre-dosed pens; some compounded programs offer pens too, at higher prices. Vials are cheaper and let a clinician prescribe any dose, which is the legal rationale for compounding; pens are simpler and remove the conversion step. If you are anxious about drawing a dose, ask the provider whether a pen option exists and what it costs, or ask for a first-dose video call, which several providers offer.

sections.heading: Your first 90 days: the checklist
sections.body:
Everything above, compressed into the order you will actually do it. Print it, or save the page.

Before you apply

  • Calculate your BMI and note any weight-related condition; the thresholds are 30, or 27 with a condition.
  • Check the disqualifiers: thyroid cancer history, MEN 2, pancreatitis, severe GI disease, pregnancy plans.
  • List every medication and supplement you take, with doses.
  • Decide the molecule: semaglutide first unless you have a specific reason for tirzepatide.
  • Decide the commitment: month to month to start if this is your first GLP-1.
  • Pick the provider by the twelve checks, and read the refund-if-declined and cancellation terms on its own site.
  • Find the regular price behind any promotion and write down what month four will cost.

Week 1

  • Complete the intake honestly; have your ID and, if you have them, recent labs ready.
  • Answer any clinician follow-up within the day.
  • On delivery: refrigerate, check the label (your name, pharmacy name, drug, concentration, beyond-use date), confirm the units-to-milligrams instruction in writing.
  • First injection on a day you can rest and eat lightly; log the date, dose and how you felt.

Weeks 2-4

  • Same day each week, rotate sites, log every dose.
  • Protein first at every meal; two to three liters of water; a daily walk.
  • Expect mild nausea and early fullness; avoid fried and very sweet food on injection day.
  • Message the clinician before the next dose if side effects are more than mild.
  • Set the refill reminder; confirm the next shipment date in the portal.

Weeks 5-8

  • First dose step-up if tolerated; expect two or three days of returning side effects.
  • Start or continue resistance training, two to three sessions a week.
  • Watch for constipation; fiber and fluids first.
  • Check your month-two charge against what you wrote down before you applied.

Weeks 9-12

  • Second step-up if tolerated; weight loss should now be steady.
  • Review protein intake honestly; reduced appetite makes under-eating it the default.
  • If you prepaid or committed to a plan, this is the point to decide whether the medication suits you well enough to stay; if you started month to month and are staying, this is the point to re-run the year-one math and consider the committed plan.
  • Book the maintenance conversation with your clinician now, before you are anywhere near your goal.

Three months in, you will know three things no guide can tell you in advance: how you tolerate the medication, how you respond to it, and whether the provider you chose is the one you want for the year. Those three answers, not any ranking, decide the rest.

sections.heading: What changed in 2025-2026, and what to watch next
sections.body:
This market moves faster than most medical categories, and a guide written in 2024 would already be wrong in four places. Here is what has changed recently and what is likely to change next, so you can tell a current page from a stale one.

The shortage era ended

The FDA's December 2024 and February 2025 decisions that tirzepatide and semaglutide were no longer in shortage, and the end of the enforcement grace periods in spring 2025, closed the window in which compounding pharmacies could produce copies of the approved drugs at scale. The programs that survived did so by returning to patient-specific compounding with a documented clinical rationale, by naming their pharmacies, and in several cases by adding a brand-name shelf. Expect continued FDA attention to marketing language, as the June 2026 warning letter over "FDA-approved" claims showed, and expect the legitimate providers to keep tightening how they describe the product.

The pills arrived

The Wegovy pill in December 2025 and Foundayo in April 2026 turned "I will not inject" from a hard stop into a pricing question. Both are brand-name and priced in the $149-$349 range by dose through the manufacturers and telehealth, which is three to seven times the cheapest compounded injection and a fraction of a brand-name pen. The likely next move is pressure on compounded prices from the bottom and brand-name pen prices from the top; our price-change log is where that will show first.

Prices fell, then settled

The verified compounded floor for semaglutide is $41 a month on a committed plan (welludr, lowered from $49 on October 28, 2026) and $49 month to month at embody during its pre-Black Friday sale (previously $69), with tirzepatide at $71 and $99 (previously $89 and $119). The committed-plan floor has been stable through the period we have logged; the movement has been in promotions, which appear and expire, and in the commitment structures behind the headline rates. The pattern to watch is a low headline price attached to a longer plan - that is where the "cheapest" claims will come from, and the year-one math in this guide is the way to read them.

Medicare moved

The GLP-1 Bridge pilot, reported at a flat $50 a month for the approved medications through December 2027, is the first meaningful Medicare route to these drugs for weight management. We report that figure from dated third-party sources and have not verified it; the eligibility conditions are the part to confirm with your plan, and our over-65 guide tracks them.

Brands rename, molecules do not

One of the providers in this guide, welludr, became welludr in October 2026 without changing its plans or prices, and the industry's churn in company names, parent companies and pharmacy partners is going to continue. The anchor that does not move is the molecule: semaglutide and tirzepatide, from a named, licensed pharmacy, on a patient-specific prescription, at a price with its conditions attached. Judge every provider, and every future version of this guide, against that.

How we will keep this page current

Prices are re-verified on a schedule and on every change we catch, and the "verified" date in the price table is the date of the last check. Clinical and regulatory statements are updated when the labels or the FDA's guidance change, and the update date at the top of the page moves only when something on it actually changed. If you find a figure that no longer matches a provider's site, the contact details on our about page reach the people who maintain it.

sections.heading: Frequently asked questions
sections.body:
Can I get Ozempic online for weight loss? Ozempic is approved for type 2 diabetes; for weight loss the approved semaglutide product is Wegovy, which telehealth providers such as ro prescribe. Most people searching for "Ozempic for weight loss" end up with compounded semaglutide at $41 to $199 a month or Wegovy at brand-name prices. How to get Ozempic online walks through each option.

Can I get a GLP-1 without seeing a doctor? No. Every legal route requires a licensed clinician to review your history and prescribe. The review can be entirely online and asynchronous, which is what "no clinic visit" means. Can you get Ozempic without a doctor explains the law.

What is the cheapest GLP-1 online? At verified prices on October 16, 2026: compounded semaglutide at $41 a month on welludr's 12-month plan (a pre-Black Friday rate), or $49 a month at embody with no commitment. Compounded tirzepatide: $71 at welludr on the plan, $99 at embody month to month. The cheapest GLP-1 page is updated on every price change.

Is compounded semaglutide safe? It is the same active ingredient prepared by a state-licensed pharmacy on a prescription. It is not FDA-approved, has no trials of its own, and its quality depends on the pharmacy; the FDA has documented adverse events, dosing errors and wrong-ingredient products from the wider market. The protection is a named, licensed pharmacy, a patient-specific prescription and a labeled product.

Does the price go up as my dose goes up? Not at the providers in this guide, every one of which publishes one price per medication at every dose. What changes the price is a promotion ending (altRx, Medvi, SHED) or, at welludr and Sprout, whether you are on the 12-month plan, and at HealthRx the end of the $39 first month.

How much weight will I lose? The trial averages are about 15% of body weight on semaglutide at 68 weeks and 15% to 21% on tirzepatide at 72 weeks depending on dose, with wide individual variation. Most of the loss happens between months three and nine.

How fast will it arrive? Published windows from the providers we track: 1-2 days at DirectMeds, free expedited delivery with no stated window at embody, often next-day at TrimRx, overnight at HealthRx, within 2 days at Sprout, 3-5 business days at welludr, 5-7 days at altRx. Add one to three days for the clinician review before shipping.

Do I need insurance? No. The compounded prices here are cash prices, and embody, altRx and DirectMeds state that no insurance is required. Insurance rarely covers compounded medication; it sometimes covers brand-name.

Can I use my HSA or FSA? Generally yes for a prescribed medication; Medvi and SHED state eligibility explicitly. Keep the itemized receipt.

What happens if I stop? Appetite returns, and in the semaglutide extension study participants regained about two-thirds of their lost weight within a year. Plan for maintenance from the start.

Which is better, semaglutide or tirzepatide? Tirzepatide produced more weight loss in its trials; semaglutide costs $40 to $100 a month less at the same provider, has a longer record and comes as a pill. For a first course, most people start with semaglutide and switch only if they plateau.

Can I switch providers mid-treatment? Yes. The new provider runs its own intake and writes a new prescription; most will continue your current dose with documentation. Check the cancellation terms at the provider you are leaving, especially on a 12-month plan.

Are the "pills" and "drops" the same as the Wegovy pill? No. The Wegovy pill and Foundayo are FDA-approved formulations with their own trials. Compounded tablets, drops and troches are unstudied compounded preparations.

Is there a money-back guarantee anywhere? embody refunds the unused portion, less services rendered, if a clinician does not approve you. SHED guarantees 5% body-weight loss in 120 days or your money back. Everything else is governed by each provider's cancellation terms, which the review pages quote.

Can I buy semaglutide from overseas or without a prescription? Not legally, and not safely. Products sold without a prescription or shipped from unlicensed sources are the category in which the FDA has found counterfeits, wrong ingredients and unlabeled vials. The verified prices in this guide start at $49 a month; there is no legitimate product meaningfully cheaper than that.

Can I take a GLP-1 with metformin or other weight-loss medication? Often, under supervision; metformin is commonly co-prescribed. Insulin and sulfonylureas need dose adjustment because of hypoglycemia risk, and combining two GLP-1 products is never appropriate. The intake is where every medication gets declared.

What if I move to another state? Tell the provider. Prescribing requires a clinician licensed in your state, and the prescription may need to be rewritten; most providers list the states they serve.

How do I travel with it? Keep vials or pens refrigerated with a small cold pack; most labels allow a period at room temperature (the Wegovy pen, for example, up to 28 days below 86°F), and your pharmacy's instructions govern a compounded vial. Carry the labeled prescription through airport security.

What is the difference between a vial and a pen? A pen is pre-filled and pre-dosed; you dial and inject. A vial requires drawing the dose into a syringe using a units conversion the provider supplies. Vials are what most compounded programs ship and are why compounded is cheaper; pens are what the brand-name products use.

How do I know a telehealth provider is legitimate? It names its pharmacy and its clinicians' licensing, requires a real intake, labels its medication with a pharmacy name, publishes a physical address and phone number, and never calls a compounded product FDA-approved. LegitScript certification, which embody carries, is an independent check of the same points.

sections.heading: How this guide was researched, and what to do next
sections.body:
Every provider price, shipping window, plan condition and refund term in this guide comes from our verified price index, which is read from each provider's own site on a dated schedule - most recently October 16, 2026 - and logged on every change. Where a figure comes from a manufacturer, a government program or a third-party tracker, it is dated, linked and marked as unverified by us. Clinical statements are drawn from the FDA-approved labels and the peer-reviewed trial reports linked inline, and the medical and scientific content has been reviewed for accuracy by our named medical reviewer under the policy described on our medical review policy page. We earn commissions from some of the providers we link to; it affects neither the prices shown nor the facts stated, and our how we rank page sets out exactly how the ranking is built.

This guide is for information only. It is not medical advice, and whether a GLP-1 medication is right for you is a decision for you and a licensed clinician who knows your history. Compounded medications are not FDA-approved.

Where to go from here

  • If you know what you want and want the shortest path to a provider: the provider ranking, or the matching quiz.
  • If price is the decider: cheapest GLP-1 online and what you will really pay.
  • If you are choosing the molecule: tirzepatide vs semaglutide and best tirzepatide online.
  • If you want the brand-name product: the Zepbound and Wegovy pill price guides and the ro review.
