articles.title: Stopping GLP-1s: Weight Regain and How to Keep It Off (2026)
articles.description: What happens when you stop semaglutide or tirzepatide: regain data from every major trial and 2026 meta-analysis, maintenance doses, tapering, muscle and cost.
articles.author: Treatments Hub Research Team
keyTakeaways: In every randomized trial that has switched people from semaglutide or tirzepatide to placebo, most of the lost weight came back within a year: about two-thirds in the STEP 1 extension, 6.9 percentage points in 48 weeks in STEP 4 and 14.0 points in 52 weeks in SURMOUNT-4. A January 2026 BMJ meta-analysis of 37 studies puts the average regain at 0.4 kg a month, roughly 0.8 kg a month for the newer drugs, with weight projected back at baseline in about a year and a half to two years.

Real-world data are less bleak than the trials, for a telling reason. In a Cleveland Clinic study of 7,938 adults who stopped within a year, the obesity group had regained only 0.5% of body weight on average a year later, and 45% had maintained or kept losing, largely because more than half restarted the drug or switched to another treatment.

The first randomized evidence on a lower maintenance dose arrived in May 2026: in SURMOUNT-MAINTAIN, people who dropped to 5 mg of tirzepatide after 60 weeks kept most of their loss (16.6% below baseline at week 112) versus 21.9% on the full dose and 9.9% on placebo. There is still no randomized trial of a slow taper, of 'microdosing' or of a reduced-frequency schedule, and no professional guideline recommends a stopping protocol.

What you can control: how much of the loss was fat rather than muscle (resistance training and protein during treatment), whether you switch rather than stop (to a cheaper compounded plan, a different molecule or an oral GLP-1), and whether you plan the off-ramp with your prescriber instead of letting a lapsed refill decide it. At verified prices, staying on compounded semaglutide costs $41 to $199 a month; the cheapest year is $492.

sections.heading: The short answer, and what this guide covers
sections.body:
This is the long version of the question that every person on a GLP-1 eventually asks, usually around month nine, when the scale has slowed, the budget has not, and a refill lapses. It is written for someone who wants the full picture before deciding: what the trials actually measured when people stopped, what the two big 2026 meta-analyses added, why the real-world numbers look different, what the biology is doing, who regains least, what the evidence says about maintenance doses, tapering and the "microdosing" trend, how much of the weight you lose is muscle and what to do about it, what else reverses when the drug stops, what staying on costs at verified prices, how to switch rather than stop, and how to build a 90-day off-ramp with your prescriber if you do stop.

Three rules govern everything that follows. Every clinical number has a dated, linked source, and where the source is a press release, a preprint or a secondary report rather than a peer-reviewed paper, we say so. Every provider price is one we checked on the provider's own site, most recently on October 16, 2026, and carries its conditions. Where the evidence does not exist, we say that too, because the gap between what is marketed about "coming off" these drugs and what has been studied is wide, and the gap itself is useful information.

Who this guide is for

It is for the person who has reached a goal weight and wonders whether they can stop; the person whose insurance or budget has changed and who feels forced to stop; the person who has stopped already and is watching the scale climb; the person who is deciding whether to start at all and wants to know what the commitment really is; and the clinician-curious reader who wants the trial names, dates and numbers in one place. It is not medical advice. Dose changes, tapers and restarts are decisions for you and a licensed prescriber who knows your history, and nothing here replaces that conversation. It should make it a better one.

A note on the drugs

"GLP-1" in this guide means the two molecules that account for almost all weight-loss prescribing in 2026: semaglutide (a GLP-1 receptor agonist sold as Wegovy, Ozempic and the Wegovy pill, and compounded by 503A pharmacies) and tirzepatide (a dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist sold as Zepbound and Mounjaro, and compounded). Orforglipron (Foundayo), the daily non-peptide GLP-1 pill approved on April 1, 2026, appears where it is relevant to maintenance. Older drugs such as liraglutide and the non-GLP-1 medications appear only inside the meta-analyses that pooled them. How these drugs work is covered in our guide to how GLP-1 medications work; this guide starts from the day the last dose wears off.

sections.heading: Why 'what happens when I stop' is the most important question in obesity medicine
sections.body:
For most of the history of weight-loss treatment, the hard part was losing the weight. GLP-1 medications changed that. In the pivotal trials, semaglutide 2.4 mg produced a mean loss of 14.9% of body weight at 68 weeks (STEP 1, New England Journal of Medicine, March 18, 2021) and tirzepatide 15 mg produced 20.9% at 72 weeks (SURMOUNT-1, New England Journal of Medicine, July 21, 2022), against 2% to 3% on placebo. Those are numbers that no diet programme and no earlier drug approached. So the hard part moved. In 2026 the defining question is no longer whether these drugs work but what happens afterwards, and that question is where the science, the economics and the marketing all collide.

It matters at scale. A consulting analysis reported by CBS News on October 22, 2026 estimated that roughly half of American semaglutide users now take it primarily for weight loss rather than diabetes, a population that largely pays cash or faces coverage that can end at a plan renewal. Every one of those people will, at some point, stop, pause, lapse or be forced off. The trials that follow tell us what happens when they do, and they are unusually consistent.

Three ways to frame the drugs, and why only one is right

The first frame is the diet frame: a GLP-1 is a tool that helps you lose weight, after which you keep it off with the habits you built. This is how most people start, and it is the frame the withdrawal trials contradict most directly. The second frame is the cure frame: enough time on the drug "resets" something, and you can stop. There is no evidence for this; the extension studies show appetite and weight returning regardless of how long people had been treated, within the durations studied. The third frame is the chronic-disease frame: obesity involves a biology that defends a higher weight, the drug offsets that biology while it is present, and stopping removes the offset. This is the frame the data support, the frame the FDA labels use when they describe the drugs as being for "chronic weight management," and the frame that makes the rest of this guide make sense. It is also, importantly, not a counsel of despair. Blood pressure medication works the same way, and nobody considers a person who needs it long term to have failed.

sections.heading: What the randomized trials showed when people stopped
sections.body:
Four trials have randomized or followed people off semaglutide or tirzepatide after substantial weight loss and measured what happened. They are the foundation of everything written about regain, and they are worth knowing by name because much of what is written about them is wrong in the details.

Trial (publication)DrugDesignLoss before stoppingWhat happened off drugWhat happened staying on
STEP 1 extension (Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, April 19, 2022)Semaglutide 2.4 mg327 participants followed for 52 weeks after 68 weeks of treatment ended17.3% (semaglutide arm)Regained 11.6 percentage points, about two-thirds; net 5.6% below baseline at week 120Not studied in the extension
STEP 4 (JAMA, March 23, 2021)Semaglutide 2.4 mg803 randomized after a 20-week run-in to continue or switch to placebo for 48 weeks10.6%Regained 6.9 percentage points; net 5.0% below baseline at week 68Lost a further 7.9 points; 17.4% below baseline
SURMOUNT-4 (JAMA, December 11, 2023)Tirzepatide 10 or 15 mg670 randomized after a 36-week lead-in to continue or switch to placebo for 52 weeks20.9%Regained 14.0 percentage points; net 9.9% below baseline at week 88Lost a further 5.5 points; 25.3% below baseline
SURMOUNT-MAINTAIN (The Lancet, May 12, 2026)Tirzepatide378 randomized after a 60-week lead-in to full dose, 5 mg or placebo for 52 weeksAbout 22% (open-label phase)Placebo: 9.9% below baseline at week 112, with rescue allowed after regaining halfFull dose 21.9%, 5 mg 16.6% below baseline

Sources: Wilding et al., Weight regain and cardiometabolic effects after withdrawal of semaglutide: the STEP 1 trial extension, Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, 2022; Rubino et al., Effect of continued weekly subcutaneous semaglutide vs placebo on weight loss maintenance (STEP 4), JAMA, 2021; Aronne et al., Continued treatment with tirzepatide for maintenance of weight reduction (SURMOUNT-4), JAMA, 2023; Horn et al., Tirzepatide for maintenance of bodyweight reduction (SURMOUNT-MAINTAIN), The Lancet, 2026. SURMOUNT-MAINTAIN is covered in its own section below.

STEP 1 extension: the two-thirds figure

This is the study behind the sentence you have read everywhere: "people regained two-thirds of the weight within a year." The detail matters. STEP 1 treated people for 68 weeks with semaglutide 2.4 mg plus lifestyle counselling; at the end, both the drug and the counselling stopped, and 327 of the original 1,961 participants were followed for another year without either. The semaglutide group had lost 17.3% at week 68 and had regained 11.6 percentage points by week 120, leaving them 5.6% below where they started. The placebo group, who had lost 2.0%, regained 1.9 points. So two-thirds of the loss returned, one-third did not, and the regain happened without any structured support, which is more like real life than the trial itself was. The authors also reported that the improvements in blood pressure, blood lipids and HbA1c seen on treatment had reverted toward baseline by week 120, a point we come back to.

STEP 4: the cleanest test

STEP 4 is the better-designed study of the stopping question because it was randomized at the moment of stopping. Everyone took semaglutide for 20 weeks, reaching the full 2.4 mg dose and losing 10.6% on average. Then 803 people were randomly assigned either to keep taking it or to switch to a placebo injection, without knowing which, for 48 more weeks. Those who continued lost a further 7.9%. Those who switched regained 6.9 percentage points. The gap between the arms at week 68 was 14.8 percentage points of body weight, and it opened within weeks of the switch. Because the placebo group did not know they had been switched and kept receiving the same lifestyle counselling, this trial isolates the drug effect from motivation, support and expectation. The weight came back anyway.

SURMOUNT-4: tirzepatide, larger loss, larger regain

SURMOUNT-4 ran the same design with tirzepatide. A 36-week open-label lead-in at 10 or 15 mg produced a mean loss of 20.9%. Then 670 people were randomized to continue or to switch to placebo for 52 weeks. Continuing produced a further 5.5% loss, for 25.3% in total. Switching produced a regain of 14.0 percentage points, leaving that group 9.9% below baseline. Two things are worth noticing. The regain was larger in absolute terms than in STEP 4 because the loss had been larger; as a share of the loss it was similar, roughly two-thirds. And the placebo group was still carrying a weight loss at week 88 that would count as a success for most diet programmes, which is the optimistic reading of the same data. A post hoc analysis of the trial published in JAMA Internal Medicine in December 2025 (summarized in an American College of Cardiology journal scan) reported that more than four in five of those switched to placebo had regained at least a quarter of their lost weight within the year, which is the distribution behind the average: regain was the norm, not the result of a few outliers.

What the trials have in common

Regain began within the first month off the drug in every study, continued through the whole follow-up period without clearly flattening, was proportional to the weight lost, and occurred despite continued lifestyle counselling in the trials that provided it. Nobody in these studies was told how to taper, because nobody was tapered: the switch to placebo was abrupt by design. Whether a taper changes the curve is a separate question with, as of October 2026, no randomized answer; we cover what is registered below.

sections.heading: The 2026 meta-analyses: how fast, how much, and when it stops
sections.body:
Individual trials tell you what happened to the people in them. Two meta-analyses published in 2026 pooled every study they could find and answered the questions patients actually ask: how fast does weight come back, how much of it, and does the regain ever plateau?

BMJ, January 2026: 0.4 kg a month, 0.8 for the new drugs

The larger of the two was led by Sam West at the University of Oxford's Nuffield Department of Primary Care Health Sciences and published in The BMJ on January 7, 2026 (doi 10.1136/bmj-2025-085304; the university's summary gives the headline figures). It pooled 37 studies with 9,341 adults who had taken a weight-management medication for an average of 39 weeks and were then followed for an average of 32 weeks after stopping. Its findings:

  • Weight rose by an average of 0.4 kg (about 0.9 lb) per month after the drugs were stopped, across all medications.
  • For the newer drugs, semaglutide and tirzepatide, regain was faster, at about 0.8 kg per month.
  • Regain after stopping a medication was faster than regain after ending a behavioural weight-loss programme by about 0.3 kg per month, regardless of how much weight had been lost.
  • Extrapolating the pooled rate, the authors estimated that weight would return to its starting point roughly a year and a half to two years after stopping, with the improvements in blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol projected to revert sooner.

Two cautions, both the authors' own. The return-to-baseline estimate is a projection beyond the average follow-up, not an observation, because few studies followed people for two years. And the pooled studies differ in drugs, doses and populations, so 0.4 kg a month is a central tendency, not a forecast for an individual.

eClinicalMedicine, 2026: the shape of the curve

A second group used a different method, meta-regression, to reconstruct the regain curve over time from 48 studies and published it in eClinicalMedicine, a Lancet journal (doi 10.1016/j.eclinm.2026.103796). Its model found that about 60% of the lost weight had been regained by 52 weeks after stopping, and that the curve flattened at around 60 weeks with roughly three-quarters of the loss regained, implying that about a quarter of the loss might be sustained. The plateau is a model projection drawn from the available follow-up and the authors present it as such; it is consistent with the one-third sustained in the STEP 1 extension and the roughly half of the loss still present in SURMOUNT-4's placebo arm at a year, and it is the most optimistic reading of the pooled data that the evidence supports. An accompanying commentary in the same journal made a point that recurs throughout this guide: at the time of writing, there were no randomized trials of tapering regimens or structured maintenance protocols, and clinical guidelines offered no recommendations on how to stop.

A third model: half the loss back in about seven and a half months

A smaller analysis in Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism reconstructed time-point data from six randomized trials with 1,776 participants and estimated that half of the treatment-related weight loss returns within about 7.5 months of discontinuation. Its inputs overlap heavily with the trials in the table above, so it is not independent confirmation so much as another way of reading the same curves, but the number is a useful rule of thumb: whatever you lost, expect the midpoint of regain somewhere around the eighth month off treatment if nothing else changes.

How to use these numbers

Put together, the three analyses say the same thing from different angles. Regain starts immediately, runs at something like 0.4 to 0.8 kg a month, reaches half of the loss in well under a year, and may flatten in the second year with a fraction of the loss, perhaps a quarter to a third, still in hand. For a person who lost 20 kg (44 lb) on tirzepatide, that is roughly 13 to 15 kg back within about a year and a half, and perhaps 5 to 7 kg kept. For someone who lost 12 kg on semaglutide, it is roughly 8 kg back and 4 kept. Those are arithmetic on the pooled averages, not predictions, and the next section explains why individual experience in the real world is often better.

sections.heading: What happens in the real world: the Cleveland Clinic cohort
sections.body:
Trials are designed to measure a drug, so they switch people to placebo abruptly and forbid them from restarting. Real life has no such rule. The most important real-world study of stopping was published in Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism in March 2026 by Hamlet Gasoyan and colleagues at Cleveland Clinic (Cleveland Clinic newsroom, March 12, 2026), and it changes the picture in an instructive way.

The study

The researchers followed 7,938 adults with overweight or obesity in Ohio and Florida who started injectable semaglutide or tirzepatide between 2021 and 2023, for obesity or for type 2 diabetes, and who stopped within three to twelve months. They then tracked weight for a year after discontinuation using the health system's own records.

What they found

  • Patients in the obesity group had lost an average of 8.4% of their body weight before stopping, which is less than the trials because they stopped early, typically before reaching a full maintenance dose.
  • One year after stopping, the obesity group had regained an average of just 0.5% of body weight. The diabetes group had, on average, lost a further 1.3%.
  • Averages hide the split. About 55% of the obesity group gained weight after stopping, and about 45% either maintained their weight or kept losing. In the diabetes group the split was roughly 44% gained, 56% maintained or lost.
  • The explanation the authors offer, backed by their own data, is that stopping was often not permanent: about one in five restarted the same drug within the year, and more than a third transitioned to an alternative obesity treatment. "Many patients who stop semaglutide or tirzepatide restart the medication or transition to another obesity treatment, which may explain why they regain less weight than patients in randomized trials," Gasoyan said in the clinic's release.

Why this matters more than the headline

The optimistic reading is that nearly half of real patients kept their weight off for a year. The accurate reading is that nearly half kept their weight off because a large share of them did not actually stay off treatment. Both are true, and the second is the actionable one: the single most common thing that distinguished real-world patients from trial participants was that they were allowed to go back on, and many did. The study also had limits the authors state plainly. It came from one health system in two states, it could not capture every intervention patients used, it measured people who stopped early rather than at a goal weight, and a year is short.

What "early stoppers" tell us

The population here is worth dwelling on because it describes most online GLP-1 patients. People who stop within a year usually stop for cost, side effects or supply, not because they reached a goal, and they stop having lost less than the trials' 15% to 21%. Smaller losses mean smaller absolute regain, and a lower dose at the time of stopping may mean a gentler return of appetite, though the study did not test that. If you are three to nine months in and weighing whether to stop, this is the study that most resembles your situation, and its central lesson is that the people who did best were those who treated stopping as a pause with an exit back onto treatment rather than as the end.

sections.heading: Why the weight comes back: the biology, not the willpower
sections.body:
People who regain weight after stopping a GLP-1 almost always describe it the same way: the hunger came back, the food noise came back, portions that had felt like plenty stopped feeling like enough. That is not a character change. It is the predictable result of removing a drug from a body that has been adapting, the whole time, to the weight it lost.

First, the drug leaves

Semaglutide has an elimination half-life of about one week and tirzepatide about five days, according to their prescribing information. A drug is essentially gone after about five half-lives, so semaglutide's effect fades over roughly five weeks and tirzepatide's over roughly three to four. That is why most people feel nothing different in the first week or two after a missed dose and then notice appetite returning in the third and fourth week. The slowing of stomach emptying reverses on the same timeline, which is why fullness after meals shortens. Nothing about this is a withdrawal syndrome; it is the drug's effect ending.

Second, the adaptations to weight loss do not leave

The more important fact is what the drug was holding back. In 2011, Priya Sumithran and colleagues at the University of Melbourne published a study in the New England Journal of Medicine (Long-Term Persistence of Hormonal Adaptations to Weight Loss) in which 50 adults lost an average of 13.5 kg on a ten-week very-low-energy diet. The researchers measured appetite hormones before, after, and a year later. At 62 weeks, leptin, peptide YY, cholecystokinin and insulin (hormones that signal fullness or energy sufficiency) were still significantly below baseline, while ghrelin (the hunger hormone), gastric inhibitory polypeptide and pancreatic polypeptide were still significantly above it, and participants' reported hunger was still higher than before they dieted. The authors' conclusion was that the circulating mediators of appetite that encourage weight regain "do not return to pre-weight-loss levels" a year later, and that long-term strategies to counteract them would be needed to prevent relapse. That study did not involve a GLP-1. It describes what happens to anyone who loses a substantial amount of weight by any means, and it is the backdrop against which the GLP-1 withdrawal trials should be read: the drug does not create the hunger that follows stopping, it had been suppressing hunger that weight loss itself amplified.

Third, the body burns less than its new size predicts

Energy expenditure falls with weight loss, partly because a smaller body needs less, and partly, in many people, beyond what the smaller size explains. The most cited evidence is Fothergill and colleagues' six-year follow-up of fourteen contestants from the television programme The Biggest Loser, published in Obesity in 2016 (Persistent metabolic adaptation 6 years after "The Biggest Loser" competition). Six years after losing an average of 58 kg, participants had regained an average of 41 kg, yet their resting metabolic rate was still about 700 kcal a day below where it had started, roughly 500 kcal a day lower than their body composition and age predicted. Two caveats belong next to that number. The intervention was extreme and the sample tiny, and co-author Kevin Hall has written that the finding was widely over-read as proof that dieting "destroys metabolism," when the contestants had in fact kept off a clinically meaningful average of about 12% of their starting weight. The sober version is that some degree of metabolic adaptation is real, persistent and proportional to the effort to stay lighter, and that it is one of several forces a person who stops a GLP-1 is leaning against.

Fourth, the brain's set point does not move on the drug's schedule

The language of a "set point" is a simplification, but the evidence that the body defends a weight range through appetite, satiety and expenditure is robust, and there is no evidence that eighteen months of pharmacological weight loss moves that defended range downward. The withdrawal trials are, in effect, a test of the hypothesis that it does, and they came back negative within their durations. Whether longer treatment, say three to five years, would be different is unknown, because no trial has withdrawn people after that long.

What this means for you

If you stop, you should expect hunger to return within about a month and to be somewhat stronger than you remember from before you started, because your body is now defending a weight it has lost. You should expect your maintenance calorie needs to be lower than a calculator predicts for your new size. And you should treat both as facts to plan around rather than failures to feel ashamed of. The plateau guide covers the same adaptations as they show up during treatment; off treatment they are simply unopposed.

sections.heading: Who regains least? What the data can and cannot tell you
sections.body:
Everyone wants to know whether they will be in the minority who keep the weight off. The honest answer is that the studies were not designed to find out, and the predictors that have been reported are modest. Here is what can be said with support, and what cannot.

Supported by data

  • Staying on something. The single strongest predictor of holding weight in the Cleveland Clinic cohort was not stopping for good: restarting the same drug or switching to another treatment. In SURMOUNT-MAINTAIN, a lower dose held most of the loss. This is not a loophole; it is the finding.
  • How much you lost. Regain in the trials was proportional to the loss, so larger losers regained more kilograms but ended up further below baseline. In SURMOUNT-4 the placebo arm was still 9.9% down a year after stopping; in STEP 4 the equivalent figure was 5.0%. If you lost a lot, you are likely to keep more in absolute terms even if you regain the typical share.
  • Having diabetes. In the Cleveland Clinic study, the type 2 diabetes group lost further weight after stopping on average. The authors do not claim to know why; plausible explanations include other glucose-lowering drugs, continued care and different reasons for stopping. It is an observation, not a mechanism.
  • Stopping early at a smaller loss. Also from Cleveland Clinic: people who stopped within a year, having lost about 8%, regained very little on average. Part of this is restarting, part may be that there was less to regain.

Plausible but not demonstrated

  • Preserving muscle during the loss. Muscle is metabolically active, and people who lose proportionally more fat and less lean mass should, in principle, face a smaller drop in resting expenditure. The body-composition data from the trials and from the muscle-preserving drug studies are covered below. What does not yet exist is a trial showing that people who protected lean mass regained less after stopping.
  • Habits built during treatment. Every clinician will tell you, and the trials' lifestyle counselling was premised on it, that the eating patterns, protein intake, resistance training and sleep routines established while appetite was suppressed are what you fall back on. It is sensible, and the STEP 1 extension, where counselling stopped with the drug, is consistent with it mattering. It has not been isolated in a randomized comparison.
  • A slow taper rather than an abrupt stop. Untested in any published randomized trial as of October 2026, though trials are registered. See the tapering section.

Not supported

  • "Being disciplined." The placebo arms in STEP 4 and SURMOUNT-4 were full of people who had just lost 10% to 21% of their body weight under supervision, who did not know they had been switched, and who were still receiving counselling. They regained anyway. Discipline was not the variable.
  • Length of time on the drug "resetting" appetite. No withdrawal study has found that longer treatment produced less regain, within the durations studied.

The practical reading: you cannot reliably predict in advance whether you will hold your weight off treatment, and the people who ask the question are often those who have lost the most, who face the largest absolute regain. What you can do is stack the modest, plausible factors in your favour (muscle, habits, a planned rather than accidental stop) and, above all, keep the door back onto treatment open. The next sections are about the forms that door can take.

sections.heading: The maintenance-dose question: what SURMOUNT-MAINTAIN finally answered
sections.body:
For years the most common clinical compromise, stepping down to a lower dose once a goal weight is reached, rested on experience rather than evidence. On May 12, 2026, The Lancet published the first randomized trial designed to test it (Horn, Aronne, Wharton et al., SURMOUNT-MAINTAIN; the American College of Cardiology summary and the trial's published design paper give the details used here).

The design

441 adults with obesity in the United States took tirzepatide open-label for 60 weeks, titrating to the maximum dose they tolerated. The 378 who had lost at least 5% were then randomized 3:3:2, double-blind, to one of three arms for a further 52 weeks: continue at their maximum tolerated dose (140 people), step down to 5 mg (144) or switch to placebo (94). From week 24 of the maintenance phase, anyone who had regained more than half of their lost weight could be rescued back onto tirzepatide. 91% completed the study.

The results

Arm (weeks 60 to 112)Weight change from original baseline at week 112Difference vs placebo
Maximum tolerated dose-21.9%-12.0 points
5 mg-16.6%-6.6 points
Placebo (rescue allowed from week 24)-9.9%-

At 24 weeks after randomization, before any rescue was permitted, the arms stood at 22.4%, 18.8% and 12.3% below baseline respectively, so the placebo group had already regained close to half its loss in six months, matching the pattern in SURMOUNT-4. The 5 mg group gave back a few percentage points and then held. Adverse events were in line with the drug's known profile, which has consistently clustered around dose increases rather than stable or reduced doses.

How to read it

Three conclusions are safe. A reduced dose of tirzepatide preserves most, but not all, of the weight lost at a higher dose over one year; the 5 mg arm kept about three-quarters of the full-dose arm's advantage over placebo. Stopping entirely produced the familiar regain, blunted here by rescue. And the comparison that most people care about, 5 mg versus full dose, is a trade of roughly five percentage points of body weight for the lowest marketed dose, which for someone paying by the milligram is a substantial saving. Two cautions belong alongside. A year of maintenance is short for a lifelong condition, as the Lancet commentary noted; and the trial tested one lower dose of one drug in people who had tolerated and responded to it. It does not tell you the lowest dose that works for you, and it does not transfer automatically to semaglutide, for which no equivalent randomized dose-reduction trial has reported.

What exists for semaglutide

Less. The strongest published evidence on reduced semaglutide regimens is a retrospective case series from Scripps Clinic in San Diego, published in Obesity in early 2026 (Scripps summary). Of 38 patients who had plateaued on weekly dosing, 30 moved to a less frequent schedule, most commonly every other week; four declined to step down and four returned to weekly dosing after regaining. Across an average of 36 weeks on the reduced schedule, mean weight went from 74.1 kg to 72.4 kg, body fat continued to fall and muscle mass was stable. It is a small, uncontrolled, single-centre series and its authors call for proper trials, but it is a proof of concept that some people maintain on less, and that the ones who do not can be identified quickly and put back on the full schedule. A randomized non-inferiority trial comparing a semaglutide taper with full-dose maintenance (NCT07783854, 72 participants, 24-week primary endpoint) was listed to start in September 2026 and had not reported as of this writing.

What a maintenance dose means in practice

If you are considering it, the conversation with your prescriber has three parts: which dose to step down to (SURMOUNT-MAINTAIN tested 5 mg of tirzepatide; clinicians prescribing semaglutide often discuss 1 mg or 1.7 mg, without randomized support), how you will measure whether it is working (weekly weights for the first three months, with an agreed threshold, perhaps a 3% to 5% regain, that triggers a return to the previous dose), and what it costs. On price, the picture is favourable in one specific way: several of the providers we track charge the same flat price at every dose, so stepping down saves nothing with them, while others and the brand-name products price by dose. The true-cost guide sets out who prices how.

sections.heading: Tapering off: what clinicians do, and what has actually been tested
sections.body:
A taper, meaning a planned reduction in dose or frequency over weeks or months with the intention of eventually stopping, is different from a maintenance dose, which is a planned reduction with the intention of staying on. The two are often confused in articles about "weaning off Ozempic," so it is worth being precise: the evidence for a maintenance dose now includes a randomized trial; the evidence for a taper as a way of preventing regain after full discontinuation does not.

Why there is no evidence

Every withdrawal trial to date switched people to placebo abruptly, because the question those trials asked was whether the drug was still doing anything, and an abrupt switch is the cleanest way to find out. The eClinicalMedicine commentary on the 2026 meta-analysis noted the absence of randomized tapering studies and the silence of clinical guidelines on how to stop, and a 2025 review of the metabolic rebound after discontinuation in the same journal made the same observation about the major obesity guidelines: they do not offer tapering recommendations because there are no data on which to base them. A 2026 narrative review in Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism (doi 10.1111/dom.71075) catalogued the de-escalation strategies in use, dose reduction, extended dosing intervals, switching agents and structured discontinuation, and reached the same conclusion: they are being used far ahead of their evidence.

What is registered

That is changing. Trials now on the US registry include a comparison of tapered versus abrupt discontinuation of GLP-1 therapy (NCT07859176) and the semaglutide taper-versus-maintenance study mentioned above. Neither had results as of October 2026. If you are reading this in 2027 or later, search those identifiers; this is the single area of the guide most likely to be overtaken.

What clinicians actually do

In the absence of trials, prescribers who help people stop tend to borrow the logic of titration in reverse. The pattern our medical reviewer and the published reviews describe is: step down one dose level at a time, hold each level for at least four weeks (long enough for the drug to reach a new steady state and for appetite at that level to become apparent), and move on only if weight is stable; if weight rises more than an agreed amount at any step, hold there or go back up. Some prescribers extend the interval between injections instead of lowering the dose, as in the Scripps series. The purpose is less about the pharmacology, which does not require a taper for safety, and more about information: a stepwise descent shows you, dose by dose, where your appetite and weight begin to move, which an abrupt stop does not.

What not to do

Do not taper by splitting doses, stretching a vial beyond its beyond-use date, or improvising a schedule from an online forum. Compounded vials in particular have a labelled beyond-use date (usually 28 days from first puncture; see the 28-day rule explainer), and using a vial for two or three months to "stretch" it means injecting a product past its tested stability. If cost is the reason you are stretching, the cheaper verified plans in the cost section are a safer answer than a slower vial.

Abrupt stopping is not dangerous in itself

Unlike some medications, GLP-1s do not produce a withdrawal syndrome and there is no safety requirement to taper; the trials stopped people cold without harm. The risks of an abrupt stop are the return of appetite and weight and, for people with type 2 diabetes, the loss of glucose control, which needs a plan with the prescriber managing the diabetes. If you must stop suddenly, because of pregnancy, surgery, an adverse event or a lost supply, you are not endangering yourself by doing so; you are simply starting the clock described earlier.

sections.heading: Microdosing GLP-1s: the trend, the evidence gap and the risks
sections.body:
"Microdosing" is the term that spread through social media and some telehealth marketing in 2025 and 2026 for taking a GLP-1 at a dose well below the lowest labelled dose, often a fraction of the 0.25 mg starting dose of semaglutide or the 2.5 mg starting dose of tirzepatide, either to maintain weight, to blunt appetite with fewer side effects, or for claimed benefits unrelated to weight. Because it is pitched specifically at people who want to come off a full dose, it belongs in this guide, and the evidence section is short because the evidence is.

What has been studied

No randomized trial has tested a sub-starting dose of semaglutide or tirzepatide for weight maintenance or for anything else. The starting doses themselves were chosen in the development programmes as the lowest that could be tolerated as a ramp, not as effective doses; in the dose-ranging studies the lowest doses produced the least weight loss, and nothing below them was tested. The reduced-dose evidence that does exist (SURMOUNT-MAINTAIN's 5 mg arm, the Scripps every-other-week series) used labelled doses at labelled or extended intervals, which is a different thing from a fraction of a starting dose. Professional societies have not endorsed sub-therapeutic dosing, and academic medical centres including Cleveland Clinic and Cedars-Sinai have published cautions pointing out that it is untested. Any claim that microdosing "maintains weight loss" is, as of October 2026, a hypothesis.

Why it is mostly a compounded-product phenomenon

Brand-name pens deliver fixed doses and cannot easily be microdosed. Compounded vials can be drawn to any volume, which is why the microdosing market and the compounded market overlap almost entirely. That matters because it combines two uncertainties: an unstudied dose and a product that is not FDA-approved. The FDA's page on its concerns with unapproved GLP-1 drugs specifically lists dosing errors among the adverse events it has received for compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide, including patients drawing up the wrong volume from a vial. Industry reporting of the agency's tally (Becker's Hospital Review, citing the FDA's figures as of May 31, 2026) put the reports at roughly a thousand for compounded semaglutide and over seven hundred for compounded tirzepatide, figures we repeat as reported and have not verified against the agency's database. Microdosing, by definition, asks the patient to measure very small volumes precisely, which is exactly the task the reports describe going wrong.

The regulatory backdrop

Compounded GLP-1s remain legal in 2026 only as patient-specific prescriptions from a state-licensed 503A pharmacy for a documented clinical need, since the FDA declared the shortages of tirzepatide (December 19, 2024) and semaglutide (February 21, 2025) resolved. "A lower dose than is marketed" is one of the clinical needs some prescribers document, which is why some telehealth programmes can offer microdosing at all; whether a given prescription meets the standard is a matter between the prescriber, the pharmacy and their state boards. Reporting in 2026 described FDA proposals to further restrict large-scale compounding of these drugs; we have not been able to confirm the current status of those proposals and do not rely on them here. Our guide to compounded vs brand-name semaglutide covers the framework in detail.

sections.heading: Muscle: the part of the weight you lose that you most want to keep
sections.body:
Of all the things that determine what happens after you stop, the composition of the weight you lost is the one most within your control while you are still losing it. Weight lost as fat is the point of treatment. Weight lost as lean mass, which is mostly skeletal muscle, lowers your resting energy expenditure, your strength and, in older adults, your resilience, and it is not automatically regained as muscle when weight returns. Here is what the trials measured, what the newer studies show, and what to do.

How much of the loss is lean mass in the trials?

Both pivotal trials ran sub-studies using DXA body scans. In STEP 1, 140 participants were scanned at baseline and week 68 (Wilding et al., conference abstract; the trial's registry results report the same data): on semaglutide, total body weight fell 15.0%, fat mass fell 19.3%, visceral fat fell 27.4% and lean mass fell 9.7%, so the share of the body that was lean rose by three percentage points. In SURMOUNT-1, 160 participants were scanned at baseline and week 72 (Look et al., Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, 2025): tirzepatide reduced fat mass by roughly a third and lean mass by roughly a tenth, and the proportion of weight lost as lean versus fat was consistent across subgroups and comparable to the placebo group's, which is to say comparable to ordinary weight loss. The widely quoted claim that "40% of the weight lost on GLP-1s is muscle" is a derived figure from these sub-studies, not a number either paper reports, and it conflates lean mass (which includes water and organ tissue) with muscle. The accurate statement is that a quarter to perhaps 40% of the weight lost in the trials was lean mass, that this is similar to the proportion lost with diet alone, and that because the absolute losses were large, the absolute lean loss (around 5 to 6 kg in both sub-studies) was large too.

Does it matter?

For most adults under 60 who lose 15% of their weight and keep their ratio of lean to fat improving, the lean loss is a feature of substantial weight loss rather than a hazard. It matters more for older adults, for anyone starting with low muscle mass, and for the question this guide is about: when weight returns after stopping, it returns disproportionately as fat unless something is done to rebuild muscle, so each cycle of loss and regain can leave a person with a higher fat percentage than before. A 2026 preprint on medRxiv (not yet peer-reviewed, and reported here with that caveat) analysed body composition in GLP-1 patients and reported that about a third lost more than 5% of their lean mass, with a minority showing larger "depletive" losses; the proportion differed between the two drugs but the finding needs confirmation in a reviewed study before it should change anyone's choice of molecule.

What protects muscle: the evidence

Two interventions have data. The first is the obvious one: resistance training and adequate protein. A 12-month study of 115 adults on semaglutide published in Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism (SEMALEAN, full text) tracked body composition and strength through treatment: fat mass fell 14% by month seven and 18% by month twelve, lean mass fell about 3 kg by month seven and then stabilised through month twelve, grip strength rose by about 4.5 kg, and the proportion of participants meeting criteria for sarcopenic obesity fell from 49% to 33%. In other words, with attention to strength and nutrition, lean loss was modest, stopped early and came with gains in function rather than losses. A dedicated randomized trial of resistance training alongside GLP-1 therapy, led from the University of Exeter, is registered as NCT07457437.

The second is pharmacological and not yet available. Bimagrumab, an antibody that blocks the activin receptor and increases muscle mass, was tested with semaglutide in the phase 2b BELIEVE trial (presented at the American Diabetes Association meeting in June 2025 and published in Nature Medicine in 2026). Over 72 weeks, the combination produced 22.1% weight loss versus 15.7% for semaglutide alone, with fat mass falling 45.7% on the combination versus 27.8% on semaglutide; lean mass fell 7.4% on semaglutide alone, 2.9% on the combination, and rose 2.5% on bimagrumab alone. Side effects on the combination included acne and muscle spasms. A trial pairing bimagrumab with tirzepatide is registered (NCT05933499). None of this is approved or prescribable in 2026; it is included because it confirms, in a controlled setting, that the lean-mass loss on GLP-1s is modifiable and that modifying it does not blunt fat loss.

What to do, in order

  • Lift something twice a week, starting now. The evidence for resistance training preserving lean mass during caloric restriction predates GLP-1s and is consistent; SEMALEAN is what it looks like with the drug. Two or three sessions a week of progressive, whole-body resistance work (bodyweight, bands or weights) is the pattern the trials and guidelines use. Walking is good for you and does not do this job.
  • Eat protein deliberately, because the drug will not make you want to. Appetite suppression hits protein-rich meals as hard as anything else, and people on GLP-1s commonly under-eat protein. Your prescriber or a dietitian can set a target for your weight and kidney function; the point is to have one and to hit it at every meal rather than once a day.
  • Measure something other than weight. A monthly waist measurement, a grip-strength or sit-to-stand test, or periodic body-composition scans tell you whether what you are losing is fat. If you are losing strength, that is a signal to slow the loss, eat more protein and train, not to stop the drug.
  • Keep lifting after you stop. If weight returns, training determines how much of it returns as muscle. This is the one factor that influences not just how much you regain but what you regain.

Our guide to "Ozempic face" covers the related, more visible question of facial volume loss, which follows the same logic: pace, protein and training.

sections.heading: What else reverses when you stop: blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol and heart risk
sections.body:
Weight is the number people watch, but it was never the only thing the drug was doing. The withdrawal studies measured the cardiometabolic markers too, and they moved back with the weight.

The STEP 1 extension findings

In the year after semaglutide and the lifestyle programme stopped, the improvements in systolic and diastolic blood pressure, HbA1c, C-reactive protein and blood lipids that had been seen at week 68 reverted toward their baseline values by week 120 (Wilding et al., Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, 2022). The authors' phrasing was careful: "toward" baseline, because at week 120 participants were still 5.6% lighter and some markers remained slightly better than at the start. But the direction was uniform, and the BMJ meta-analysis a few years later projected, across its pooled studies, that the cardiometabolic improvements would return to baseline somewhat before weight did, roughly in the range of a year and a half.

For people with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes

This is the group for whom stopping has the most immediate consequence. GLP-1s lower blood glucose directly, independent of weight, so a person with type 2 diabetes who stops will usually see glucose rise within weeks, before much weight has returned, and will need their diabetes regimen reviewed by the prescriber who manages it. In STEP 1, which excluded people with diabetes, a large share of participants with prediabetes at baseline had returned to normal glucose regulation on treatment; the extension showed that benefit eroding off treatment. If you were told your prediabetes had resolved on a GLP-1, treat that as "controlled" rather than "cured" when you weigh stopping.

The heart: why the long-term data push toward staying on

The SELECT trial (Lincoff et al., New England Journal of Medicine, November 11, 2023) randomized 17,604 adults with overweight or obesity and established cardiovascular disease, but without diabetes, to semaglutide 2.4 mg or placebo and followed them for a mean of about 40 months. Semaglutide reduced the composite of cardiovascular death, heart attack and stroke by 20% (hazard ratio 0.80). That result is the basis of Wegovy's cardiovascular indication and it has a direct bearing on the stopping decision for anyone in that population: the benefit was measured in people who kept taking the drug, and there is no evidence that it persists after discontinuation. For a person with prior heart disease, the question "should I stop" is a cardiology question as much as a weight question, and the answer from the trial data leans toward continuing in some form.

What does not reverse

The weight you keep off keeps its benefits. In SURMOUNT-4's placebo arm, people were still almost 10% below baseline after a year off, and a 10% loss carries meaningful improvements in blood pressure, glucose and lipids by any standard. The habits, the muscle you built and anything structural you changed, such as a medication for blood pressure that you no longer need, are yours. The point of this section is not that stopping undoes everything; it is that the markers follow the weight, so the plan to stop should include rechecking them at three and twelve months rather than assuming they held.

sections.heading: The cost of staying on: what maintenance actually costs at verified prices
sections.body:
Cost is the most common reason people stop, and it is the one where the facts have changed most in the past two years. If you started on a brand-name pen at $1,000 or more a month and your coverage ended, the alternatives below are what the decision to stop should be weighed against. Every provider price here was checked on the provider's own site on October 16, 2026 and is shown with its condition; prices change, and the provider's page is the live source.

Compounded maintenance: the verified floor
