The full index of every provider we track, including the $149 to $199 tier, is on the weight-loss comparison; the true-cost guide explains which prices rise after month one and which do not. Two points specific to maintenance. First, several providers charge the same price at every dose, so stepping down to a maintenance dose saves nothing with them but costs nothing extra either; with per-dose pricing the lower dose is cheaper. Second, the 12-month plan that produces the $41 figure is a commitment, which suits someone who has decided to stay on and does not suit someone testing whether they can come off. Our before-you-prepay guide lists the questions to ask.

Brand-name maintenance

Brand-name Zepbound bought for cash through telehealth runs $1,249 a month at altRx and $1,599 at welludr. At ro, the Wegovy pill is $149 for the first month and then $299 a month plus a membership of $39 and then $74 to $149 a month, prices verified in August 2026. Those are the figures against which "I can't afford to stay on" is usually measured, and they are ten to twenty times the compounded floor. Manufacturer programmes narrow the gap: Foundayo lists self-pay prices of $149 to $349 a month by dose, and the manufacturers' savings offers are reported to bring brand-name products to $25 a month for people with commercial insurance that covers them. Those manufacturer figures are as reported by the dated sources in our Zepbound and Wegovy pill price guides and are not verified by us.

Medicare

Since July 1, 2026, the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge pilot has let eligible beneficiaries get the Wegovy injection and pill, the Zepbound KwikPen and Foundayo for a flat $50 a month copay, unchanged as the dose rises, through December 31, 2027. For a Medicare patient weighing whether to stop because of cost, this programme is the first thing to check; our Medicare guide covers eligibility. Medicare does not cover compounded GLP-1s.

The arithmetic that should frame the decision

A year on the cheapest verified compounded semaglutide plan costs $588. A year of tirzepatide at the cheapest month-to-month price costs $1,188 at the current sale rate. Against those figures, the withdrawal data say that stopping is likely to return most of the lost weight within a year to eighteen months and to take the cardiometabolic improvements with it. Whether staying on is worth it is a personal decision, but it should be made against the compounded price, not the brand-name one, and it should be made knowing that the trade is not "pay or stop" but "pay $41 to $199 a month or accept the regain curve." For many people reading this, that reframing is the whole answer.

sections.heading: Switching instead of stopping: a different molecule, a cheaper plan or a pill
sections.body:
The Cleveland Clinic data made a point that deserves its own section: more than a third of real-world patients who "stopped" semaglutide or tirzepatide transitioned to another obesity treatment, and that group is part of why real-world regain looked so much better than the trials. Switching is the most under-discussed alternative to stopping. There are four forms.

Same drug, cheaper source

The most common switch in 2026 is from a brand-name pen to a compounded version of the same active ingredient when coverage ends. A licensed clinician at the new provider runs an intake, reviews your current dose and, where appropriate, continues it rather than restarting at the bottom, though some providers insist on their own titration. The product changes from a factory pen to a pharmacy vial, which is a real difference covered in the compounded vs brand-name guide, and the price changes by an order of magnitude. If the reason you are stopping is money, this is the switch to evaluate first.

Semaglutide to tirzepatide, or back

People who plateau or who struggle with side effects on one molecule are sometimes moved to the other. Head-to-head, tirzepatide produced more weight loss in SURMOUNT-5 (NEJM, 2025), so a switch from semaglutide to tirzepatide at a plateau has a rationale; a switch the other way is usually about cost or tolerability, since compounded semaglutide is $40 to $100 a month cheaper at the same provider. Switching molecules means a new titration, with the side effects that accompany it, and should be planned with the prescriber. The tirzepatide vs semaglutide guide covers the comparison.

Injection to pill: the maintenance case for oral GLP-1s

This is the switch with the newest evidence. Eli Lilly's ATTAIN-MAINTAIN trial (topline results in a press release of December 18, 2025; full data were promised for a later meeting and journal, and these figures should be read as company-reported until then) took people who had lost weight on injectable Wegovy or Zepbound and randomized them to switch to daily orforglipron or to placebo for 52 weeks. People switched from Wegovy to orforglipron held their weight almost exactly (a difference of about 0.9 kg over the year); people switched from Zepbound regained about 5 kg of a much larger loss; and in a post hoc look at 24 weeks, the placebo groups had already regained about 9 kg while the orforglipron groups had regained almost nothing from Wegovy and a modest amount from Zepbound. Discontinuation for adverse events was under 8% in both switch arms. Orforglipron is now Foundayo, approved April 1, 2026, with self-pay list prices of $149 to $349 a month by dose as reported in our Foundayo vs Wegovy pill guide. A separate registered trial of switching from injectable to oral GLP-1 therapy for maintenance (NCT07729332) was listed to begin in November 2026. The practical reading: a pill that holds most of an injectable's loss at a brand-name price below the injectables' brand-name price is a genuine third option between "keep injecting" and "stop," and it will suit people whose barrier was the needle or the cold chain rather than cost itself.

How to switch without a gap

The error that turns a switch into a stop is the gap: a month between the last brand-name pen and the first compounded shipment, during which the drug clears and appetite returns, after which the new provider starts you at the lowest dose and you spend two months re-titrating through side effects to get back to where you were. To avoid it, start the new intake while you still have two to three weeks of supply, tell the new clinician your current dose and how long you have been on it, ask whether they will continue it, and check the provider's shipping window (the verified windows range from one to two days at embody and DirectMeds to five to seven days at altRx). The complete guide to GLP-1 weight loss online covers the intake process step by step.

sections.heading: Stopping because of side effects: what to try before you quit
sections.body:
Side effects are the second most common reason for stopping, and the one where a conversation with the prescriber most often changes the outcome, because most GLP-1 side effects are dose-dependent and most dose-dependent side effects have a dose-based answer.

Gastrointestinal effects

Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, constipation and reflux are the leading adverse events on both labels and cluster around dose increases. The options before stopping, in the order clinicians usually try them: hold the current dose for an extra four weeks or more before stepping up (the labels' titration schedules are minimums, not requirements); step back down one level and stay there, since a lower dose that you can tolerate for a year beats a higher one you abandon in month three; adjust eating (smaller meals, less fat, no eating close to lying down); treat constipation and reflux directly; and, if a specific molecule is the problem, switch, because tolerability of semaglutide and tirzepatide is individual and not predictable. The side-effects guide covers management in detail.

When stopping is the right call

Some effects end treatment regardless of dose: pancreatitis, gallbladder disease needing intervention, a serious allergic reaction, symptoms of a bowel obstruction, kidney injury from dehydration, or a diagnosis that makes the drug contraindicated (a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2 is an absolute contraindication on both labels, and should have been caught at intake). In those cases, stop as directed and treat the regain question separately: the weight is a problem to solve later with a different tool, and the acute problem comes first.

The 'I just don't feel like myself' stop

A proportion of people stop because they dislike the absence of pleasure in food, the flatness, the social friction of not eating. That is a legitimate reason and no data can argue with it. The relevant information is that these effects are also dose-dependent for many people, and that a maintenance dose often preserves most of the weight effect with less of the flattening. It is worth trying before stopping entirely, with the understanding, set out above, of what stopping entirely tends to bring.

sections.heading: Stopping because you reached your goal: how to think about it
sections.body:
The happiest reason to stop is also the one the evidence treats most harshly, because the people in the withdrawal trials had, by any reasonable definition, reached their goals, and they regained anyway. This section is about how to make the decision with clear eyes rather than about talking anyone out of it.

What "goal" means after a GLP-1

In the trials, weight loss slowed and plateaued at around 60 to 72 weeks at the full dose. That plateau is not the drug "wearing off"; it is the point at which the drug's effect on appetite and the body's adaptations to the new weight balance. If you have reached a plateau at a weight you are happy with, you have reached what the drug can do at that dose, and the plateau is itself the maintenance phase: you are no longer losing, you are holding. The question "should I stop now that I've reached my goal" is therefore better phrased as "should I remove the thing that is currently holding me here."

Three tests before you decide

  • Have you been at the plateau for at least three months? Weight that has been stable for a season on a stable dose is a better foundation than a goal number touched last week.
  • Have you already stepped down? If you are at a full dose, the lower-risk experiment is a maintenance dose first (randomized evidence for tirzepatide 5 mg; uncontrolled for semaglutide). If you hold your weight on less for three to six months, you have learned something about how your body behaves with less drug, and you can decide about stopping from there. If you regain on less, you have learned that too, cheaply.
  • Do you have a restart threshold agreed with your prescriber? Not a vague intention, but a number: for example, if I regain 5% of my body weight, or if my waist returns to a given measurement, I go back on without treating it as a failure. The Cleveland Clinic data are the evidence that people who do this fare best.

A middle path many clinicians now describe

Rather than stop at goal, stay on a maintenance dose for a year, during which you consolidate training, protein and the eating patterns you want to keep, and reassess with twelve months of stable weight behind you. If at that point you want to try coming off, you will do it from a stronger position, with a known maintenance dose to return to. It costs a year of a lower dose at, on this site's verified prices, $41 to $199 a month for compounded semaglutide. For a person who has lost 15% to 20% of their body weight, that is a small insurance premium on a large result.

sections.heading: When you have to stop: pregnancy, surgery, illness and supply
sections.body:
Not every stop is a choice. These are the situations in which the drug must be paused or ended, with what the labels and guidance say and how to handle the regain question when the stop is non-negotiable.

Pregnancy and trying to conceive

Both semaglutide and tirzepatide labels advise against use in pregnancy, because of harm in animal studies and because weight loss offers no benefit in pregnancy and may harm the fetus. The Wegovy prescribing information specifically advises discontinuing at least two months before a planned pregnancy because of the drug's long half-life. Tirzepatide's label additionally warns that it can reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives for four weeks after starting and after each dose increase, which is directly relevant to anyone not planning a pregnancy. If you become pregnant while on either drug, stop and tell your prescriber and obstetric provider; do not taper. The regain that follows is expected and, in pregnancy, beside the point; the plan for afterwards is a conversation for after delivery and, if relevant, after breastfeeding, for which the labels advise caution and limited data.

Surgery and procedures requiring anaesthesia

Because GLP-1s slow stomach emptying, anaesthesia societies have issued guidance on managing them before procedures, concerned with the risk of regurgitating stomach contents under sedation. The guidance has changed since 2023, when holding a weekly dose for a week before elective procedures was recommended, toward more individualized advice in later multi-society statements, and it is your surgical and anaesthesia team's call. Tell every proceduralist, including dentists and endoscopists, that you take a GLP-1 and when your last dose was. A one-week hold is not a stop in any meaningful sense; appetite will not have changed much, and you resume as directed.

Acute illness

Vomiting, diarrhoea or inability to keep fluids down from any cause is a reason to pause and call the prescriber, because dehydration on a GLP-1 can injure the kidneys, and the labels advise it. Restart when you are eating and drinking normally, at the dose the prescriber advises; after more than two or three missed weekly doses, many will restart at a lower dose to avoid the side effects of a full dose on a cleared system.

Lost supply

Shortages that drove 2023 and 2024 have eased, but individual pharmacies and providers still run out, and shipments fail. If you will miss more than one dose, the fix is a switch rather than a stop: another provider, another pharmacy or another form of the same drug, arranged before the gap opens. The shipping windows in the cost section and the provider review pages tell you who can fill fastest. Treat the first missed shipment as the trigger to line up an alternative, not the third.

sections.heading: A 90-day off-ramp: how to stop deliberately if you and your prescriber decide to
sections.body:
If, after everything above, you are going to stop, do it on purpose. The worst version of stopping, and the most common one, is the lapsed refill: the drug runs out, appetite returns three weeks later, the scale starts moving in week six, and by month four a person who meant to "see how it goes" has regained a third of their loss without ever having decided anything. The alternative is a planned descent with measurements, thresholds and an agreed route back. What follows is a structure, not a protocol, since no protocol has been tested; it is built from the trial timelines, the pharmacology and the practices described in the published reviews, and it is for discussion with your prescriber, not for self-administration.

Before day one: set the terms

  • Record a baseline. Weight, waist, a strength measure (grip or how many times you can stand from a chair in 30 seconds), blood pressure, and if your prescriber agrees, fasting glucose or HbA1c and lipids. These are the numbers you will compare against, and the cardiometabolic ones are the ones most people forget.
  • Agree the restart threshold in writing. A specific regain, commonly 3% to 5% of body weight, or a waist measurement, that triggers a return to the last effective dose without a new deliberation. Also agree what the restart looks like: the prescriber may want to restart at a lower dose and step up, so the route back is not instant.
  • Decide between a step-down and a stop. The step-down path (dose by dose, four weeks or more at each) gives information; the direct stop is reasonable if you are already at a low dose or have a reason to clear the drug quickly. Either is safe pharmacologically.
  • Fix the eating structure now, while appetite is still suppressed. Decide what three meals a day look like, with protein in each, and start eating that way on the drug, so that when appetite returns it returns into a pattern rather than a vacuum.
  • Start or intensify resistance training now. If you have not been lifting, the three months before stopping are when it matters most, for the reasons in the muscle section.

Days 1 to 30: the quiet month

Semaglutide takes about five weeks to clear and tirzepatide three to four, so the first month after the last full dose (or at a reduced dose) feels deceptively easy. Appetite is still mostly suppressed, weight is stable and it is tempting to conclude that you are fine. You are not fine yet; you are still partly medicated. Use the month to weigh weekly, keep the meal structure, train, and notice when hunger first changes, which for most people is in the third or fourth week. Write the date down; it marks the real start of the test.

Days 31 to 60: the test

This is when appetite returns toward, and often beyond, its pre-treatment level, as the Sumithran data predict, and when the regain curves in the trials begin to rise. Expect to be hungrier than you remember. Expect portions to feel smaller. The tools are the ones built in advance: protein at every meal, meals at set times rather than grazing, foods with volume and fibre, water before meals, sleep, and continued training. Weigh weekly and track the trend rather than the day. If by day 60 you are within your threshold, continue. If you have crossed it, this is where the agreed restart applies, and the single most useful thing you can do is apply it without renegotiating, because the data on people who wait are not good.

Days 61 to 90: the verdict

By three months the drug has been gone for two of them, and your trajectory is visible. The three outcomes: weight stable within threshold (continue, and recheck the cardiometabolic markers at this point and again at twelve months); weight rising slowly but within threshold (continue with a closer look at what has slipped, usually protein, training frequency or evening eating, and shorten the review interval to two weeks); or threshold crossed (restart as agreed, at the dose and schedule the prescriber set, and regard the three months as a successful experiment that produced an answer). None of these is a failure. The third is the most common, and the people who handle it by restarting promptly are, by the real-world evidence, the ones who keep most of what they lost.

Months 4 to 12

If you are still off treatment at three months, the pooled data say the risk period is far from over; the midpoint of regain in the modelled curves falls around month seven or eight, and the BMJ projection runs the return to baseline to a year and a half or more. Keep weighing weekly through the first year, keep the threshold, and keep training. Review the markers at twelve months. If you reach a year within threshold, you are in the minority the trials could not identify in advance, and the maintenance habits that got you there are the ones to protect.

sections.heading: Restarting: when to go back on, and what it looks like
sections.body:
Restarting after a stop is common, it is not a defeat, and it has its own logistics worth knowing before you need them.

When

The right time to restart is when you cross the threshold you set, not after you have regained everything. There are two reasons. The first is arithmetic: the regain curves are steepest early, so the difference between restarting at a 5% regain and at a 15% regain is months of re-titration and, often, a return to the higher doses. The second is the one the Cleveland Clinic data point to: the people who restarted or switched promptly were the ones whose year looked good on average. Restarting is also the reasonable response when a marker, not the weight, is what moved: a rising HbA1c, a blood pressure that needs its medication back, or the return of sleep apnoea symptoms.

How

After more than a few weeks off, the drug has cleared and the gut has lost its tolerance, so most prescribers restart at the lowest dose and step up, rather than resuming the maintenance dose directly; restarting at a full dose on a cleared system produces the side effects of a first titration all at once. The labels' schedules (four weeks at each step for semaglutide, four weeks for tirzepatide) are the minimums, and the step-up can be faster in someone who tolerated the drug before, at the prescriber's discretion. Expect two to three months to get back to a previous maintenance dose. Expect the appetite effect to return quickly; the weight effect, at a lower restart dose, follows more slowly than the first time only because the dose is lower.

Where

If you restart through the provider you left, check whether your account and prescription are still active; many will resume with a brief check-in. If you restart elsewhere, the new provider runs a fresh intake, and you should bring your previous dose and timeline. If you are restarting because of cost, restart on the plan you can sustain rather than the one you had. The provider comparison and the matching quiz are built for exactly that choice.

sections.heading: What is coming: drugs and trials that will change the maintenance picture
sections.body:
This guide describes the evidence as of October 2026. Several developments in the pipeline bear directly on the stopping question and are worth knowing about, with the caveat that none of them is available and the figures are from trial reports and company announcements rather than approved labels.

Retatrutide

Eli Lilly's triple agonist (GLP-1, GIP and glucagon receptors) reported a mean weight loss of 28.3% at 80 weeks at the 12 mg dose in the phase 3 TRIUMPH-1 trial, with filing expected in the first quarter of 2027 according to the company. Larger losses raise the stakes on regain, and no withdrawal or maintenance data for retatrutide have been published. It is not approved.

CagriSema

Novo Nordisk's combination of cagrilintide (an amylin analogue) with semaglutide was submitted to the FDA on December 18, 2025 with a decision expected in the fourth quarter of 2026. Amylin acts on satiety through a different pathway, and whether the combination behaves differently on withdrawal is unknown. It is not approved as of this writing.

Muscle-preserving combinations

Bimagrumab with semaglutide (BELIEVE) and the registered combination with tirzepatide, covered in the muscle section, would change what the weight lost consists of and therefore, plausibly, what regain looks like. Phase 3 programmes have not reported.

The maintenance and switching trials

The trials that will answer this guide's open questions are registered: tapered versus abrupt discontinuation (NCT07859176), semaglutide taper versus full-dose maintenance (NCT07783854), injectable-to-oral switching for maintenance (NCT07729332), and resistance training during treatment (NCT07457437). Their results, together with the full publication of ATTAIN-MAINTAIN, will be the first real evidence on how to come off rather than whether coming off causes regain. We will update this guide when they report.

What will not change

The biology in the Sumithran and Fothergill studies predates every one of these drugs and will outlast them. Whatever is approved next, the adaptations to weight loss will still be there when the next drug stops, and the frame that the evidence supports, treatment of a chronic condition rather than a course of therapy with an end date, is unlikely to be overturned by a more powerful molecule. It may be softened by cheaper and more convenient ones, which is the trend that the oral GLP-1s and the compounded market already represent.

sections.heading: Frequently asked questions about stopping GLP-1s
sections.body:
How long after stopping Ozempic or Wegovy does the weight come back? Appetite begins returning in the third or fourth week as semaglutide clears (half-life about a week). In the trials, weight began rising within the first month and continued through the year; the pooled regain rate in the January 2026 BMJ meta-analysis was about 0.8 kg a month for semaglutide and tirzepatide, with half of the loss back in roughly seven to eight months in one model and most of it within a year to eighteen months.

Does everyone regain the weight? No. Averages hide a range. In the STEP 1 extension about a third of the loss was kept on average; in the Cleveland Clinic real-world study 45% of people with obesity maintained or kept losing a year after stopping, though many of them had restarted or switched. There is no reliable way to predict in advance who will hold.

Is it better to taper or stop cold turkey? Nobody knows yet. Every published withdrawal trial stopped people abruptly, and there is no randomized comparison of tapering versus stopping as of October 2026; trials are registered. Stopping abruptly is not dangerous. A step-down gives you information about where your appetite and weight start to move.

Can I stay on a lower dose instead of stopping? For tirzepatide, yes, with randomized evidence: in SURMOUNT-MAINTAIN (The Lancet, May 2026), people who stepped down to 5 mg after 60 weeks were 16.6% below baseline a year later, against 21.9% on the full dose and 9.9% on placebo. For semaglutide, the evidence is a small uncontrolled series in which every-other-week dosing held weight in most patients. Discuss the dose, the measurement plan and the threshold for going back up with your prescriber.

Does microdosing work for maintenance? It has not been tested. No trial has studied doses below the labelled starting dose for weight maintenance, professional societies have not endorsed it, and it is usually delivered via compounded vials, for which the FDA has received reports of dosing errors. The tested lower-dose options are labelled doses at labelled or extended intervals.

Why am I hungrier than before I started? Because weight loss itself raises hunger hormones and lowers satiety hormones, and the changes persist for at least a year (Sumithran et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2011). The drug was suppressing that response; stopping unmasks it. It is biology, not a lack of discipline, and it is the reason maintenance needs a plan.

Will my blood sugar and blood pressure go back up? In the STEP 1 extension, blood pressure, HbA1c, lipids and inflammatory markers reverted toward baseline over the year off treatment, and the BMJ meta-analysis projected the same. People with type 2 diabetes should expect glucose to rise within weeks and should have their regimen reviewed before stopping.

How much muscle did I lose, and can I get it back? In the trial sub-studies about a quarter to 40% of the weight lost was lean mass, similar to diet-induced loss, with absolute losses of around 5 to 6 kg. Resistance training and adequate protein limit it during treatment (in the SEMALEAN study lean loss stopped by month seven and strength rose) and determine how much of any regain comes back as muscle rather than fat.

I lost coverage. Do I have to stop? Usually not. The options, in order of cost, are a compounded version of the same drug (verified from $41 a month for semaglutide and $71 for tirzepatide), the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge at $50 a month if you are eligible, manufacturer savings programmes, Foundayo at $149 to $349 self-pay as reported, or brand-name for cash at $1,249 and up. See the cost section.

Can I switch from the injection to a pill to maintain? The evidence is new and company-reported: in ATTAIN-MAINTAIN (topline, December 2025), people switched from Wegovy to daily orforglipron (now Foundayo) held their weight almost exactly over a year and those switched from Zepbound regained about 5 kg, while placebo groups regained around 9 kg within six months. Full publication is pending. The Wegovy pill (oral semaglutide) has no published maintenance-switch trial.

If I restart, will it work again? Re-treatment has not been formally studied after regain, but the pharmacology gives no reason to expect a smaller effect and the rescue arm of SURMOUNT-MAINTAIN worked as intended. Most prescribers restart at the lowest dose and step up over two to three months.

Is there any way to stop without regaining? Not one that has been demonstrated in a trial. What the evidence supports is minimizing regain: a maintenance dose or a switch rather than a full stop, muscle preserved during the loss, structured eating and training built before appetite returns, and a prompt restart at an agreed threshold. The quarter to a third of the loss that the pooled data suggest can be sustained is real, and the habits are what protect it.

sections.heading: How this guide was researched, and where to go next
sections.body:
Every clinical figure in this guide is taken from the peer-reviewed trial report, meta-analysis, label or registered trial linked next to it, with its publication date. Where a figure comes from a press release (ATTAIN-MAINTAIN), a preprint (the 2026 lean-mass analysis) or secondary reporting (the FDA's compounded-product adverse-event tally), we say so in the sentence that carries it and we do not build conclusions on it. Where the evidence does not exist, for tapering protocols, for microdosing, for re-treatment after regain and for semaglutide dose reduction, we say that it does not exist rather than filling the gap with practice. Every provider price is our verified price index, read from each provider's own site most recently on October 16, 2026, and shown with its conditions; manufacturer and programme prices are as reported by the dated sources in the linked guides and are not verified by us. The medical and scientific content is reviewed under the policy on our medical review policy page. We earn commissions from some providers we link to, which affects neither the prices shown nor the facts stated; our how we rank page explains the ranking.

This guide is for information only. It is not medical advice. Whether, when and how to change or stop a GLP-1 medication is a decision for you and a licensed clinician who knows your history, and the registered trials described above may change the evidence after this was written. Compounded medications are not FDA-approved.

Primary sources

  • Wilding et al., STEP 1 trial extension, Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, April 19, 2022.
  • Rubino et al., STEP 4, JAMA, March 23, 2021.
  • Aronne et al., SURMOUNT-4, JAMA, December 11, 2023.
  • Horn et al., SURMOUNT-MAINTAIN, The Lancet, May 12, 2026.
  • West et al., weight regain after stopping weight-management medication, The BMJ, January 7, 2026.
  • Meta-regression of weight regain after discontinuation, eClinicalMedicine, 2026.
  • Gasoyan et al., real-world weight trajectories after discontinuation, Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, March 2026, via the Cleveland Clinic newsroom.
  • Sumithran et al., New England Journal of Medicine, October 27, 2011.
  • Fothergill et al., Obesity, 2016.
  • Look et al., SURMOUNT-1 body composition, Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, 2025; STEP 1 DXA sub-study registry results.
  • SEMALEAN, Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism; BELIEVE, Nature Medicine, 2026.
