Two practical points. First, Medicare's GLP-1 Bridge pilot covers the approved Wegovy, Zepbound and Foundayo products at a flat copay through 2027, as covered in our GLP-1s after 65 guide; a newly approved drug would not automatically join it. Second, new drugs usually take time to win insurance coverage after approval. For most people paying cash, the first year of a new drug is likely to cost more than the approved options do now. Our cheapest GLP-1 page keeps the verified prices current, and the insurance guide explains how to check coverage.

sections.heading: What do the new drugs mean if you are on semaglutide or tirzepatide today?
sections.body:
For most people, very little in the next twelve months, and a set of options worth knowing about after that. The answer depends on where you are now.

You are on semaglutide (Wegovy or compounded) and doing well

Nothing in the pipeline is a reason to change. A drug that works and that you tolerate is the best drug for you. Stopping to wait for something stronger risks regaining weight; our guide to stopping GLP-1s sets out the regain evidence.

You are on semaglutide and have plateaued

The approved options are already here: Wegovy HD for people on 2.4 mg for at least four weeks, or a switch to tirzepatide, which beat a semaglutide-based combination head to head in REDEFINE 4. If CagriSema is approved, it becomes a third option built on the drug you already take. Talk to your prescriber about which fits; our Zepbound vs Wegovy guide covers the switch.

You are on tirzepatide and doing well

You are on the drug that set the current benchmark: 23.6% at 84 weeks in REDEFINE 4, counting everyone randomised. Retatrutide may eventually offer more, and EloraTZP is being developed specifically as a tirzepatide add-on, but neither is available, and both had more people stopping at their top doses in the trials reported so far.

You are on tirzepatide and have plateaued at 15 mg

This is the group with the most to gain from the pipeline and the least available today. Retatrutide is the obvious future candidate, from 2027 at the earliest on Lilly's filing timeline. Until then, a prescriber can review diet, activity, sleep and other medicines, and that review is the useful step while the pipeline matures.

You stopped a GLP-1 because of side effects

Watch the amylin drugs. Petrelintide's phase 2 tolerability and the companies' framing of amylin as gentler are aimed at you. They are phase 2 and early phase 3. In the meantime, the approved pills, and a slower titration on an injection under a prescriber, are worth discussing; our side-effects guide covers what helps.

You dislike injections

Two approved pills exist now, compared in our Foundayo vs Wegovy pill guide. Oral amycretin and aleniglipron are years from approval, and MariTide's monthly injection is still in phase 3.

You are worried about muscle

Bimagrumab is phase 2. Protein and resistance training work now, as our muscle-loss guide explains.

You have fatty liver disease, knee osteoarthritis or sleep apnoea

The pipeline is increasingly built around these conditions. Retatrutide's planned filing includes knee osteoarthritis pain and obstructive sleep apnoea; survodutide's case is the liver. Ask your clinician whether any approved option already has evidence for your condition, and whether a trial is relevant.

Do the new drugs help with keeping weight off?

That is the question the pipeline answers least well, and the one that matters most for anyone already on treatment. Every GLP-1 trial that has stopped the drug has seen weight return; our guide to stopping GLP-1s sets out that evidence. A new drug that produces more weight loss does not change the underlying pattern unless it is easier to stay on, cheaper to stay on, or works as a lower-burden maintenance option.

Switching and maintenance trials.

  • Orforglipron (Foundayo). Lilly's ATTAIN-MAINTAIN trial switched people from Wegovy or Zepbound injections to the daily pill, as covered in our Foundayo guide. It is the only switch-to-maintenance result for an approved drug in this guide, and it was company-reported.
  • MariTide. Amgen is running MARITIME-SWITCH, enrolling adults moving from weekly tirzepatide or semaglutide to MariTide. A monthly or less frequent injection is, in principle, the kind of option that suits long-term maintenance.
  • Long-term extensions. MariTide's MARITIME-1 extension, with an estimated primary completion in late 2027, shows the companies collecting longer follow-up, but an extension is not a maintenance trial in the sense of stepping down or switching after weight loss.

Time's reporting that about 40% of people stop within a year is the real-world limit on every drug in this guide. The amylin drugs' case is that a gentler drug is easier to stay on for years. That case has not yet been tested in a long-term trial. Until it is, the best maintenance plan is the one you and a prescriber can sustain with the approved drugs, at a dose you tolerate, alongside the protein and training that protect muscle.

sections.heading: Should you wait for a new drug or start an approved one now?
sections.body:
Talk to a prescriber, and do not wait without a reason. The approved drugs work now. The new ones may work better, but the earliest of them is a company's plan away from approval, and approval is not the same as coverage, supply or a prescription.

A decision framework

  1. Do you have a weight-related health problem now? High blood pressure, type 2 diabetes or prediabetes, sleep apnoea, fatty liver, joint pain. If yes, the cost of waiting a year or two is measured in your health, and the approved drugs have evidence for several of those conditions. Start the conversation now.
  2. Is the only drug you would accept one that is not approved? If so, ask why. If the reason is side effects, the amylin drugs may suit you later; if it is effect size, tirzepatide and Wegovy HD already produce averages in the high teens to low twenties in their trials; if it is injections, the pills exist.
  3. Is cost the barrier? A new drug will not be cheaper than today's options at launch on any evidence we found. Our cheapest GLP-1 page shows what is available now.
  4. Would you switch later if something better is approved? Usually that is possible. MariTide is being tested in people switching from weekly GLP-1s, and orforglipron's ATTAIN-MAINTAIN trial tested switching from injections. Starting an approved drug now does not lock you out of a future one.
  5. Are you tempted by an online "research" product to get there early? Do not. It is not the trial drug, and the FDA has said so.

Worked example: two people, same pipeline

A 52-year-old with a BMI of 36, prediabetes and knee pain reads that retatrutide reduced knee pain in TRIUMPH-1 and decides to wait. On Lilly's timeline, the earliest US decision falls in 2027 or later, and coverage after that is unknown. Over that time, an approved drug with a trial average in the 15% to 21% range could have been treating both the weight and the blood sugar. Waiting is the expensive choice here, and the person can still ask about retatrutide when it is approved.

A 40-year-old who has been on tirzepatide 15 mg for a year, lost 18%, tolerates it and has stalled reads the same news. There is no approved next step above tirzepatide 15 mg, so for this person the pipeline genuinely matters. The sensible plan is to stay on treatment, work with a prescriber on the plateau, and revisit when retatrutide's label is known. Stopping now would not bring retatrutide any closer.

Our best GLP-1 for weight loss guide compares the approved options, and the provider guide covers how to find a prescriber.

sections.heading: Who is this guide for, and who isn't it for?
sections.body:
This guide is for adults on, or considering, a prescribed weight-loss medication who want to understand what is coming and whether it should change their plans. It is written for US readers, and its approval statements are about the FDA.

It is not for:

  • Anyone looking for a way to get an unapproved drug. We do not describe sources, doses or preparation for retatrutide, cagrilintide or any other pipeline drug, and the only legitimate route is a clinical trial.
  • Anyone planning to stop a current treatment to wait. That is a decision for you and a prescriber, and the regain evidence argues against doing it without a plan.
  • Investors. We report trial results for patients. Company timelines here are quoted to explain access, not to forecast markets.
  • Children and adolescents, pregnant people and anyone with a history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2. The trials in this guide enrolled adults, and the approved labels carry specific restrictions for these groups; a specialist needs to be involved.
  • People outside the US. Approval status differs elsewhere; ecnoglutide, for example, is approved in China and not here.

sections.heading: What don't we know yet about the next-generation drugs?
sections.body:
A great deal, and it is worth being specific, because the headlines suggest more certainty than the evidence supports.

  • Long-term safety. The longest phase 3 trials in this guide ran 80 to 84 weeks. The approved drugs have years of use behind them; the new mechanisms do not. Glucagon activation, GIP blockade and amylin combinations each need long-term data.
  • What dysesthesia is. It appeared with retatrutide and with high-dose semaglutide, more at higher doses. Its cause and whether it matters long term are not established.
  • Cardiovascular outcomes. Semaglutide has outcome data; most pipeline drugs do not yet. Lilly has said TRIUMPH-3's cardiovascular data will be presented later.
  • Head-to-head results. Only one pipeline drug, CagriSema, has reported a phase 3 head-to-head against tirzepatide, and it lost; EloraTZP's phase 2b included a tirzepatide arm, in people with diabetes. Retatrutide, amycretin, MariTide and the amylin drugs have no published head-to-head against the best approved drug.
  • Real-world persistence. Trials keep people on drug with support. Time's reported figure that about 40% stop within a year applies to the current drugs; whether the new ones are easier to stay on is unknown.
  • What happens when they stop. With every GLP-1, weight returns after stopping. There is no reason yet to expect the new drugs to be different, and little data either way.
  • Price and coverage. No company has published a US price for any pipeline drug in the sources we found.
  • Whether timelines hold. Retatrutide's filing has already moved once. FDA decisions can bring requests for more data. Company dates in this guide are plans.
  • Which estimand to believe. Companies lead with on-treatment figures; journals lead with everyone-randomised figures. Both are honest answers to different questions. We give both where we have them, and the comparison tables use like-for-like figures where possible.

We will update this guide as results are published and decisions are made.

sections.heading: Questions to ask your clinician about the new weight-loss drugs
sections.body:
Take this list to your next appointment. A good prescriber will be glad you asked.

  1. Given my health and my results so far, is there an approved option I should consider now, such as a dose change, Wegovy HD, a switch to tirzepatide or a pill?
  2. If CagriSema or retatrutide is approved, would I be a likely candidate, and what would we need to see on the label first?
  3. What would switching involve: a new titration, a gap in treatment, a change in side effects?
  4. Is there a clinical trial I might be eligible for, and would joining mean stopping my current drug or risking a placebo arm?
  5. Are my side effects a reason to look at a different mechanism later, such as an amylin drug, or can they be managed now?
  6. Do I have a condition, such as fatty liver, sleep apnoea or knee osteoarthritis, where a pipeline drug has specific data, and is there an approved option with evidence for it?
  7. How should we protect muscle on my current treatment?
  8. If I see a "new drug" offered online, how do I tell whether it is legitimate? (The answer for any unapproved drug is that it is not.)
  9. What will my insurance cover now, and how do I find out whether it will cover a new drug after approval?
  10. When should we review my plan again, and what result would make us change it?

sections.heading: Final verdict and next steps
sections.body:
The next generation of weight-loss drugs is real and close, and it is not here yet for new mechanisms. Retatrutide is the strongest result in phase 3, 25.0% at 80 weeks counting everyone randomised, with a filing Lilly plans for early 2027 and a new skin-sensation side effect to understand. CagriSema is the only new mechanism under FDA review, with a decision the company expects in late 2026, but it lost to tirzepatide head to head. Amylin is the mechanism to watch for tolerability, and the drugs built on it range from early phase 3 to phase 2. MariTide aims at fewer injections, survodutide at the liver, bimagrumab at muscle.

Meanwhile, the approved options improved: two GLP-1 pills and a 7.2 mg semaglutide dose arrived between December 2025 and April 2026, joining tirzepatide, which remains the benchmark every pipeline drug is measured against. None of the pipeline drugs can be legally compounded, and online "research" versions are not the trial drugs.

  1. If you are not on treatment and have a weight-related condition: talk to a prescriber now about the approved drugs. Start with our best GLP-1 guide and the provider guide.
  2. If you are on treatment and doing well: stay on it. Revisit when a new drug's label is known.
  3. If you have plateaued: ask about Wegovy HD or tirzepatide, compared in our tirzepatide vs semaglutide guide.
  4. If you want a pill: read Foundayo vs Wegovy pill and pills vs injections.
  5. If cost is the barrier: the cheapest GLP-1 page lists verified prices; the compounded vs brand-name guide explains the trade-offs.
  6. If you are following retatrutide: our retatrutide page tracks its status.

This article is general information, not medical advice. Investigational drugs are not approved for any use outside clinical trials. Do not start, stop or change a prescribed medicine without a licensed clinician who knows your history.

articles.title: GLP-1 Coverage in 2027: Employers Dropping Wegovy, Zepbound
articles.description: Survey data on employers dropping Wegovy and Zepbound for weight loss in 2027, an open-enrollment checklist, appeals, Medicare's $50 Bridge and cash costs.
articles.author: Treatments Hub Research Team
keyTakeaways: Employer coverage of GLP-1s for weight loss fell in WTW's 2026 survey for the first time in three years, from 57% to 53% of employers with 100 or more workers, and 30% of those still covering are considering dropping it. Business Group on Health reports large-employer coverage down from 72% in 2025 to 60% in 2026, with about 14% having dropped or planning to drop it in 2027.

Demand is moving the other way: Gallup found 11% of US adults were taking a GLP-1 for weight loss in 2026, up from 3% in 2024. Cost is the stated reason for cuts, cited by 91% of employers that have dropped or are weighing dropping coverage in the WTW survey.

Open enrollment is the moment to check, not January. Search your 2027 formulary for Wegovy and Zepbound, read the prior-authorization and BMI rules, ask whether coverage continues for heart disease, sleep apnea or liver indications, and compare plans if you have a choice. Diabetes coverage is usually untouched.

If coverage goes, routes remain at very different prices: Medicare's GLP-1 Bridge at $50 a month through December 31, 2027 if you qualify, brand-name cash at $1,149-$1,799 a month at the providers we track, the Wegovy pill at ro from $149 then $299 plus membership, or compounded semaglutide from $41 a month and tirzepatide from $71 at verified sale prices, which are not FDA-approved products.

sections.heading: Is your employer dropping GLP-1 coverage for weight loss in 2027?
sections.body:
The short answer

Possibly, and fewer employers are covering these drugs each year. WTW's 2026 survey found the share of employers covering GLP-1s for weight loss fell from 57% to 53%, the first decline in three years, and 30% of those still covering are considering dropping it. Business Group on Health reports 14% of large employers have dropped or plan to drop coverage in 2027. The only reliable answer for you is your own 2027 formulary, which you can check now, during open enrollment, before your choices lock. Diabetes coverage usually continues.

For three years the direction of travel for employer coverage of Wegovy and Zepbound was up. In 2026 it turned. The surveys published between June and October 2026, from WTW, Mercer, Business Group on Health, KFF and the International Foundation of Employee Benefit Plans, all point the same way: coverage for weight loss is flat at best and falling at many large employers, and a sizeable minority of those still paying are weighing an exit for 2027. Bloomberg reported on October 30, 2026 that fewer US employees will have these drugs covered next year; CNBC's October 27 report described plans dropping coverage as premiums rise.

This guide is the data-led version of that story, written for the weeks when it matters. Most employer open-enrollment windows run in October and November, Medicare's runs to December 7, and the HealthCare.gov window opened on November 1. Decisions made in those windows decide what you pay for a GLP-1 in 2027. We set out what each survey actually measured, which public plans have already cut coverage, what a "dropped" benefit looks like in plan documents, how to check yours, how appeals work, and what every remaining route costs over a year at prices we have verified.

If you have already received a letter saying your coverage has ended, our shorter guide to what to do when you lose coverage for Zepbound or Wegovy covers the immediate options. This page is about 2027: reading the numbers, checking the plan you are about to choose, and planning a year rather than a month.

Two rules apply throughout. First, survey figures are for the employers each survey sampled, which differ in size and definition, so we show them side by side and never average them. Second, nothing here is a reason to change or stop a prescribed medicine on your own. Coverage decides how you pay; a licensed clinician decides what you take.

sections.heading: The 2026-2027 coverage numbers at a glance
sections.body:
Seven sources, each with its own population. Read across a row, not down a column: a 53% figure for employers with 100 or more workers and an 18% figure for firms with 200 or more workers are not in conflict, because the surveys ask different questions of different samples. KFF, for example, asks whether a firm's largest plan covers GLP-1s used primarily for weight loss, across firms of all industries; the benefits consultancies survey their own client and member bases, which skew toward larger and more generous employers.

StatisticFigureSource and populationDate

How to read the WTW 30% and 16% figures

They describe the same respondents with different denominators. WTW reports that 16% of all employers in its sample cover GLP-1s for weight loss now but are considering removing them, up from 9% a year earlier. Since 53% cover at all, 16 divided by 53 is about 30%, which is the "30% of those still covering" figure in the WTW release and in Bloomberg's report. Neither figure says 30% of employers will drop coverage in 2027; "considering" is a survey answer, not a decision.

Why the Business Group on Health figures look high

Business Group on Health surveys its own members, who are among the largest employers in the country, so its coverage rate starts far above KFF's. The trend is what matters: a drop from 72% to 60% in a year among the employers most likely to cover these drugs. A separate Business Group on Health survey, released June 10, 2026 from 105 member employers surveyed in February and March, put coverage for weight management at 67%, with 72% of those covering saying they were likely to continue in 2027 and 10% saying they likely would not. The two surveys used different samples and dates, so the 60% and 67% figures should not be read as a contradiction.

sections.heading: Why are employers dropping Wegovy and Zepbound coverage?
sections.body:
Cost, by their own account, and the arithmetic is not mysterious. Every additional person who starts a GLP-1 adds a recurring monthly claim that, on current evidence, continues for as long as the weight loss is meant to last. Use has climbed quickly: Gallup's 11% current-use figure for US adults in 2026 compares with 3% in 2024 (Gallup). An employer that covered the drugs in 2023 for a small group of eligible employees may now be paying for several times as many.

What the employer surveys say about spending

  • Cost is the stated reason. In WTW's 2026 survey, 91% of employers that have dropped coverage or are weighing it cited cost (WTW).
  • GLP-1s are a measurable slice of total claims. Among employers covering weight loss, GLP-1s averaged 11.4% of total annual claims in 2026, up from 6.9% in 2023, according to the IFEBP survey.
  • The spending impact is felt most at the largest firms. Among KFF respondents that cover the drugs for weight loss, 29% said the coverage had a significant impact on prescription drug spending and 27% a moderate impact (KFF).
  • Most large employers link GLP-1s to rising costs. Nearly eight in ten employers in Business Group on Health's June 2026 survey said GLP-1s are driving an increase in their health care costs (Business Group on Health).
  • The whole benefit is getting more expensive. Mercer's preliminary 2026 survey projects an 8.2% rise in health benefit cost per employee in 2027, the largest increase since 2003, with growing GLP-1 use for weight management accounting for roughly one percentage point of it (Mercer; Fierce Healthcare). Business Group on Health's members expect a median cost trend of 9.2% for 2027 before plan changes (Business Group on Health).

Why lower list prices have not stopped the cuts

Novo Nordisk has announced a lower US list price for Wegovy and Ozempic taking effect on January 1, 2027. It is reasonable to ask why that does not rescue coverage. Mercer's analysis is that the manufacturer is likely to offset a lower list price with smaller rebates, so what an employer actually pays may change less than the headline suggests, and that rebates may still be limited in 2027 for plans that cover GLP-1s only for obesity-related use (Mercer). Mercer also notes that the list-price change does not affect the manufacturers' direct-to-consumer self-pay prices, which are set separately. For an employee, the practical point is that a lower list price is not a promise of renewed coverage.

Why weight loss is cut and diabetes is not

Almost every cut in 2026 targets the weight-management indication. Type 2 diabetes is a long-established covered condition with a clear treatment pathway, and dropping its medicines would be a different decision. The IFEBP survey's 60% "diabetes only" figure shows how common that split already is (IFEBP). Walmart illustrates the pattern in reverse: for 2027 it will offer Ozempic and Mounjaro at no charge to employees with type 2 diabetes under most of its medical plans, after a new prior authorisation, while GLP-1s for weight loss remain outside the benefit (CNBC, October 13, 2026).

sections.heading: Which employers and public plans have already cut GLP-1 weight-loss coverage?
sections.body:
Private employers rarely announce benefit cuts, so the public record is dominated by state employee plans and Medicaid programmes, whose decisions are made in public meetings. They are worth knowing because they show how a cut is usually structured: an end date months ahead, a carve-out for diabetes, sometimes an exception for other conditions, and a transition period for people already on treatment.

State employee plans

  • Massachusetts. The Group Insurance Commission, which covers state employees and retirees, voted 10-7 in February 2026 to end coverage of GLP-1 drugs for weight loss for its non-Medicare plans from July 1, 2026 (WGBH, February 26, 2026). About 22,000 members were taking the drugs for weight loss, according to commission staff as reported by Becker's. The commission's June 2026 update says some members may still qualify through other medical conditions; Becker's reports these as cardiovascular disease, sleep apnea and the liver condition MASH.
  • North Carolina. The State Health Plan's board voted 4-3 to stop covering GLP-1s for weight loss from April 1, 2024 (WFAE, January 2024). In 2026 the state treasurer said the expected budget would not restore that coverage (WRAL).
  • Ohio. The state ended weight-loss GLP-1 coverage for state employees on July 1, 2025, citing escalating costs despite cost-containment measures; coverage for diabetes continued (CW Columbus).

Medicaid

KFF Health News reported in December 2025 that California, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania and South Carolina would stop covering GLP-1 prescriptions for obesity in adults on January 1, 2026, citing budget strain (KFF Health News via Medical Xpress). By April 2026, Stateline reported that more states were considering the same step. Medicaid rules differ by state and change with each budget, so anyone covered by Medicaid should check with their state programme directly.

Private employers

The surveys above are the best evidence for private employers, and they say most changes for 2027 are cuts or restrictions rather than additions. Business Group on Health's vice president was quoted by Reuters as saying not a single employer in its survey would add GLP-1 coverage for weight management in 2027 (Reuters via U.S. News). Among employers that do not cover the drugs, the IFEBP found 9% considering adding coverage, and 19% said they would not cover weight-loss indications even though they had covered them before (IFEBP).

The public examples share one feature worth copying into your own planning: each gave members months of notice. If your employer is dropping coverage for 2027, the notice is most likely in this year's open-enrollment materials, which is why the next sections are about reading them now.

sections.heading: What does a dropped or tightened benefit look like in a 2027 plan?
sections.body:
"Dropping coverage" can mean several different things in plan documents, and they have different consequences for you. The first job during open enrollment is to work out which one you are facing.

What the plan doesHow it appears in plan materialsWhat it means for you
Full exclusion for weight management"Weight loss drugs" or "anti-obesity medications" listed under exclusions; Wegovy and Zepbound absent from the formulary or marked not coveredNo appeal reverses a plan-design exclusion. Plan for another route, unless another covered indication applies to you
Coverage with tighter prior authorisationDrug listed with "PA" and new criteria: a higher BMI threshold, documented conditions, a minimum time on a programmeStill covered if you meet the criteria; your prescriber files the paperwork. Re-authorisation may be required each year
Required lifestyle or care programmeCoverage "through" a named digital or clinical weight-management programmeYou must enrol and stay engaged. Massachusetts' plan, for example, required members to join a programme to keep coverage before the cut (Mass.gov)
Step therapy"ST" on the formulary; a requirement to try another drug or approach firstA documented trial of the first-step option may be required before the GLP-1 is approved
Prescriber limitsOnly certain specialists or an in-network programme may prescribeA telehealth or primary care prescription may not satisfy the plan
One preferred drugOnly one of Wegovy or Zepbound listed as preferredSwitching to the preferred drug may keep you covered; a clinician decides whether that is appropriate
Higher cost shareDrug moves to a higher tier or coinsurance rather than a flat copayStill covered, but your monthly cost can rise sharply until the deductible and out-of-pocket maximum are met

Tightening is more common than outright removal. Mercer found 27% of large employers tightened utilisation controls in 2026 or plan to in 2027 (Mercer), and Business Group on Health has described employers tying eligibility to clinical criteria, requiring lifestyle programmes and limiting who can prescribe as alternatives to a full cut (Business Group on Health). KFF reports that the large firms that do cover the drugs for weight loss often attach restrictions (KFF).

The labelled criteria plans build on

Prior-authorisation criteria usually start from the FDA labels. Wegovy is approved for chronic weight management in adults with a BMI of 30 or more, or 27 or more with at least one weight-related condition (Wegovy prescribing information, FDA), and Zepbound's approval for chronic weight management uses the same thresholds (FDA, November 2023). Many plans add their own requirements on top, such as documented attempts at diet and exercise or a minimum weight loss at the first renewal to continue coverage. Your plan's criteria document, not the label, is what the reviewer applies.

Other indications can keep a drug covered

Wegovy and Zepbound are no longer approved for weight management alone. The FDA approved Wegovy in March 2024 to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death, heart attack and stroke in adults with established cardiovascular disease and either obesity or overweight (FDA), and granted it accelerated approval in August 2025 for adults with noncirrhotic MASH with moderate to advanced liver fibrosis (Managed Healthcare Executive). Zepbound was approved in December 2024 for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity (FDA). A plan that excludes "weight loss" may still cover these uses, as the Massachusetts example shows. Whether one applies to you is a clinical question with a documented diagnosis behind it, not a box to tick; ask your clinician, and ask the plan how it treats each indication.

sections.heading: How do you check your 2027 plan during open enrollment?
sections.body:
Plan documents for the coming year are usually published at the start of open enrollment, and the formulary is the document that answers the question. It takes about half an hour to work through the steps below, and doing so before your window closes is the difference between choosing a plan and finding out in January.

StepWhat to look forWhere to find itDone
1. Find the 2027 formulary, not 2026The drug list dated for the new plan year; employers often change PBM or tier rules on January 1Benefits portal, PBM website, or the open-enrollment packet☐
2. Search for each drug by nameWegovy (injection and pill), Zepbound (pen, vial and KwikPen), and any GLP-1 you take nowFormulary PDF or online drug lookup☐
3. Read the codes next to itPA (prior authorisation), ST (step therapy), QL (quantity limit), tier or coinsuranceFormulary key, usually on the first pages☐
4. Read the exclusions list"Weight loss drugs", "anti-obesity medications" or "drugs for cosmetic or weight loss purposes"Summary Plan Description or Evidence of Coverage☐
5. Get the PA criteria in writingBMI threshold, required conditions, programme enrolment, renewal requirements (such as a minimum weight loss)Call the PBM number on your card and ask for the criteria document☐
6. Ask about other indicationsWhether coverage continues for cardiovascular risk reduction, sleep apnea or MASH, and for diabetesPBM or HR benefits team☐
7. Ask about current usersAny transition period or grandfathering for people already on treatmentHR benefits team; plan change notice☐
8. Price the covered routeDeductible, coinsurance and out-of-pocket maximum applied to a brand GLP-1 for 12 monthsSummary of Benefits and Coverage; PBM cost estimator☐
9. Compare every plan you can chooseDifferent plans from the same employer can carry different drug rules; a spouse's or partner's plan may differ againEach plan's formulary and SPD☐
10. Decide your HSA or FSA amountIf you may pay cash in 2027, the amount you set aside now is the pre-tax money availableOpen-enrollment election form☐
11. Ask about direct-to-employer programmesWhether your employer contributes to a manufacturer-direct programme outside the planHR benefits team☐
12. Save the evidenceScreenshots or PDFs of the 2027 formulary entry and criteria, datedYour own files☐

Questions to put to the benefits team

  1. Is Wegovy or Zepbound covered for chronic weight management in each 2027 plan option, and on what tier?
  2. What are the 2027 prior-authorisation criteria, and do they differ from 2026?
  3. If I am covered today, will my current authorisation carry over, and until when?
  4. Are Wegovy and Zepbound covered for cardiovascular risk reduction, obstructive sleep apnea or MASH if weight management is excluded?
  5. Does the plan require enrolment in a weight-management programme, and which one?
  6. Does the company offer or contribute to a direct-to-employer GLP-1 programme outside the plan?

Medicare and marketplace windows

The same method applies outside employer plans. Medicare's Open Enrollment runs from October 15 to December 7, and changes take effect on January 1 (Medicare.gov). The HealthCare.gov open-enrollment period for 2027 coverage opened on November 1, 2026 (NPR, November 1, 2026); check your state exchange for its deadline and for each plan's formulary before you choose. Our guide to GLP-1s with insurance explains formularies and prior authorisation in more detail.

sections.heading: Should you switch plans to keep GLP-1 coverage?
sections.body:
Sometimes, and the only way to know is to run the numbers for a full year. Three situations come up repeatedly.

Your employer offers several plans with different drug rules

Large employers often offer two or three plan designs, and the drug benefit can differ between them, particularly when one plan is administered by a different carrier or PBM. If one option still covers Wegovy or Zepbound for weight management and another does not, compare the annual premium difference with what you would otherwise pay in cash. A plan that costs more in premiums but covers a brand GLP-1 can come out ahead, because the cash price of a brand pen at the providers we track runs to four figures a month (see the cost table below). The reverse is also possible: a high-deductible plan that covers the drug may still leave you paying the full price until the deductible is met.

A spouse or partner has access to a different plan

Family coverage decisions are rarely made on one drug, and they should not be. But if a partner's employer still covers GLP-1s for weight loss and the rest of the comparison is close, it is a legitimate tie-breaker. Check that plan's 2027 formulary and criteria, not its 2026 version, and confirm that dependants are treated the same as employees for the drug benefit.

You are choosing a Medicare or marketplace plan

For Medicare, the GLP-1 Bridge operates outside the regular Part D benefit, so plan choice matters less for the Bridge drugs than it would for a normal Part D drug; you still need Part D coverage, and the next section covers what we could verify. For marketplace plans, read each plan's formulary for the drug by name.

When switching is not worth it

  • When the plan that covers the drug requires criteria you do not meet. Coverage you cannot use is not coverage.
  • When the premium difference is larger than the cost of an alternative route you would accept.
  • When other medical needs, doctors or hospitals point clearly to a different plan.

A plan decision lasts a year. Our GLP-1 cost calculator totals the verified cash prices so you can put a number on the alternative before you compare premiums.

sections.heading: Can you appeal if your plan stops covering Wegovy or Zepbound?
sections.body:
It depends on why the drug is not being paid for. An appeal is a request to reverse a decision made under the plan's rules. It is a strong tool against a prior-authorisation denial and a weak one against a rule the plan has chosen to write.

Denial versus exclusion

  • Prior-authorisation denial. The drug is covered, but the reviewer decided you did not meet the criteria. This is the case where appeals succeed, usually with better documentation: BMI measurements with dates, the weight-related conditions on record, the programme you completed, and a letter from your prescriber explaining medical necessity.
  • Plan exclusion. The 2027 plan does not cover drugs for weight management at all. An internal appeal will usually confirm the exclusion. The exception is when you have another indication the plan does cover, in which case the request is for coverage under that indication, not an appeal of the exclusion.

The two stages

Federal rules give most plan members two levels of review. An internal appeal asks the plan to reconsider; you generally have at least 180 days from the written denial to file one (CMS). An external review sends the decision to an independent reviewer, so the plan no longer has the final say. HealthCare.gov says external review is available for denials that involve medical judgment, and that you generally have four months after the plan's notice or final determination to request it (HealthCare.gov). Because external review is about medical judgment, it rarely helps against a plain benefit exclusion. Your denial letter states your plan's exact deadlines and process; follow those. HealthCare.gov's appeals page also points to state consumer assistance programmes that help people file.

Making an appeal stronger

  1. Ask the plan for the specific criteria the reviewer applied and the reason for denial in writing.
  2. Ask your prescriber to address each criterion directly, with dated records rather than a general statement.
  3. If you have a covered condition such as established cardiovascular disease, sleep apnea or MASH, make sure the request and the diagnosis code reflect it, when your clinician agrees it applies.
  4. Ask for an expedited review if a delay would seriously harm your health; urgent cases can move faster.
  5. Keep copies of everything and note each call: date, name, reference number.

An appeal can take weeks. If you are mid-treatment, talk to your prescriber early about how to avoid a gap, and do not ration or stretch doses to make a supply last. That is a clinical decision, and the labels do not support it.

sections.heading: What does Medicare's $50 GLP-1 Bridge mean for 2027?
sections.body:
For people on Medicare, 2027 looks better than it does for many employees. Since July 1, 2026, the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge has let eligible beneficiaries get covered obesity drugs for a flat $50 copay a month, and the programme runs through December 31, 2027 (CMS; CMS Bridge page). The drugs named in reporting on the programme are the Wegovy pill and injection, the Zepbound KwikPen and Foundayo, and the $50 does not rise as the dose does (NPR via St. Louis Public Radio; NPR via WLRN).

Why the Bridge runs through 2027

The Bridge was meant to lead into a longer-term arrangement called the BALANCE model. In April 2026, CMS said the Part D portion of BALANCE would not go ahead in 2027 because not enough Part D plans agreed to take part, and extended the Bridge instead (American Hospital Association, April 22, 2026). Because the Bridge sits outside the Part D benefit, it does not depend on your plan sponsor opting in. KFF has noted that it is uncertain how beneficiaries will keep coverage of these drugs for obesity after the Bridge ends at the end of 2027 (KFF).

Who qualifies

Eligibility runs through clinical criteria and an approval step. We have not seen the full eligibility rules in a form we can verify, so we will not summarise them; CMS's page and your Part D plan are the right sources. Our guide to GLP-1s after 65 covers the questions to ask. Medicare does not cover compounded GLP-1s under the Bridge or anywhere else.

What to do in this Open Enrollment

  • Keep or choose Part D coverage (a stand-alone drug plan or a Medicare Advantage plan with drug coverage), since the Bridge is for Part D enrollees; confirm this with your plan.
  • Ask your plan whether you are eligible for the GLP-1 Bridge and what documentation the approval needs from your prescriber.
  • If you take a GLP-1 for diabetes, it is covered under Part D's normal rules, not the Bridge; check its tier in the 2027 formulary.
  • Make Open Enrollment changes by December 7 for a January 1 start (Medicare.gov).

Retirees on employer or state retiree plans should check both sets of rules. Massachusetts, for example, treated Medicare and non-Medicare members differently in its 2026 change (WGBH).

sections.heading: What are direct-to-employer GLP-1 programmes, and can they replace coverage?
sections.body:
A new middle route appeared in 2026. Instead of covering a GLP-1 through the insurance plan, some employers contribute to its cost through a manufacturer-direct channel outside the plan. Both manufacturers have built one.

Lilly Employer Connect

Eli Lilly launched a direct-to-employer programme for Zepbound in March 2026. Employers buy the Zepbound KwikPen at a flat monthly price across doses and decide how to split the cost with employees, through third-party administrators that at launch included GoodRx, Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company and Teladoc Health (CNBC, March 5, 2026). What an employee pays depends on the share the employer chooses to cover.

Novo Nordisk and Andel

On October 28, 2026, the direct-to-employer marketplace Andel announced a collaboration with Novo Nordisk to bring the Wegovy injection and Wegovy pill to employers. The company says employers contribute an amount of their choosing, members get manufacturer-direct pricing, and Andel handles prescription verification through delivery (Andel press release). AJMC described it as a workaround for employers pulling back on coverage. These are company descriptions; we have not seen independent data on what employees pay.

What to ask

  • Does my employer offer or contribute to one of these programmes in 2027, and how much does it contribute per month?
  • What will I pay at each dose, and does that change during the year?
  • Who prescribes, and can my current prescriber continue?
  • Can I pay my share with HSA or FSA money?

The IFEBP found 27% of employers already encourage employees to obtain GLP-1s through a direct-to-consumer platform (IFEBP). Whether that is a helpful alternative or a cost shift depends on the contribution. An employer that pays a meaningful share through a direct programme may leave you better off than a plan with a high deductible; one that only points you to a website has not replaced coverage.

sections.heading: Every route if your plan drops coverage
sections.body:
When the formulary says no, six routes remain. They differ by an order of magnitude in price and also in what you are buying, so the cost basis and the caveats belong in the same row. Prices below are the providers' and manufacturers' published figures as they appear on this site; provider rows come from our verified price index.

RouteProductCost basisMain caveats

Direct-to-employer programmeZepbound KwikPen (Lilly Employer Connect) or Wegovy (Andel with Novo Nordisk)Depends on your employer's contribution; we have not verified employee pricesOnly if your employer takes part
Manufacturer savings offer with commercial coverageBrand pills and pensReported as low as $25 a month for the Wegovy pill where your plan covers it; Foundayo $25 with commercial insurance (Scientific American)Eligibility rules apply; government-plan members excluded; we have not verified current Zepbound and Wegovy pen card terms
Brand-name for cashWegovy, Zepbound, Ozempic; Wegovy pill; FoundayoPens $1,149-$1,799 a month at providers we track; ro's Wegovy pill $149 first month, then $299, plus membership; Foundayo $149-$349 self-pay by dose (reported)The FDA-approved product with no change; the most expensive route
Compounded semaglutide or tirzepatidePharmacy-prepared, same active ingredientSemaglutide from $41 a month (12-month plan, sale) and tirzepatide from $71 (sale) at verified pricesNot FDA-approved, no trials of its own, never covered by insurance or Medicare; ask which pharmacy fills it

Brand-name cash, in detail

At our last verification, altRx lists Zepbound at $1,249 a month, Wegovy at $1,579 and Ozempic at $1,149; welludr lists Zepbound at $1,599 and Ozempic at $1,399; and Sprout lists Wegovy at $1,799. ro sells the Zepbound KwikPen from $299 for the first month, then $399-$449 a month, plus its membership of $39 for the first month and then $74-$149 a month, prices verified in August 2026. Because ro bills the medication separately, a plan that still covers the drug can pay its share. The full ladder is in what Zepbound costs online.

The pills

The two FDA-approved GLP-1 pills sit between the pens and compounded injections at cash prices. ro sells the Wegovy pill at $149 for the first month and $299 a month after, plus the same membership; Novo Nordisk's direct-pay tiers are reported by third-party trackers in the same $149-$299 range, which we have not verified. Eli Lilly's Foundayo lists $149 to $349 a month self-pay by dose through LillyDirect, as reported by Scientific American. Details are in the Wegovy pill price guide.

Manufacturer direct pens and vials

Both manufacturers also sell their injectable weight-loss drugs direct to self-paying patients: Lilly through LillyDirect, including Zepbound in single-dose vials, and Novo Nordisk through its NovoCare Pharmacy. We have not published verified prices for those injectable self-pay offers, so we do not quote them here; check the manufacturer's page for your dose and get the price for the dose you will stay on, not only the first fill.

Compounded

At verified published prices, compounded semaglutide runs from $41 a month at welludr (12-month plan, pre-Black Friday sale) and $49 at embody (month to month, sale) up to $199, and compounded tirzepatide from $71 (welludr, sale) and $99 (embody, sale) up to $299. The trade-offs are covered below and in compounded vs brand-name.

sections.body:
Monthly prices hide the number that matters for a plan decision, which is the annual total. The table below multiplies each verified monthly figure by twelve, or adds a first month and eleven later months where the price steps up, and states the condition attached to each price. It is a price comparison, not a recommendation: the routes are not equivalent products, and the cheapest row is not the right one for everyone.

How to use the table

  • Sale prices may not last the year. The welludr and embody figures are pre-Black Friday sale prices with no end date stated. Where a regular price is published, we show the annual total at that price as well, so you can budget for the worse case. Our Black Friday GLP-1 deals page tracks the windows as providers publish them.
  • Dose changes matter on some routes and not others. Several compounded prices are flat at every dose, which keeps the total predictable. The pills and ro's pens step up after the first month, and Foundayo's reported price rises with the dose.
  • Insurance totals are personal. If your plan still covers the drug, your annual cost is your copays or coinsurance until the out-of-pocket maximum, which only your plan's documents can give you. Price that number and set it against the rows above.
  • Premiums are part of the comparison. If choosing a plan that covers the drug costs more in premiums, add the difference to that route's total before you compare.

A worked example

Take an employee whose 2026 plan covered Zepbound and whose 2027 plan excludes it. Staying on brand-name tirzepatide for cash costs $14,988 over 2027 at altRx's published price. ro's KwikPen route costs $5,541 to $6,916 with membership. Compounded tirzepatide costs $852 at welludr's sale price, or $1,188 at embody if its sale price holds. The gap between the brand cash route and the cheapest compounded route is $14,136 a year ($14,988 minus $852). That gap is the price of staying on the FDA-approved product, and only the employee, with a clinician, can decide whether it is worth paying. Our cost calculator runs the same arithmetic for any provider and dose.

sections.heading: Can you use an HSA or FSA to pay for a GLP-1 in 2027?
sections.body:
Usually, for a prescribed medicine used to treat a diagnosed condition. The IRS treats the cost of a weight-loss programme as a medical expense only when it treats a specific disease diagnosed by a physician, such as obesity, diabetes, hypertension or heart disease; a programme for general health or appearance does not qualify (IRS, March 2023). Prescription medicines for a diagnosed condition are generally qualified expenses. CNBC's October 2026 report lists using FSA or HSA money for medically necessary GLP-1s among the options for workers losing coverage.

Why it matters during open enrollment

If you expect to pay cash for some or all of 2027, the amount you elect for a health FSA, or plan to contribute to an HSA, is set or planned now. Pre-tax money reduces the effective cost of any route in the year-cost table by your marginal tax rate. Ask your benefits team about your FSA's rules for unused balances before you elect, because over-electing can cost you money.

What to check

  • Whether your administrator accepts the expense. Some administrators ask for a letter of medical necessity for weight-related prescriptions. Ask before you rely on the card.
  • Whether the provider accepts the card. In our price index, Medvi lists HSA/FSA payment and SHED describes its plans as HSA/FSA approved. Other providers may accept cards too; check at checkout.
  • Bundled fees. A telehealth price that bundles the clinician visit, medication and shipping is easier to document than a membership fee alone. Keep itemised receipts.
  • HSA eligibility. You can contribute to an HSA only with a qualifying high-deductible health plan, so the plan you choose this month decides whether an HSA is available.

This is general information about how the rules are framed, not tax advice. Your plan administrator and, for complex situations, a tax professional decide what qualifies for you.

sections.heading: Is compounded semaglutide or tirzepatide a safe substitute for lost coverage?
sections.body:
It is the route most people who lose coverage consider, because the prices are a small fraction of brand cash prices. It is a different kind of product, and that should be understood before the price is.

What a compounded GLP-1 is

A compounded GLP-1 contains the same active ingredient as the brand drug but is prepared by a pharmacy for an individual prescription rather than manufactured as an FDA-approved product. The FDA does not review compounded drugs for safety, effectiveness or quality before they are sold, and it has set out its concerns about unapproved GLP-1 products used for weight loss (FDA). In 2026 the agency sent warning letters to telehealth companies objecting to marketing that described compounded products as generic versions of the brand drugs or as coming from an "FDA-approved pharmacy" (Mondaq). Compounded products have no trials of their own, and no insurer or Medicare programme pays for them.

What a legitimate route looks like

  • A licensed clinician reviews your history and decides whether to prescribe, and at what dose. No guaranteed approval.
  • The provider names the pharmacy that fills the prescription and its state licence, which you can check on the state board's website. Our guide to 503A and 503B pharmacies explains the difference.
  • The vial carries a beyond-use date and arrives cold-packed.
  • The price is published, with the plan length and any promotion stated.

The providers in our index

The providers in our verified price index each have genuine strengths for someone leaving a covered plan. welludr has the lowest ongoing price, flat at every dose, on a 12-month plan. embody is the cheapest with no commitment and ships in one to two days. altRx keeps one price at every dose, which makes the annual total predictable as the dose rises. Medvi includes clinician visits, a dietitian and coaching in its all-inclusive price, and SHED includes coaching with a money-back guarantee tied to results. A person leaving a covered brand drug should tell the new prescriber their current drug, dose and date of last injection; whether to continue at a similar dose or step down is the clinician's decision.

What not to do

Losing coverage is not a reason to leave the licensed system. "Research peptides" and vials sold without a prescription are not compounded medicines, carry no pharmacy accountability, and are outside anything a clinician can supervise.

sections.heading: Who this guide is for, and who it isn't for
sections.body:
This guide is for:

  • Employees choosing a 2027 plan who take, or plan to start, Wegovy or Zepbound for weight management.
  • People who have been told their employer, state plan or Medicaid programme is ending coverage and want to plan a year ahead.
  • Medicare beneficiaries deciding what to do in Open Enrollment before December 7.
  • HR and benefits staff who want the survey figures in one place with their sources.

It is not for:

  • Anyone looking for a way to qualify for coverage they do not meet. A covered indication such as sleep apnea or established heart disease needs a real diagnosis made by a clinician. Misstating a condition to a plan is not a route we describe.
  • Anyone thinking of stretching, splitting or skipping doses to make a supply last. Dosing follows the label and the prescriber's plan. Our guide to stopping a GLP-1 and weight regain covers what the evidence says about stopping.
  • People taking a GLP-1 for type 2 diabetes, whose coverage is usually unaffected by the cuts described here. Check your formulary, but do not assume the weight-loss changes apply to you.
  • Anyone wanting tax or legal advice on HSA, FSA or appeal rights in a specific case.

sections.heading: What we don't know yet about 2027 coverage
sections.body:
Honest limits, because several of the numbers above will move.

  • How many employers will actually drop coverage. The WTW and Mercer figures for 2027 are about employers "considering" or "planning" a change in surveys fielded months before open enrollment. Final plan decisions may be larger or smaller.
  • Whether the surveys represent your employer. The consultancy and Business Group on Health samples skew toward large employers. Small employers, which KFF's survey shows cover these drugs far less often, are under-represented in the headline figures.
  • What lower list prices do to net costs. Mercer and others expect lower list prices to be offset partly by lower rebates. Whether that makes coverage cheaper for employers in practice will not be clear until 2027 claims come in (Mercer).
  • What direct-to-employer programmes cost employees. The Lilly and Novo channels are new and the employee share depends on each employer. We have not seen independent data.
  • What happens to Medicare coverage after 2027. The Bridge ends on December 31, 2027. CMS has said it will gather more data before any Part D rollout of the BALANCE model, and KFF calls the post-2027 picture uncertain (KFF).
  • How long sale prices last. The lowest compounded figures in our tables are sale prices with no end date stated. We re-verify the index and log every change.
  • Some survey details come from summaries. Where a figure, such as KFF's firm-size breakdown or the IFEBP claims share, reached us through a summary of the report rather than the report itself, we have said so. If the full report differs, the report wins.

sections.heading: Questions to ask HR, your insurer and your clinician
sections.body:
Three conversations, in this order.

HR or the benefits team

  1. Which 2027 plan options cover Wegovy or Zepbound for weight management, and on what terms?
  2. Is there a transition period for people already on treatment?
  3. Does the company offer a direct-to-employer GLP-1 programme, and how much does it contribute?
  4. What are the FSA rules for unused balances, and which plans are HSA-eligible?

The insurer or PBM (number on your card)

  1. What are the 2027 prior-authorisation criteria for each drug, in writing?
  2. Is the drug covered for cardiovascular risk reduction, sleep apnea or MASH if weight management is excluded?
  3. What would 12 months cost me under this plan after deductible and coinsurance?
  4. If I am denied, what are the internal appeal and external review deadlines?

Your clinician

  1. Do I have a condition, such as established heart disease, sleep apnea or MASH, that a plan would treat as a separate covered use?
  2. If my coverage ends, which route do you recommend for me, and why?
  3. If I switch drug or route, how will you decide my dose, and what should I tell a new prescriber?
  4. If I stop altogether, what should I expect and how should we monitor it?
  5. Will you write a letter of medical necessity for an appeal or for my HSA or FSA administrator?

For the provider side, our provider checklist covers what to ask a telehealth company before you pay.

sections.heading: Final verdict and next steps
sections.body:
The data are clear about direction. Employer coverage of GLP-1s for weight loss stopped growing in 2026 and fell in several surveys: from 57% to 53% at WTW's employers, from 72% to 60% among Business Group on Health's large employers, and from 43% to 33% at the largest firms in KFF's survey as reported. Cost is the reason employers give, and demand is still rising. For 2027, expect more exclusions, more prior-authorisation rules and more employers pointing to programmes outside the plan, with diabetes coverage largely untouched.

For an individual, the advice is simple and time-limited: check now. Open enrollment is the one point in the year when you can see next year's rules and still choose. After that, the routes are known and their annual costs differ by more than $20,000, from a $600 year on Medicare's Bridge, if you qualify, to $21,588 for brand Wegovy at the highest cash price we track.

  1. This week: find your 2027 formulary, search for Wegovy and Zepbound, and work through the checklist above. Save the pages.
  2. Before your window closes: compare plan options and premiums against the year-cost table, set your FSA or HSA amount, and ask HR about direct-to-employer programmes.
  3. If you are on Medicare: ask your Part D plan about the GLP-1 Bridge and make any changes by December 7. See GLP-1s after 65.
  4. If coverage ends: start with our lost-coverage guide, then compare routes in weight-loss medication without insurance and the verified price ladder.
  5. If you are weighing compounded: read compounded vs brand-name first, then compare providers in the full ranking.
  6. If you want to stay on the brand: compare cash routes in Zepbound price online and Wegovy pill price online.

This article is general information about insurance coverage and prices, not medical, tax or legal advice. A licensed clinician decides whether a GLP-1 is appropriate for you and at what dose. Survey figures, programme rules and prices change; each is dated, and we re-verify.
