articles.title: Are altRx, embody and welludr the Same Company? (2026)
articles.description: altRx, embody, welludr, TrimRx and Medvi are separate companies. Why some feel alike: a shared clinician network, per their own published documents.
articles.author: Treatments Hub Research Team
keyTakeaways: altRx, embody, welludr, TrimRx and Medvi are separate companies. Their own documents name different operating entities, and each sets its own prices, plans, support and guarantees.
altRx, embody and welludr each name OpenLoop as the clinician network behind their prescriptions, which is why patients sometimes notice similar intake steps or portals.
None of them is a pharmacy. Prescriptions are filled by independent, state-licensed pharmacies, and which pharmacy fills an order can differ by brand, treatment and state.
A shared clinician network is a common, legitimate telehealth structure. What separates the brands for you is price, commitment, shipping speed and support.

sections.heading: Are altRx, embody and welludr the same company?
sections.body:
The short answerNo. altRx, embody and welludr (formerly wellmedr) are separate companies with different operating entities, prices and plan terms. They can feel alike because each one names the same telehealth clinician network, OpenLoop, in its own published documents, and none of them is a pharmacy: licensed clinicians in that network decide whether to prescribe, and independent licensed pharmacies fill the prescriptions. TrimRx and Medvi are also separate companies.

The question comes up because patients who try more than one of these services notice overlaps: a similar health questionnaire, a similar sequence of steps, sometimes a familiar-looking patient portal. The overlaps are real, and they have a plain explanation. Most online GLP-1 brands do not employ their own doctors or run their own pharmacies. They are consumer-facing companies that contract with a licensed clinician network and with licensed pharmacies, and several of the best-known brands contract with the same network.

Everything below comes from each company's own terms, privacy policy, about page or refund policy, linked in place, as published when we checked on November 2, 2026. Companies can change partners, so the documents themselves are the place to confirm the current arrangement.

sections.heading: Who runs each provider, and who prescribes?
sections.body:
BrandOperating company (own documents)Who prescribesWho fills prescriptions
altRxTrinity HealthCare Supply, LLC d/b/a altRx, which provides the technology platform and administrative services (altRx about page)OpenLoop Healthcare Partners, PC (altRx about page)Independently owned, state-licensed 503A compounding pharmacies in the altRx pharmacy network (altRx terms)
embodyModern Metabolic Medicine, Inc. (embody terms)Clinicians from OpenLoop Health (embody terms)Independent third-party pharmacies (embody terms)
welludr (formerly wellmedr)welludr, which collects payment on behalf of the medical group (welludr terms)OpenLoop Health (welludr privacy policy)Named licensed pharmacies, including Logos Pharmacy, Emerald Compounding Pharmacy and Center City Pharmacy, varying by treatment and location (welludr refund policy)
TrimRxA technology and administrative services platform (TrimRx terms)Independent, affiliated physician groups (TrimRx terms)A participating pharmacy, paid by TrimRx out of the fees it collects (TrimRx terms)
MedviA separate companyNot confirmed from Medvi's own documentsNot confirmed from Medvi's own documents

Two things stand out. First, the operating companies are different: there is no shared parent named in any of these documents, so "sister brands" is not an accurate description on the evidence available. Second, three of the five name the same clinician network. That is the "cousins by infrastructure" relationship people sense when they compare portals.

sections.heading: Why do these providers look so similar?
sections.body:
Because the parts a patient touches first are often supplied by the same partners. The clinician network sets how an intake is reviewed, and network-wide tools can shape what the questionnaire and follow-up messages look like. The pharmacy side is similar: compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide are prepared by state-licensed compounding pharmacies, a regulated channel the FDA describes on its human drug compounding pages, and several brands work with pharmacies from the same pool.

What each brand controls is the part you pay for and live with: the price, whether you commit to a plan, how fast it ships, how support works and what guarantees apply. Those differ a lot, which is why choosing between them is a real decision rather than a choice between labels on the same box.

sections.heading: Is the medication the same if I switch between them?
sections.body: The active ingredient is the same molecule, semaglutide or tirzepatide, but the specific compounded product depends on the pharmacy that fills the order, and that can differ by brand, by treatment and by state. welludr, for example, says the dispensing pharmacy varies with treatment and location (welludr refund policy). If consistency matters to you, ask the provider which pharmacy will fill your prescription before you switch, and tell your new prescriber your current dose so they can decide how to continue. Do not change or stretch a dose on your own; the prescriber decides.

sections.heading: Is a shared clinician network a red flag?
sections.body: No. It is the standard structure for direct-to-consumer telehealth. A licensed clinician network provides the prescribers, the brand provides the service around them, and licensed pharmacies dispense. The legitimacy checks are the same as for any provider: a licensed clinician who reviews your history and can decline treatment, a licensed US pharmacy, published prices with their conditions, and clear cancellation terms. Each brand's page on our site walks through those checks: is altRx legit, is embody legit, is welludr legit and is TrimRx legit.

sections.heading: If they share a network, how do they actually differ?
sections.body:
On the things you will notice every month. Verified prices from our price index, with the condition attached to each:

ProviderSemaglutideTirzepatideCommitment
welludr$41/month$71/month12-month plan for the lowest rate (pre-Black Friday sale)
embody$49/month$99/monthMonth to month (pre-Black Friday sale)
altRx$89/month$149/monthPause or cancel anytime; Buy Now, Pay Later
Medvifrom $99/monthNot listedNo membership; dietician and coaching included
TrimRxPlans from $179/month (TrimRx site, read Nov 22, 2026); not tied to one drugMonth to month

Beyond price: altRx is the one with a brand-name shelf (Ozempic, Zepbound, Wegovy) alongside compounded plans; embody offers free expedited delivery (no timeline guaranteed) and a partial refund if you are not approved; welludr includes a coach and a weight-loss warranty; Medvi bundles video visits and a dietician; TrimRx has the cleanest exit terms. Prices change, so check the cheapest GLP-1 comparison or the cost calculator before you decide.

sections.heading: Which one should I choose?
sections.body: Choose on what differs, not on the shared network. Lowest price and happy to commit: welludr. Lowest price without a commitment: embody. A path to brand-name medication in the same account: altRx. The most hands-on support: Medvi. Flexibility above all: TrimRx. Side-by-side detail is in embody vs welludr, altRx vs embody and embody vs altRx vs welludr, and the full ranking is on our weight loss comparison. This article is general information, not medical advice.

articles.title: GLP-1 Weight Loss Results: How Much Weight Do People Lose?
articles.description: How much weight people lose on semaglutide and tirzepatide, from the STEP and SURMOUNT trials: averages, pounds, who loses more, and what happens if you stop.
articles.author: Treatments Hub Research Team
keyTakeaways: In the main trials, people on semaglutide 2.4 mg lost 14.9% of their body weight on average over 68 weeks (STEP 1), against 2.4% on placebo.
Tirzepatide produced 15.0% to 20.9% average loss over 72 weeks depending on dose (SURMOUNT-1), against 3.1% on placebo.
In the only head-to-head trial, SURMOUNT-5, tirzepatide averaged 20.2% and semaglutide 13.7% at 72 weeks.
Results vary widely between people, are lower on average with type 2 diabetes, and most of the weight returned within a year of stopping in the STEP 1 extension.

sections.heading: How much weight do people lose on GLP-1 medications?
sections.body:
The short answerIn the pivotal trials, adults without diabetes lost about 15% of their body weight on average with semaglutide 2.4 mg (Wegovy's dose) over 68 weeks, and 15% to 21% with tirzepatide (Zepbound) over 72 weeks, depending on the dose. For someone starting at 220 lb, that is roughly 33 lb on semaglutide and up to about 46 lb on the top tirzepatide dose. These are averages: some people lose much more, some much less, and the loss builds over a year or more, not weeks.

The numbers on this page come from the large randomized trials that led to FDA approval, each linked to the published paper. They describe what happened to the average participant, who was also given diet and exercise counseling, under trial conditions with brand-name medication. Nothing here is a prediction for any one person; a licensed clinician is the right person to set expectations for you.

sections.heading: What did the main clinical trials find?
sections.body:
TrialMedication and doseWho took partLengthAverage weight loss
STEP 1 (NEJM, 2021)Semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly1,961 adults with obesity or overweight, no diabetes68 weeks14.9% vs 2.4% on placebo
SURMOUNT-1 (NEJM, 2022)Tirzepatide 5, 10 or 15 mg weekly2,539 adults with obesity or overweight, no diabetes72 weeks15.0%, 19.5% and 20.9% vs 3.1% on placebo
STEP 2 (Lancet, 2021)Semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly1,210 adults with type 2 diabetes68 weeks9.6% vs 3.4% on placebo
SURMOUNT-2 (Lancet, 2023)Tirzepatide 10 or 15 mg weekly938 adults with type 2 diabetes72 weeks12.8% and 14.7% vs 3.2% on placebo
SURMOUNT-5 (NEJM, 2025)Tirzepatide vs semaglutide, highest tolerated dose751 adults with obesity, no diabetes72 weeks20.2% (tirzepatide) vs 13.7% (semaglutide)

The placebo groups matter: they received the same lifestyle counseling, so the gap between the medication and placebo columns is the effect of the drug itself. The tirzepatide figures above are the trials' main "treatment-regimen" results, which count everyone who was randomized, including people who stopped early. Counting only people who stayed on treatment, SURMOUNT-1 reported up to 22.5% at 15 mg, which is the figure you will often see quoted.

sections.heading: What share of people reach 5%, 10%, 15% or 20% weight loss?
sections.body:
Averages hide the spread, so the trials also report how many people crossed set thresholds. In STEP 1, 86.4% of people on semaglutide lost at least 5% of their weight, 69.1% lost at least 10% and 50.5% lost at least 15%, against 31.5%, 12.0% and 4.9% on placebo. Put the other way, about one in seven people on semaglutide did not reach 5%.

In SURMOUNT-1, about half of the people on tirzepatide 10 mg and 57% of those on 15 mg lost 20% or more, against 3% on placebo. In the head-to-head SURMOUNT-5 trial, 81.6% on tirzepatide and 60.5% on semaglutide lost at least 10%, and 48.4% and 27.3% lost at least 20%.

Losing 5% to 10% of body weight is the range usually described as clinically meaningful, because it is where improvements in blood pressure, blood sugar and other markers tend to show. You do not need to match the trial average for treatment to be worthwhile.

sections.heading: How many pounds is that?
sections.body:
The trial results are percentages, so the pounds depend on where you start. This table applies the trial averages to three starting weights. It is arithmetic on an average, not a forecast for anyone.

Starting weightPlacebo plus lifestyle (STEP 1, 2.4%)Semaglutide 2.4 mg (STEP 1, 14.9%)Tirzepatide 15 mg (SURMOUNT-1, 20.9%)
180 lbabout 4 lbabout 27 lbabout 38 lb
220 lbabout 5 lbabout 33 lbabout 46 lb
260 lbabout 6 lbabout 39 lbabout 54 lb

Check where you start with our BMI and GLP-1 eligibility check, which uses the same label criteria a prescriber starts from.

sections.heading: Does tirzepatide cause more weight loss than semaglutide?
sections.body:
On the published evidence, yes, on average. SURMOUNT-5, the only trial so far to compare them directly, gave 751 adults the highest dose each could tolerate for 72 weeks: average weight loss was 20.2% with tirzepatide and 13.7% with semaglutide, a gap of 6.5 percentage points. The trial was open label (participants knew which drug they were on) and was run by tirzepatide's manufacturer, Eli Lilly, so it is strong evidence but not the last word.

The separate trials point the same way: about 15% for semaglutide in STEP 1 against 15% to 21% by dose for tirzepatide in SURMOUNT-1, though those were different trials in different people. More weight loss is not the only consideration. Side effects, cost and how you respond matter too; our tirzepatide vs semaglutide comparison covers the full picture and the GLP-1 price tracker has current verified prices for both.

sections.heading: How much weight do people lose per month on a GLP-1?
sections.body:
Spread evenly across the trials, about 0.9% of body weight a month on semaglutide 2.4 mg (STEP 1: 14.9% over 68 weeks) and about 1.3% a month on tirzepatide 15 mg (SURMOUNT-1: 20.9% over 72 weeks). For someone starting at 220 lb, that works out to roughly 2.1 lb a month on semaglutide and 2.8 lb a month on tirzepatide, against about 0.3 lb a month on placebo with the same diet and exercise counseling.

Treat those as averages over a year and a half, not a monthly target. The trials reported where people ended up, not a steady rate, and the loss isn't spread evenly: the dose is still being raised for the first four to five months, and individual results vary widely. Our cost calculator shows what the same months cost at verified prices.

sections.heading: How fast does the weight come off?
sections.body:
Gradually. Both medications start at a low dose that is raised step by step to limit side effects: semaglutide over 16 weeks to the 2.4 mg maintenance dose, per the Wegovy prescribing information, and tirzepatide over a 20-week escalation period in SURMOUNT-1. The trial averages above were measured after 68 to 72 weeks, so the loss in the first month or two is much smaller.

For a month-by-month view of what usually happens, see how long semaglutide takes to work and what to expect in your first month. Our dose schedule timeline maps the labelled dose steps onto a calendar.

sections.heading: Why do results vary so much between people?
sections.body:
• Type 2 diabetes. People with diabetes lose less on average: 9.6% on semaglutide in STEP 2 and 12.8% to 14.7% on tirzepatide in SURMOUNT-2, against about 15% and up to 21% in the trials without diabetes.
  • The dose reached. In SURMOUNT-1 the average rose from 15.0% at 5 mg to 20.9% at 15 mg. Some people stay on a lower dose because of side effects.
  • Staying on treatment. The gap between the 20.9% and 22.5% tirzepatide figures is largely people who stopped early. Consistency over months is part of the result.
  • Diet and activity. Every trial group, placebo included, had lifestyle counseling. The medication works alongside those changes, not instead of them; see what to eat on a GLP-1 and how to protect muscle while losing weight.
  • Individual biology. Even with everything else equal, response differs, which is why about one in seven people in STEP 1 lost less than 5%.

If progress stalls, that is a conversation for your prescriber; our guide to weight-loss plateaus covers the usual causes.

sections.heading: What happens to the weight if you stop?
sections.body:
For most people, much of it comes back. In STEP 4, people who had taken semaglutide for 20 weeks were randomly switched either to placebo or to continued treatment: from week 20 to week 68, the placebo group regained 6.9% of their body weight while the continued group lost a further 7.9%. In the STEP 1 extension, which followed people for a year after they stopped, participants regained about two-thirds of the weight they had lost, and most of the improvements in blood pressure and blood sugar faded with it.

That is why prescribers treat these as long-term medications. Planning for maintenance, whether that means staying on a dose, tapering under supervision or something else, is covered in our guide to stopping GLP-1s and keeping the weight off.

sections.heading: Do compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide give the same results?
sections.body:
Nobody knows for certain, because they have not been studied in these trials. Every result on this page comes from FDA-approved, brand-name medication made by the manufacturer. Compounded versions contain the same active ingredient but are prepared by state-licensed compounding pharmacies, and compounded drugs are not FDA-approved or reviewed for safety and effectiveness, as the FDA explains on its human drug compounding pages.

That does not mean they do not work; it means the trial numbers are the best available reference rather than a guarantee for a compounded product. Our explainer on compounded vs brand-name semaglutide covers the real differences and how to check a provider's pharmacy.

sections.heading: What about the results providers advertise?
sections.body: Many online providers publish their own figures, such as average pounds lost by their customers. Those numbers are the provider's own and are usually self-reported or drawn from people who stayed on the program, so they are not comparable with the randomized trials above. We do not repeat them on this site. When you compare providers, compare what you can check: the medication, the verified price and its conditions, the clinician review and the cancellation terms. Our guide to choosing a GLP-1 provider lists the checks, and the step-by-step guide to starting GLP-1 treatment online shows what the process looks like.

sections.heading: The bottom line
sections.body: The best evidence says the average person without diabetes loses about 15% of their body weight on semaglutide 2.4 mg and 15% to 21% on tirzepatide over roughly a year and a half, with tirzepatide ahead in the one head-to-head trial. Individual results range widely, are lower with type 2 diabetes, build slowly through the dose steps and largely depend on staying on treatment. Every number here is a published trial average, linked to its source. This article is general information, not medical advice; a licensed clinician decides whether either medication is right for you. For a wider set of figures, including prices and side-effect rates, see our GLP-1 price index and statistics.

articles.title: How to Start GLP-1 Online: The Intake Process, Step by Step
articles.description: What starting semaglutide or tirzepatide online involves: eligibility, intake questions, clinician review, pharmacy and first dose, with real screenshots.
articles.author: Treatments Hub Research Team
keyTakeaways: Starting online follows the same order at almost every provider: an eligibility check, a medical questionnaire, a licensed clinician's review, then a prescription filled by a licensed pharmacy and shipped to you.
The usual starting point is the FDA label: a BMI of 30 or more, or 27 or more with at least one weight-related condition. The clinician makes the final decision and can say no.
Have your height and weight, your medical history, a list of current medications and any recent lab results ready; the questionnaire itself usually takes a few minutes.
Treatment starts at a low dose that is raised every four weeks, so the first month is about getting used to the medication, not about the scale.

sections.heading: How do you start GLP-1 treatment online?
sections.body:
The short answerPick a licensed telehealth provider, answer its online health questionnaire (height, weight, medical history, current medications), and a licensed clinician reviews your answers. If they decide semaglutide or tirzepatide is appropriate, they write a prescription, a licensed pharmacy fills it and the medication ships to your door. You start on a low dose that is raised step by step. No office visit is needed, but a prescription always is.

This guide walks through each step with screenshots of real provider sites, captured on November 5, 2026, so you can see what the screens look like before you start. The screenshots show how each provider presents its own process; every claim in them is the provider's, not ours. Providers change their sites, so details may differ by the time you read this.

sections.heading: Step 1: Check whether you are likely to qualify
sections.body:
Online providers start from the same criteria as the FDA labels: adults with a BMI of 30 or more, or 27 or more with at least one weight-related condition such as high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes or high cholesterol, per the Wegovy prescribing information. Our BMI and GLP-1 eligibility check tells you where you stand in under a minute, and our guide to who qualifies for GLP-1 medication covers the details.

Most provider homepages put this check up front. welludr's, for example, leads with an eligibility quiz:

Meeting the BMI threshold does not guarantee a prescription. Some conditions rule these medications out: the labels carry a warning against use with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, and the questionnaire will ask about pregnancy or plans to become pregnant.

sections.heading: Step 2: Choose a provider
sections.body:
You choose the provider before the intake, because each one runs its own questionnaire and sets its own prices and terms. The things worth comparing are the medication offered (compounded or brand-name, semaglutide or tirzepatide), the verified monthly price and the condition attached to it, whether the lowest price needs a prepaid plan, what happens if you are not approved, and how cancellation works. Our guide to choosing a GLP-1 provider lists the checks, the GLP-1 price tracker has every provider's current verified price, and it is worth reading what to check before you prepay.

Providers explain their process differently, but the order is the same. altRx sums it up in three steps:

sections.heading: Step 3: Complete the online health questionnaire
sections.body:
The intake is a set of screens asking about your body, your health and your goals. Expect questions on:

  • Height and weight, used to calculate your BMI
  • Weight-related conditions, such as blood pressure, blood sugar or cholesterol
  • Your medical history, including thyroid, pancreas, gallbladder and kidney conditions
  • Current medications and supplements, and any past weight-loss medication
  • Pregnancy, breastfeeding or plans to become pregnant
  • Contact and shipping details, and sometimes an ID check

Answer accurately. The clinician's decision, and your safety, depend on it, and an answer that leaves out a condition or a medication can lead to a prescription that is wrong for you. Having a list of your medications and any recent lab results to hand makes the questionnaire quicker.

sections.heading: Step 4: A licensed clinician reviews your answers
sections.body:
A licensed clinician (a physician, nurse practitioner or physician assistant, depending on the provider and state) reviews your intake and decides whether a GLP-1 is appropriate, which medication and what starting dose. They may message you with follow-up questions, ask for recent lab work or arrange a video or phone visit; requirements differ by provider and by state. They can also decline, and a legitimate provider will.

welludr's site shows what happens after its intake, from plan activation to the clinician building the treatment plan:

Before you pay, check what happens to your money if you are not approved, because the terms differ: embody, for example, says it refunds the unused portion, less services rendered, if you are not approved.

sections.heading: Step 5: The pharmacy fills your prescription and ships it
sections.body:
Once prescribed, the order goes to a licensed pharmacy. Compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide are prepared by state-licensed compounding pharmacies, a regulated channel the FDA describes on its human drug compounding pages; compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. Brand-name Wegovy or Zepbound come from the manufacturer through a regular pharmacy. The medication usually arrives in an insulated package with supplies and instructions:

Delivery speed varies a lot between providers. Our provider comparison sets each provider's published shipping promise side by side. Refills follow the same route; welludr, for example, says it ships the next supply before you run out:

sections.heading: Step 6: Your first dose and the dose schedule
sections.body:
You start low. Semaglutide is raised every four weeks over 16 weeks to the 2.4 mg maintenance dose, per the Wegovy prescribing information, and tirzepatide was raised over a 20-week escalation period in SURMOUNT-1. Your clinician sets your actual schedule and may hold or slow increases if side effects are hard to manage. Our dose schedule timeline maps the labelled steps onto a calendar.

The first weeks are mostly about adjustment: appetite usually changes before the scale does, and nausea is most common around dose increases. Read what to expect in your first month and the side effects guide before your first injection. For what the trials found over the longer run, see how much weight people lose on GLP-1s.

sections.heading: Step 7: Check-ins, dose changes and refills
sections.body:
Treatment is ongoing, so the relationship with the provider matters after the first box arrives. Expect periodic check-ins (a form or a message with your weight and any side effects) before each dose increase or refill, and a way to reach the care team between them. Providers describe their support differently; embody, for example, lists 24/7 messaging and the option to pause or adjust:

If you want to stop, pause or switch provider later, our guide to switching GLP-1 providers or medications covers how to do it without a gap, and what happens when you stop explains why that decision belongs with your prescriber.

sections.heading: How long does it take to get started?
sections.body: The questionnaire itself usually takes a few minutes; the three providers in the screenshots above say 2 to 3 minutes. After that, the time to your first dose is the clinician's review plus shipping, and both vary: a review can be finished the same day or take longer if the clinician needs more information or labs, and shipping ranges from a day or two to about a week depending on the provider. Ask the provider for its current review and shipping times if timing matters to you.

sections.heading: What are the warning signs of an unsafe online GLP-1 seller?
sections.body:
• No medical questions, or a prescription "guaranteed". A legitimate provider asks about your health and lets a clinician decline.
  • No prescription needed. Semaglutide and tirzepatide are prescription-only in the US; a seller that skips the prescription is not operating legally.
  • "Research use only" or "not for human consumption" labels. These products are not made for patients.
  • No named, licensed pharmacy. You should be able to find out which licensed pharmacy fills your order.
  • Prices with no conditions shown. A low price that turns out to need a long prepaid plan should be disclosed up front; compare with the verified conditions on our cheapest GLP-1 comparison.

For a full walkthrough of the legal route, see whether you can get Ozempic without a doctor (no, but you can without an office visit).

sections.heading: The bottom line
sections.body: Starting GLP-1 treatment online comes down to seven steps: check you are likely to qualify, choose a provider on verified price and terms, answer the questionnaire accurately, let a licensed clinician decide, receive the medication from a licensed pharmacy, start at a low dose, and keep up with check-ins. The screens differ from one provider to the next, but the order and the safeguards should not. This article is general information, not medical advice; a licensed clinician decides whether a GLP-1 is right for you. For the full background on the online route, our complete guide to GLP-1 weight loss online goes deeper.

articles.title: GLP-1s and Alcohol: Can You Drink on Ozempic or Zepbound?
articles.description: Is it safe to drink on semaglutide or tirzepatide? The real risks, who should skip it, and what the 2026 studies found about GLP-1s and drinking less.
articles.author: Treatments Hub Research Team
keyTakeaways: There's no blanket ban on alcohol with semaglutide or tirzepatide, but the two overlap on the side effects that matter: an upset stomach, dehydration, pancreatitis and, on diabetes medication, low blood sugar.
Skip alcohol entirely if you've had pancreatitis, take insulin or a sulfonylurea without your prescriber's OK, are pregnant or trying, or think your drinking is out of control.
Many people simply want to drink less on a GLP-1: 44% of drinkers in a 2026 JAMA Psychiatry survey said they cut back in the first three months.
In a 2026 Lancet trial, semaglutide plus therapy cut heavy drinking days more than therapy alone, but no GLP-1 is approved to treat alcohol use disorder.

sections.heading: Can you drink alcohol on Ozempic, Wegovy or Zepbound?
sections.body:
The short answerFor most people, an occasional drink isn't off-limits. Neither semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) nor tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) comes with a rule against alcohol. The catch is that alcohol and these medications can cause some of the same problems: nausea and vomiting, dehydration, pancreatitis and, if you also take diabetes medication, low blood sugar. So keep it light, never drink on an empty stomach, and ask your prescriber what's sensible for you. Many people find they want less anyway.

It's one of the first questions people ask once they start a GLP-1, usually just before a wedding, a work dinner or the holidays. The honest answer has two parts. There's the safety side, which is mostly common sense once you know where the overlaps are. And there's the surprising side: a growing pile of research, much of it published this year, on why so many people on these drugs lose interest in drinking.

sections.heading: What are the risks of mixing alcohol and GLP-1s?
sections.body:
None of these are reasons to panic. They're the places where a drink and a GLP-1 push in the same direction, which is worth knowing before you order a second one.

  • Your stomach. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea are the most common GLP-1 side effects, and they peak in the first weeks and after each dose increase. Alcohol irritates the gut too. A drink that was fine last month can hit differently the week you step up a dose. Our side effects guide covers how to manage nausea.
  • Dehydration. The Wegovy prescribing information warns that fluid loss from vomiting or diarrhea can lead to kidney problems. Alcohol makes you lose fluid as well, so drink water alongside it, especially if your stomach is already unsettled.
  • Pancreatitis. Acute pancreatitis is a listed warning on GLP-1 labels, and heavy alcohol use is one of the main causes of pancreatitis, per the NIH's digestive diseases institute. Severe stomach pain that spreads to your back needs urgent care, whether or not you've been drinking.
  • Low blood sugar. GLP-1s on their own rarely cause it, but the label warns the risk goes up with insulin or a sulfonylurea. Alcohol lowers blood sugar too, and on a GLP-1 you're often eating less, so an empty stomach is easier to end up with than you'd think.

sections.heading: Who should skip alcohol completely on a GLP-1?
sections.body:
• Anyone who has had pancreatitis, or has been told their triglycerides are very high.
  • People taking insulin or a sulfonylurea (such as glipizide or glyburide), unless their prescriber has said exactly how much is safe.
  • Anyone pregnant or trying to conceive. GLP-1s are usually stopped before a planned pregnancy anyway, so that's a conversation to have with your clinician early.
  • Anyone who feels their drinking is hard to control. That's not a GLP-1 question; it's a reason to get proper support. SAMHSA's free, confidential National Helpline is 1-800-662-4357, any time. If you drink heavily every day, don't stop suddenly on your own: withdrawal can be dangerous, and a clinician can help you do it safely.

sections.heading: Does alcohol feel different on a GLP-1?
sections.body:
It can. GLP-1s slow down how fast your stomach empties, and a small pilot study from Virginia Tech, reported in October 2025, found that people on these drugs absorbed alcohol into their bloodstream more slowly and said they felt less drunk. It was a pilot, and the authors described it that way.

Feeling less drunk is not the same as being less impaired. Don't use it as a reason to drink more, and never drive after drinking. The slower absorption can also mean a drink catches up with you later than you expect.

sections.heading: Why do some people drink less on a GLP-1?
sections.body:
Plenty of people notice it without looking for it: the glass of wine at dinner stops being appealing, or one drink is enough. In a JAMA Psychiatry survey of 242 people who drank when they started a GLP-1, 44.2% said they drank less in the first three months, and 52.6% said nothing changed. Among those who screened as possibly drinking at unhealthy levels, 54.1% cut back. Most of them hadn't heard it might happen: only about 10% of everyone surveyed knew GLP-1s might lower drinking, the Harvard Gazette reported in November 2026. It's self-reported, so it can't prove the drug caused the change, but it matches what clinicians hear.

The leading idea is that the same signals that quiet "food noise" also take the edge off the pull of alcohol. That's what the trials in the next section are testing. If you're comparing providers, our three highest-ranked are below. Whichever you pick, mention how much you drink when you fill in the intake.

sections.heading: What did the 2026 alcohol studies actually find?
sections.body:
StudyWhoWhat happenedHow strong
Lancet trial (May 2026)108 adults with alcohol use disorder and obesity, 26 weeks, all given cognitive behavioral therapyWeekly semaglutide 2.4 mg cut heavy drinking days by 41.1%, a 13.7% bigger reduction than placebo, per the NIHRandomized and placebo-controlled, but small
Oral semaglutide trial (Jul 2026)50 adults with moderate to severe alcohol use disorder, 8 weeksFewer heavy drinking days, but it missed its main goal (cravings)Small and short; the authors call it hypothesis-generating
BMJ Open study (Jul 2026)40,703 adults with alcohol use disorder plus type 2 diabetes or obesityPeople on semaglutide or tirzepatide had fewer alcohol-related hospital stays over a year than people on sulfonylureas (hazard ratio 0.74), Healio reportedObservational, so it can't prove cause
JAMA Psychiatry survey (2026)242 people who drank when starting a GLP-144.2% drank less in the first three monthsSelf-reported

The pattern is consistent, but the strongest evidence still comes from small trials. Bigger ones are under way: the VA's CRAVE trial is enrolling more than 600 veterans with moderate or severe alcohol use disorder at 18 VA medical centers. None of these studies used compounded semaglutide or tirzepatide.

sections.heading: Is semaglutide approved to treat alcohol use disorder?
sections.body:
No. The American Psychiatric Association's July 2026 release says plainly that semaglutide "is not currently approved as a treatment for alcohol use disorder," and the same is true of tirzepatide. The VA, running its own trial, tells veterans not to swap proven treatment for a GLP-1 without talking to a provider.

Proven options already exist: FDA-approved medicines such as naltrexone and acamprosate, counseling and therapy. If cutting back is the goal, those are where to start, and a doctor can tell you whether a GLP-1 makes sense on top for your weight.

sections.heading: Should you tell your online GLP-1 provider how much you drink?
sections.body:
Yes, and be accurate. The intake questionnaire asks about your health history for a reason: a prescriber who knows you drink most nights, or have had pancreatitis, will make different calls on the medication and dose. You won't be judged for an honest answer, and it can't be used against you the way a wrong prescription can. If you're starting out, our step-by-step guide to starting GLP-1 treatment online shows what the questions look like.

It's also worth asking your prescriber directly: "How much is reasonable for me while I'm on this?" The answer depends on your dose, your other medications and how your stomach is handling it.

sections.heading: The bottom line
sections.body: An occasional drink on a GLP-1 is fine for most people, as long as you eat first, drink water and go easy around dose increases. Skip it altogether if you've had pancreatitis, take insulin or a sulfonylurea without your prescriber's go-ahead, or are pregnant or trying. If you find you're drinking less, you're in good company; the research is promising but early, and it's not a substitute for real treatment if alcohol is a problem. For the rest of the picture, see how much weight people lose on GLP-1s, what to eat on a GLP-1 and our guide to GLP-1s and mental health. This is general information, not medical advice.

articles.title: Compounded Semaglutide Units to mg: How to Read Your Vial
articles.description: Why '20 units' means nothing without the vial's mg/mL. The formula, conversion tables for semaglutide and tirzepatide, the 28-day rule and the FDA's error reports.
articles.author: Treatments Hub Research Team
keyTakeaways: A 'unit' on an insulin syringe is a volume (100 units = 1 mL), not a dose. The same 0.25 mg of semaglutide is 25 units from a 1 mg/mL vial, 10 units from a 2.5 mg/mL vial and 5 units from a 5 mg/mL vial. Instructions written only in units are the root of the errors the FDA has logged.

The FDA's reports include patients who drew 50 units instead of 5, a prescriber who wrote 25 units meaning 0.25 mg (5 units), and 20 units written instead of 2: doses five to twenty times too high, with vomiting, dehydration, fainting, pancreatitis and gallstones among the results.

Three numbers must appear together before you inject: the dose in mg, the vial's concentration in mg/mL, and the resulting volume in mL (and units). If any one is missing, call the pharmacy before you draw up. The formula is mL = mg ÷ mg/mL.

FDA says to discard a multi-dose vial 28 days after first use even if drug remains, so a vial's total mg rarely equals usable doses; at the labelled starting doses, that often means buying more than you inject. The FDA-approved labels (Wegovy, Zepbound) are the reference your prescriber works from for every dose step.

sections.heading: What do the 'units' on a compounded semaglutide vial mean?
sections.body:
The short answerUnits are a measure of volume, not of medicine. The insulin syringes used for compounded GLP-1 injections are "U-100" syringes: 100 units equals 1 mL, so 10 units is 0.1 mL and 5 units is 0.05 mL. How much semaglutide or tirzepatide sits in that volume depends entirely on the vial's concentration, printed as milligrams per millilitre (mg/mL). Your prescribed dose is a weight in mg. The units are only the answer to "how far do I pull the plunger," and that answer changes every time the concentration changes.

This is the single idea that explains the dosing errors the FDA alerted prescribers, compounders and patients about (content current as of July 26, 2024). The approved products hide the arithmetic: a Wegovy pen delivers a fixed dose with no measuring, and a Zepbound vial is a single dose drawn up whole. Compounded products often come as multi-dose vials in varying concentrations, and the FDA notes that instructions may tell patients to inject a number of "units," a figure whose meaning shifts with the concentration. Our own medical reviewer flagged the same point on our weight-loss hub: compounded instructions should state the dose in mg, the concentration, and the matching syringe volume, because units alone cause confusion.

This page gives you the formula, conversion tables at example concentrations for both molecules, the 28-day vial math, how to choose a syringe, and the red flags that should stop you before you inject. It is not a dosing instruction. The dose on your prescription, written by a licensed prescriber who knows your history, is the only one that applies to you; this page is for checking that the numbers on your vial, your syringe and your prescription agree. Compounded medicines are not FDA-approved, and the FDA does not verify their safety, effectiveness or quality.

sections.heading: What went wrong in the FDA's dosing-error reports?
sections.body:
The FDA's alert describes the pattern in concrete cases. Most reports involved patients drawing more than the prescribed amount from a multi-dose vial during self-injection, taking "five to 20 times more than the intended dose." The individual cases it cites:

What happenedIntendedActualMultiple
Patient told to draw 5 units (0.05 mL) on a U-100 syringe drew 50 units5 units50 units10x
Prescriber meant 0.25 mg (5 units at that concentration) but wrote 25 units; the patient had severe vomiting5 units25 units5x
Prescriber wrote 20 units instead of 2 units; three patients received the dose and had nausea and vomiting2 units20 units10x
Patient could not get clear instructions from the telemedicine prescriber, searched online, and took five times the dose1x5x5x
A patient who was also a clinician recalculated the dose in units and self-administered ten times the intended amount1x10x10x

The reported effects were nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fainting, headache, migraine, dehydration, acute pancreatitis and gallstones; some patients were hospitalised. The FDA's page on unapproved GLP-1 drugs (current as of October 1, 2026) adds that it has received "multiple reports of adverse events, some requiring hospitalization," that may relate to these errors, and that in some cases the error was the clinician miscalculating rather than the patient.

Notice what every case has in common. None involved a defective product. Each was a conversion failure: a dose in mg turned into a number of units without the concentration being carried through, or a decimal lost between a prescription and a syringe. That is why the fix is arithmetic and labelling, and why the FDA's recommendations are about syringes and instructions, not the drug.

sections.heading: How do you convert mg to mL and units?
sections.body:
Two lines, applied in order, every time:

The formula

Volume (mL) = dose (mg) ÷ concentration (mg/mL)

Units on a U-100 syringe = volume (mL) × 100

Worked example. Your prescription says 0.5 mg of semaglutide once weekly and the vial says 2.5 mg/mL. Volume = 0.5 ÷ 2.5 = 0.2 mL. Units = 0.2 × 100 = 20 units. Now the same prescription with a 5 mg/mL vial: 0.5 ÷ 5 = 0.1 mL = 10 units. Same dose, half the units, because the vial is twice as strong. A patient who moves between pharmacies, or whose pharmacy changes concentration between refills, can be given the identical mg dose and need a completely different syringe reading.

A check you can run against an FDA-approved product shows the arithmetic is not a compounded-only concern. The Zepbound label (revised August 2026) lists a multi-dose vial of 10 mg in 2.4 mL that delivers four 2.5 mg doses of 0.6 mL each. Run it through the formula: 10 ÷ 2.4 = 4.17 mg/mL; 2.5 ÷ 4.17 = 0.6 mL = 60 units. The label's own numbers reconcile, which is exactly the test to apply to a compounded vial: do the total mg, the total mL and the per-dose volume on the instructions all agree with each other?

Three habits prevent most mistakes. Write the three numbers (mg, mg/mL, mL) on the vial box in your own hand after confirming them with the pharmacist. Re-do the arithmetic whenever a new vial arrives, even from the same pharmacy. And never convert a dose into units from memory; the number you remember belongs to the last concentration, not necessarily this one.

sections.heading: Semaglutide conversion table: dose, concentration, volume, units
sections.body:
The doses in the left column are the escalation steps in the Wegovy prescribing information (revised June 2026): 0.25 mg for weeks 1 to 4, 0.5 mg for weeks 5 to 8, 1 mg for weeks 9 to 12, 1.7 mg for weeks 13 to 16, then a maintenance dose of 1.7 mg or 2.4 mg. The concentrations across the top are examples chosen to show how the volume moves; your vial may say something else, and that number, not this table, governs your draw. Units assume a U-100 syringe.

Weekly dose1 mg/mL vial2.5 mg/mL vial5 mg/mL vial
0.25 mg (weeks 1 to 4 on the label)0.25 mL = 25 units0.1 mL = 10 units0.05 mL = 5 units
0.5 mg (weeks 5 to 8)0.5 mL = 50 units0.2 mL = 20 units0.1 mL = 10 units
1 mg (weeks 9 to 12)1 mL = 100 units0.4 mL = 40 units0.2 mL = 20 units
1.7 mg (weeks 13 to 16, or maintenance)1.7 mL = 170 units (more than one syringe)0.68 mL = 68 units0.34 mL = 34 units
2.4 mg (maintenance)2.4 mL = 240 units (more than one syringe)0.96 mL = 96 units0.48 mL = 48 units

Read the table across a row and the problem the FDA describes is visible: the starting 0.25 mg dose is 5 units from one vial and 25 units from another. A "25 units" instruction written for the 1 mg/mL vial, carried over to a 5 mg/mL vial, delivers 1.25 mg, five times the intended dose, which is precisely one of the FDA's cases. Read down a column and the second point appears: the right-hand vials put maintenance doses within a single 1 mL syringe, while the 1 mg/mL vial does not, which is one reason concentrations vary between pharmacies.

The label's schedule is the reference your prescriber works from, including its instruction to consider delaying an increase by four weeks if a dose is not tolerated. Whether and when you move between rows is the prescriber's decision, not the table's; doses are increased step by step under supervision, and a missed-dose rule exists for a reason (on the injection label, two or more consecutive missed doses mean restarting escalation at a lower dose).

sections.heading: Tirzepatide conversion table: dose, concentration, volume, units
sections.body:
Tirzepatide's labelled steps are wider. The Zepbound label starts at 2.5 mg once weekly for four weeks (a starting dose only, "not approved as a maintenance dosage"), then 5 mg, with any further increase in 2.5 mg steps after at least four weeks on the current dose, to a maximum of 15 mg. Again, the concentrations are examples; the volume in your instructions must come from your own vial.

Weekly dose5 mg/mL vial10 mg/mL vial20 mg/mL vial
2.5 mg (first 4 weeks on the label)0.5 mL = 50 units0.25 mL = 25 units0.125 mL = 12.5 units
5 mg1 mL = 100 units0.5 mL = 50 units0.25 mL = 25 units
7.5 mg1.5 mL = 150 units (more than one syringe)0.75 mL = 75 units0.375 mL = 37.5 units
10 mg2 mL = 200 units (more than one syringe)1 mL = 100 units0.5 mL = 50 units
12.5 mg2.5 mL = 250 units1.25 mL = 125 units0.625 mL = 62.5 units
15 mg (label maximum)3 mL = 300 units1.5 mL = 150 units0.75 mL = 75 units

Two practical notes fall out of this table. Half-unit readings (12.5, 37.5, 62.5) only exist on syringes marked in half units; if your syringe is marked in whole or two-unit steps, a concentration that produces a half-unit volume is a reason to ask the pharmacy for a different syringe or a different concentration rather than to round. And at the top of the range, a 5 mg/mL product needs more than one full 1 mL syringe per injection, which multiplies the chances of a counting error. The Zepbound label's own guidance for its vials is to use "a syringe appropriate for dose administration (e.g., a 1 mL syringe capable of measuring a 0.5 mL or 0.6 mL dose)," and to use a new syringe and needle every time.

For the clinical side of tirzepatide dosing (why the label pauses four weeks between steps, and what the 72-week SURMOUNT results measured at each maintenance dose), see tirzepatide vs semaglutide.

sections.heading: How do you read a compounded vial label, line by line?
sections.body:
A compounded vial label is written by the pharmacy, so layouts vary, but the information you need is always the same five items. If you cannot find one of them, that is a phone call, not a guess.

Look forWhat it tells youIf it is missing
Drug name and salt formIt should say semaglutide or tirzepatide. The FDA says "semaglutide sodium" and "semaglutide acetate" are different active ingredients from the approved drug and that it is "not aware of any lawful basis for their use in compounding."Ask the pharmacy in writing which active ingredient was used.
Concentration (mg/mL)The number that converts your mg dose into a volume. Sometimes printed as total mg and total mL instead (for example 5 mg / 2 mL = 2.5 mg/mL).Do not inject. Without it, no number of units can be checked.
Total volume and total mgHow many doses the vial physically holds, before the 28-day rule (next section).Ask; it also tells you whether the vial was overfilled or underfilled relative to the price you paid.
Beyond-use dateThe pharmacy's date after which the product should not be used, separate from the 28-days-after-opening rule.Ask for it; a vial without one has no documented stability.
Dose instruction in mg, mL and unitsAll three, agreeing with each other and with the concentration. The FDA tells prescribers to be vigilant because concentrations vary, and to contact the compounder if uncertain.Call the prescriber before the first injection; ask them to confirm the mL figure, not just the units.

Keep the vial box and the pharmacy's information sheet until the vial is finished. If a refill arrives with a different concentration, or a different total volume, treat it as a new product and redo the arithmetic from the top.

sections.heading: Which syringe should you use for compounded GLP-1 injections?
sections.body:
Insulin syringes come in three common barrel sizes, and the FDA's alert asks prescribers and compounders to "provide a syringe size appropriate for the intended dose" and to counsel patients on measuring with it. The reason is precision: the smaller the barrel, the finer the markings.

U-100 syringeHoldsTypical markingsSuits volumes of
0.3 mL (30-unit)30 unitsFinest; half-unit versions existUp to 0.3 mL: most semaglutide doses at 2.5 mg/mL and above
0.5 mL (50-unit)50 unitsFine0.3 to 0.5 mL
1 mL (100-unit)100 unitsCoarsest0.5 to 1 mL: higher tirzepatide doses at 10 mg/mL

Two errors in the FDA's reports were a plain tenfold misreading (5 units drawn as 50). On a 1 mL syringe, 5 units is a sliver near the needle hub and the 50-unit line sits mid-barrel; on a 0.3 mL syringe, 5 units is a clearly visible fifth of the barrel and 50 units does not exist. Matching the syringe to the dose is not a convenience; it removes the most common wrong answer from the syringe entirely. If the pharmacy shipped syringes that cannot read your volume accurately, ask for the right size before you start.

Always use a new sterile needle and syringe for each dose, as both FDA pages state. Insulin syringes are single-use.

sections.heading: How many doses does a multi-dose vial really give you?
sections.body:
Fewer than the label's total mg suggests, because of the 28-day rule. The FDA's position, stated on its unapproved GLP-1 page, is that multi-dose sterile vials should generally be used within 28 days after first use, because the risk of contamination rises after that; discard the vial 28 days after the first puncture even if medication remains, and "do not continue using medication from the vial after 28 days" even if the compounder says it can be used longer.

At once-weekly dosing, 28 days is four injections. So the usable doses in a vial are the lesser of what it physically holds and four. The table shows what that means at the labelled semaglutide starting steps for a 1 mL vial at 2.5 mg/mL (2.5 mg total):

Weekly doseDoses the vial holdsDoses usable in 28 daysmg injectedmg discarded
0.25 mg1041 mg1.5 mg (60%)
0.5 mg542 mg0.5 mg (20%)
1 mg2 (plus a half)22 mg0.5 mg, and a third week needs a new vial

Three consequences. First, "a vial of 2.5 mg" is not "ten weeks of starting doses." Second, a plan priced per vial can cost very differently per usable dose depending on your step, which is worth knowing before you prepay; our guide to the true cost of GLP-1 treatment works through the yearly totals. Third, a vial sized so that the 28-day limit falls exactly on your fourth dose is the efficient design, and it is a fair question to ask a provider how its vial sizes line up with the labelled steps.

sections.heading: What dose schedule do the FDA-approved labels use?
sections.body:
Compounded products have no label of their own, so the approved prescribing information is the reference point for every dose step, and the document your prescriber is working from. Both labels increase slowly for a reason: gastrointestinal side effects cluster after each increase, and the labels allow a pause when a step is not tolerated.

Semaglutide injection (Wegovy label, revised 6/2026)Tirzepatide injection (Zepbound label, revised 8/2026)
Starting dose0.25 mg once weekly for 4 weeks2.5 mg once weekly for 4 weeks (starting dose only)
Escalation0.5 mg (weeks 5 to 8), 1 mg (9 to 12), 1.7 mg (13 to 16)5 mg after 4 weeks, then 2.5 mg steps after at least 4 weeks on each
Maintenance for weight reduction1.7 mg or 2.4 mg once weekly; the June 2026 label adds a 7.2 mg option (Wegovy HD) only after 2.4 mg has been tolerated for at least 4 weeks and more weight loss is clinically indicated5, 10 or 15 mg once weekly; 15 mg is the maximum
If a step is not toleratedConsider delaying escalation by 4 weeksStay at least 4 weeks on each dose before increasing
Missed doseTake it if the next dose is more than 2 days away; otherwise skip. Two or more missed in a row: restart escalation at a lower doseTake within 4 days (96 hours); after that, skip and resume on schedule
