sections.heading: How do embody and ro work?
sections.body:
The simplest way to understand embody GLP-1 vs ro Body is to look at what each company bills you for.

embody: one cash price, compounded medication

embody is a weight-loss-only telehealth program. You complete a roughly five-minute online health qualifier, a licensed medical practitioner reviews your chart (embody says usually within 24 hours, often under five), and if treatment is appropriate a prescription goes to one of the US-based 503A compounding pharmacies embody works with. The medication ships free in one to two days in temperature-controlled, tracked, insured packaging. The monthly price covers the medication, the clinician review, injection supplies and shipping. There is no membership fee, no insurance requirement and no contract; you can cancel at any time, and if a clinician does not approve you for treatment embody refunds the unused portion, less services rendered.

What you get is compounded semaglutide or compounded tirzepatide, as a weekly injection. embody does not sell brand-name Ozempic, Wegovy or Zepbound, and it does not offer a pill. Support runs through a dedicated nursing team and the patient portal, where dose adjustments are handled; there is no dietician or formal coaching layer. embody is LegitScript-certified, which is an independent certification for online healthcare merchants, and it is operated by Modern Metabolic Medicine, Inc., with prescribing clinicians from OpenLoop Health. The full write-up is in our is embody legit? guide.

ro: a membership plus brand-name medication

ro is one of the longest-established telehealth companies in the US, and weight loss is one program among several. You complete an online medical assessment, a licensed provider reviews it and decides whether treatment is appropriate, and if prescribed the medication is dispensed by ro's own integrated pharmacy and delivered to your home, with dose adjustments handled by the provider over time.

The bill has two parts. The ro Body membership costs $39 for the first month and then $74 to $149 a month depending on the plan, with $74 the rate on a 12-month prepaid plan. It pays for the provider assessment and follow-up, ongoing dose adjustments and the pharmacy service. The medication is billed separately, either through your insurance or at ro's cash price. ro's published weight-loss pricing centers on brand-name medication: the Wegovy pill and pen and the Zepbound KwikPen. Its treatment list in our review also names compounded semaglutide and metabolic support supplements, but the only medication prices we have verified at ro are the brand-name ones, so that is what this guide costs out. ro says some plans may be FSA/HSA eligible, there are no long-term contracts, and the service is not available in every state.

That two-part bill is the single most important thing to understand about ro, because the $39 is for the consultation and membership, not the medicine. Our ro cost guide walks through it line by line.

sections.heading: Which medications do embody and ro offer?
sections.body:
The price gap exists because the products differ. embody sells compounded semaglutide and compounded tirzepatide; ro's published pricing is for brand-name Wegovy and Zepbound. The compounded semaglutide vs brand Wegovy question, and the compounded tirzepatide vs Zepbound cost question, are the heart of this comparison.

Brand-name: FDA-approved, with trial results of their own

Wegovy (semaglutide) and Zepbound (tirzepatide) are finished products the FDA has reviewed and approved for chronic weight management. Their results come from large randomized trials. In the Wegovy prescribing information, adults on the 2.4 mg weekly injection lost an average of 14.9% of their body weight over 68 weeks against 2.4% on placebo, the STEP 1 result published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2021. The Zepbound label reports 20.9% average weight loss at the top 15 mg dose over 72 weeks against 3.1% on placebo. In the one large head-to-head trial, SURMOUNT-5 (NEJM, 2025), 751 adults without diabetes lost 20.2% on tirzepatide and 13.7% on semaglutide at 72 weeks; that trial was open label and run by tirzepatide's maker. All of those figures come from brand-name medication, and more detail is in our GLP-1 weight loss results guide.

ro's brand-name shelf includes the Wegovy pill (oral semaglutide), which matters if you want to avoid injections; our Wegovy pill price guide covers its $149-then-$299 pricing at ro. If you are weighing a GLP-1 injection vs weight loss pill cost, note that at ro the pill's ongoing price ($299) sits in the same range as the pen's ($299 to $399), with the same membership on top of either; GLP-1 pills vs injections sets the two formats side by side.

Compounded: the same active ingredient, a different product, no FDA approval

Compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide are prepared by licensed pharmacies from the active ingredient. The FDA's own compounding questions and answers page (content current September 16, 2025) says plainly that compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, which means the FDA does not verify their safety, effectiveness or quality before they are marketed. There are no clinical trials of the compounded products themselves, so the trial figures above cannot be assumed for them. The FDA's page on concerns with unapproved GLP-1 drugs (content current October 1, 2026) describes adverse event reports, some requiring hospitalization, linked to dosing errors with compounded injectable semaglutide, where patients drew the wrong dose from a multi-dose vial or clinicians miscalculated it. It also lists, as a telehealth red flag, a company that claims its compounded drug is the same as an FDA-approved drug.

That is the trade-off embody's price buys. What makes it a reasonable trade for many people is the pharmacy and the prescriber. embody is LegitScript-certified and fills through US-based 503A compounding pharmacies, meaning state-licensed pharmacies that compound for an individual patient on a prescription. The rules around that got tighter after the shortages ended. On the FDA's page tracking its GLP-1 compounding policy (updated April 1, 2026), the agency records that it declared the tirzepatide injection shortage resolved on December 19, 2024, after re-evaluating an October 2, 2024 decision, and the semaglutide injection shortage resolved on February 21, 2025. Its April 1, 2026 reminder says a 503A pharmacy must compound for an individual patient based on a prescription and must not compound, regularly or in inordinate amounts, products that are "essentially copies" of a commercially available drug, unless a prescriber documents a change that makes a significant difference for that patient. The same update gives an example: semaglutide combined with vitamin B12 may still be treated as essentially a copy when the strengths are within 10% of the commercial products. And it notes that tirzepatide and semaglutide do not currently appear on the 503B bulks list or the FDA's drug shortage list, which restricts the larger outsourcing facilities. Our compounded vs brand-name semaglutide guide goes through what that means in practice.

Flat-rate titration vs dose-tier pricing

One practical difference hides inside the medication question. Both semaglutide and tirzepatide are started low and stepped up over months, and the dose you stay on is the one that produced the trial results. embody prices its compounded medication flat at every dose: $49 or $99 whether you are at the starting dose or the maintenance dose. ro's brand-name prices step up after the introductory period: the Wegovy pill is $149 the first month and $299 after, the Wegovy pen from $199 at intro rates and then $299 to $399, the Zepbound KwikPen from $299 and then $399 to $449. For the pill, our Wegovy pill guide notes that the manufacturer's reported self-pay tiers also rise with dose, so the lowest price belongs to the dose you leave behind. Whichever provider you use, a clinician decides your starting dose and titration plan; neither company lets you choose a dose from a menu, and this guide gives no dosing instructions.

sections.heading: What is the consultation and intake like at embody and ro?
sections.body:
Both providers run a real clinical gate: a licensed clinician reviews your intake and can decline you. The experience around that gate differs.

embody: asynchronous, fast, self-serve

embody's intake is a roughly five-minute online health qualifier. There is no scheduled appointment; a licensed medical practitioner reviews your chart asynchronously, usually within 24 hours and often under five hours by embody's own account. If something needs clarifying you get a message. Once prescribed, orders placed before 2pm Central ship the same day, and embody quotes free expedited delivery in insured, temperature-controlled, tracked packaging; its Terms do not guarantee a delivery timeline. Ongoing care is through the patient portal and a nursing team, with dose adjustments requested and made there. It is a medication-first model: fast, low-friction and deliberately light on live contact. The step-by-step flow, with screenshots of real intake screens, is in our how to start GLP-1 treatment online guide.

ro: online assessment, provider review, in-house pharmacy

ro's stored description is an online medical assessment reviewed by a qualified provider, who decides whether treatment is appropriate, with the medication dispensed by ro's integrated pharmacy and dose adjustments handled by the provider over time. ro's review lists board-certified provider consultations and ongoing care among its features, and notes that wait times can vary during peak periods. We do not hold a published review-time promise or a published delivery window for ro, so we cannot put a number next to embody's 24 hours; "standard home delivery" is how our battle page records it. ro's size and its in-house pharmacy are real advantages for fulfilment and name recognition, and they are why ro wins the brand and pharmacy category on our embody vs ro battle page.

Labs and what to bring

Neither review in our files states whether labs are required. Across the providers we track, many ask for recent lab work and will order it if you have none, and some accept an attestation, so expect the question and have any recent results to hand. Both intakes will ask for height, weight, medical history, current medications and a government ID, because the prescription is written in your name. Answer honestly: the same answers that could get you declined are the ones that would make a GLP-1 unsafe for you.

Shipping times, side by side

embody's published promise is free expedited cold-chain delivery, with no timeline guaranteed in its Terms. ro's is home delivery from its own pharmacy without a stored window. Across every provider we track, shipping delays are the most common complaint, and the most common cause is pharmacy backlog rather than carrier time, so order before your current supply runs low whichever provider you choose. Our provider comparison sets each published shipping promise side by side.

Our three highest-ranked online GLP-1 providers are below.

sections.heading: Is embody weight loss legit and safe?
sections.body:
Is embody weight loss legit? Yes, by every signal we can check. embody is LegitScript-certified, an independent certification for online healthcare merchants. It works with US-based 503A compounding pharmacies, meaning state-licensed pharmacies that compound for an individual patient on a prescription. It requires a licensed medical review before any prescription is issued, and that review can and does decline people. Its pricing is published and flat, it refunds the unused portion (less services rendered) if you are not approved, and it is operated by a named company, Modern Metabolic Medicine, Inc., with prescribing clinicians from OpenLoop Health. Those are the markers that separate a legitimate telehealth provider from one to avoid, and embody has all of them. Our embody legitimacy guide runs through each.

Is it safe? That is a different question, and the honest answer is that the medication, not the company, carries the risk. embody's products are compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide, which the FDA does not review for safety, effectiveness or quality before sale. The FDA's October 2026 guidance on unapproved GLP-1 drugs documents dosing errors with compounded injectables drawn from multi-dose vials. A reputable provider mitigates that with a licensed pharmacy, a labelled vial with your name, the drug, the strength, the pharmacy's name and a beyond-use date, clear instructions and a nurse line for the first dose; if anything arrives unlabelled, stop and contact the provider. Beyond compounding, GLP-1s themselves have warnings on their labels, including a boxed warning on thyroid C-cell tumours seen in rodents, and warnings on pancreatitis and gallbladder disease, which is why a clinician's review of your history matters and why you should tell them everything.

So: legitimate, yes. Safe, as safe as compounded GLP-1 treatment under a licensed clinician can be, which is a real step below an FDA-approved product with trial data behind it and a real step above anything bought outside the licensed system. For an embody weight loss review covering plans and the full record, see our embody review.

sections.heading: What is the cheapest online weight loss injection provider in the US?
sections.body:
At our verified price index check on November 3, 2026, the cheapest online weight loss injection was compounded semaglutide at welludr for $41 a month, a pre-Black Friday sale price (previously $49) that requires a 12-month plan and is the same at every dose, shipped in three to five business days. The cheapest with no commitment was embody at $49 a month, flat, month to month, shipped in one to two days. For tirzepatide the same two led: $71 at welludr on the 12-month plan and $99 at embody month to month. Both companies' figures were sale prices with no end date stated, and embody's site showed a countdown to a price increase on the day we checked.

Whether $41 or $49 is the better deal depends on the commitment. welludr's $41 saves $96 over a year against embody's $588 but asks for twelve months; embody's $49 is the lowest price you can walk away from after a single month, which matters most in the first weeks when you are finding out whether you tolerate the medication. ro does not compete in this tier: at the stored rates, its cheapest semaglutide route is the Wegovy pill at $149 the first month and $299 after, plus the membership. The live ladder, every provider lowest first with its condition, is on our cheapest GLP-1 online page, and the best online GLP-1 provider in the US overall, on our criteria, is the ranking at the top of this site.

sections.heading: Does ro cover the cost of Wegovy if insurance denies it?
sections.body:
Not in any way we have verified. What our records state is this: ro bills the medication separately from its membership, so where your insurance covers Wegovy the plan can pay its share, and where it does not you pay ro's cash rate, which for the Wegovy pill is $149 the first month and then $299 a month, or from $199 and then $299 to $399 for the pen, on top of the membership. We have no stored statement from ro about absorbing the cost, matching a price, or refunding the membership after a coverage denial, so we cannot tell you that ro covers the gap, and you should not assume it does. Confirm directly with ro before paying the $39 what happens to your membership if your plan denies the medication, and what the ongoing cash price at your maintenance dose would be.

Two things we can say. First, a ro GLP-1 insurance coverage check starts with you, not ro: call the number on your card or search your plan's formulary for "Wegovy" and "Zepbound", and ask whether prior authorization is required; coverage for weight loss alone is much patchier than coverage for diabetes, and many employer plans exclude it. Our GLP-1 with insurance guide explains the formulary, prior authorization and appeals. Second, if coverage is denied, the ro Wegovy cash price without insurance is the number above, and the self-pay backup is compounded semaglutide at $41 to $49 a month, a different, non-FDA-approved product. If brand-name Wegovy is what you want regardless, our Wegovy providers page covers how to get a Wegovy pen online in the US and what each route charges.

sections.heading: Can you switch from brand Wegovy to compounded semaglutide online?
sections.body:
Often, yes, but it is a clinician's decision, not a checkout option. Both medications contain semaglutide, so a licensed prescriber at a compounded provider such as embody can review your history, including the dose you are on and how you have tolerated it, and decide whether to prescribe compounded semaglutide and at what dose. Some people switch because insurance coverage ended, some because the cash price at embody is a fraction of a brand-name pen plus membership. The reverse move, from compounded to brand-name Wegovy or Zepbound, is what ro's model is built for, and again a ro provider makes the call.

Three cautions. The compounded product is not the same as Wegovy: same active ingredient, different product, no FDA approval and no trial data of its own, as the FDA's compounding Q&A makes clear. Compounded semaglutide usually arrives as a multi-dose vial you draw from, not a prefilled pen, which is where the dosing-error reports come from, so your first dose deserves the provider's instructions and nurse line. And do not improvise a dose during the switch; tell the new provider exactly what you were taking and when your last dose was, and let them set the plan. Our switching from Ozempic guide covers moving providers or medications without a gap in treatment, and the embody vs ro battle page scores the two providers category by category.

sections.heading: The bottom line
sections.body:
embody vs ro weight loss comes down to two questions. Are you paying cash, and are you comfortable with compounded medication? If yes to both, embody is the stronger offer: $49 a month for compounded semaglutide or $99 for compounded tirzepatide at the November 3, 2026 sale prices, flat at every dose, with the clinician review, supplies and free expedited cold-chain delivery (no timeline guaranteed) included, a partial refund if you are not approved (unused portion less services rendered), and no contract. It is our top-ranked provider for exactly that combination. Does your insurance cover Wegovy or Zepbound, or do you want the FDA-approved brand-name product from a large, established platform with its own pharmacy? Then ro is the better fit: a $39-then-$74-to-$149 membership plus the medication, billed separately so your plan can pay for it, and a six-month cash cost that runs about $2,088 to $2,428 for the Wegovy pill if it does not.

Both are legitimate. Both put a licensed clinician between you and the prescription, and that clinician, not this article, decides whether a GLP-1 is right for you and which one. Compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide are not FDA-approved; Wegovy and Zepbound are. Prices are the providers' published rates at our last check and change often, so confirm them at checkout. For the full reviews, see embody and ro; for the legitimacy audits, is embody legit? and is ro legit?. This is general information, not medical advice.

articles.title: Is Compounded Semaglutide Going Away? FDA Rules, Nov 2026
articles.description: Compounded semaglutide is not FDA-approved and not banned outright. What the FDA's Empower warning letter and 503B proposal mean for your plan (Nov 2026).
articles.author: Treatments Hub Research Team
keyTakeaways: Not banned, not on a date. The FDA's own status line reads "Tirzepatide and semaglutide do not currently appear on the 503B bulks list or on FDA's drug shortage list" (compounding-policy page, current as of April 1, 2026, read Nov 18, 2026). Patient-specific 503A compounding continues where a prescriber documents a "significant difference" for that patient. Compounded semaglutide is not FDA-approved.

Warning Letter 738238 to Empower Pharmacy (September 18, 2026, posted September 22) says its SEMAGLUTIDE/CYANOCOBALAMIN (1 mL, 5/0.5 mg/mL) and two TIRZEPATIDE/NIACINAMIDE vials "appear to be essentially copies" of approved products, compounded "regularly and in inordinate amounts." No response or close-out letter was posted as of Nov 18, 2026.

On April 30, 2026 the FDA proposed leaving semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide off the 503B bulks list, having "not identified a clinical need." Comments ran to June 29, 2026. No final determination was found on fda.gov as of Nov 18, 2026; that is an absence, not a confirmation.

Prices read on the providers' own pages Nov 18, 2026: embody $49/month (compounded semaglutide, not FDA-approved, sale banner with no end date); HealthRx $39 first month then $125/month; DirectMeds $249/month sublingual. None of the three pages says what happens to a prepaid plan if compounding stops.

sections.heading: Is compounded semaglutide going away?
sections.body:
The short answerNot outright, and not on any announced date. The shortage basis for mass compounding ended in 2025. On September 18, 2026 the FDA told Empower Pharmacy its semaglutide/B12 and tirzepatide/niacinamide vials "appear to be essentially copies" of approved drugs, and on April 30, 2026 it proposed closing the 503B bulk route. Patient-specific 503A compounding continues under a prescriber's documented finding. Compounded semaglutide is not FDA-approved. Status read at fda.gov Nov 18, 2026.

The real question is not legal. It is whether you can keep the $49 to $249 a month plan you are on or about to buy, and, if the pharmacy stops, what happens to your money and your treatment. Every FDA quote below was read at fda.gov on Nov 18, 2026, and every provider price was read on the provider's own page the same day or taken from our verified price index with its date.

The FDA has not banned compounded semaglutide and has set no date on which anything ends. It has also, in writing, named the vitamin B12 co-formulation that most telehealth brands sell as a product it "may consider" essentially a copy of an approved drug, and it has told one large 503A pharmacy that its output volume makes the differences "pretextual."

What this page is not: medical advice. Nothing here tells you to stop, switch or stock up. The FDA says compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, which means the agency "does not verify the safety, effectiveness or quality of compounded drugs before they are marketed" (Compounding and the FDA: Questions and Answers, content current as of September 16, 2025, read Nov 18, 2026). Your prescriber is the person to ask about your own treatment.

sections.heading: What did the FDA's warning letter to Empower actually say?
sections.body:
Warning Letter 738238 is dated September 18, 2026 and addressed to Empower Clinic Services, LLC dba Empower Pharmacy, Houston, Texas. The FDA's warning-letter database lists it as posted September 22, 2026 under the subject "CGMP/Finished Pharmaceuticals/Adulterated/Unapproved New Drug" (database search, read Nov 18, 2026). It follows an inspection "From November 3, 2025, through November 14, 2025," a Form FDA 483 issued November 14, 2025, and firm responses dated December 8, 2025, March 18, 2026 and April 30, 2026.

The products it names, in the letter's own strings:

Product as written in the letterVialConcentrationActive drug per vial (arithmetic)
SEMAGLUTIDE/CYANOCOBALAMIN1 mL5/0.5 mg/mL5 mg semaglutide, 0.5 mg cyanocobalamin
TIRZEPATIDE/NIACINAMIDE2.5 mL8/2 mg/mL20 mg tirzepatide, 5 mg niacinamide
TIRZEPATIDE/NIACINAMIDE4 mL17/2 mg/mL68 mg tirzepatide, 8 mg niacinamide

Source: Warning Letter 738238, September 18, 2026, read Nov 18, 2026. Per-vial figures are mg/mL multiplied by mL. They are not doses and not weeks of supply; see our page on reading a compounded vial in mg, not units.

The core charge is under section 503A, the patient-specific compounding route. The FDA writes that these products "appear to be essentially copies of FDA-approved semaglutide and tirzepatide products" and that "production records collected during the inspection indicate that your firm compounded these drug products regularly or in inordinate amounts." For each of July, August, September and October 2025 the letter says the firm "compounded and filled more than (b)(4) orders" of each product; the quantities are redacted.

The sentence that matters most for anyone on a B12 or niacinamide formulation: "FDA is aware of high demand for compounded versions of FDA-approved semaglutide and tirzepatide products. The volume of products you are producing suggests that differences between products you are compounding and the FDA-approved products are pretextual."

The evidence the FDA lists is three-fold: "(1) orders/prescriptions that lack any prescriber determination of significant difference from the commercially available product; (2) orders/prescriptions with purported prescriber determinations of 'significant difference' that appear to be repeated verbatim across many records, suggesting that they may be pre-generated for selection by the prescriber, rather than written by the prescriber for an identified individual patient; and (3) the volume of particular products compounded and orders filled." It adds that such statements can arrive "through third-party technology platforms that provide prescribers with pre-selected menu options for choosing a statement of significant difference." That is a description of a telehealth workflow, and it is the reason this letter reaches further than one pharmacy.

The consequence the FDA draws: products outside 503A lose the exemptions from "the FDA approval requirement of section 505," the labeling requirement of section 502(f)(1), and CGMP under 501(a)(2)(B). The letter also alleges the products were "prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions," citing smoke studies and media fills, and lists five CGMP violations. It states, "You do not have any FDA-approved applications on file for the ineligible drug products that you compounded." The firm had "fifteen (15) working days" to respond; the letter warns that failure to address the violations "may result in legal action without further notice, including, without limitation, seizure and injunction." As of Nov 18, 2026 the database shows no response letter and no close-out letter.

Two cautions. First, a warning letter sets out what the FDA says "appears" to violate the law; it is not a court finding. Second, none of the three provider pages we read on Nov 18, 2026 names Empower as its pharmacy, and this page does not say that any provider listed here is supplied by it.

sections.heading: Does adding B12 make compounded semaglutide legal?
sections.body:
Not by itself, in the FDA's own words. The agency's compounding-policy page (FDA clarifies policies for compounders, content current as of April 1, 2026, read Nov 18, 2026) sets out when a compounded product is "essentially a copy": it "has the same active pharmaceutical ingredient(s) (API) as the commercially available drug product in the same, similar or an easily substitutable strength, and the commercially available drug product can be used by the same route of administration (regardless of how it is labeled) prescribed for the compounded drug product. This is unless a prescriber determines and documents the compounded drug product contains a change that produces a significant difference from the commercially available drug product for an identified individual patient."

The page then gives the B12 example directly: "FDA may consider a compounded drug product that combines semaglutide API and another API, such as vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin), to be essentially a copy of a commercially available drug product when the: drug products are used by the same route of administration - the compounded drug product is given the same way as the commercially available drug products, such as an injectable; drug products are the same, similar or easily substitutable strength - the amounts of semaglutide and vitamin B12 in the compounded drug product are within 10% of the strengths of the respective commercially available drug products."

So the test is not whether B12 is present. It is whether a named prescriber "determines and documents" a significant difference for a named patient. The statute, as the Empower letter quotes it, exempts a product only where "there is a change, made for an identified individual patient, which produces for that patient a significant difference, as determined by the prescribing practitioner." The Empower letter's complaint is that the statements it saw were missing or "repeated verbatim across many records." The same page also preserves a small-volume line: the FDA "does not intend to take action against a compounder" that "fills four or fewer prescriptions of that compounded drug product during a calendar month."

A B12 formulation prescribed with an individual, documented reason remains inside 503A; the same formulation produced in volume on template statements is what the FDA says appears to be a copy in the Empower letter. Which side a given plan sits on is a question for the prescriber and the pharmacy, not something a product page settles. Our page on compounded semaglutide vs brand-name covers what is and is not the same about the molecule itself; compounded products are not FDA-approved either way.

sections.heading: What is the 503B bulks-list decision, and when is it final?
sections.body:
503B outsourcing facilities are the larger, FDA-registered compounders that make batches without patient-specific prescriptions. The FDA's April 30, 2026 press release (read Nov 18, 2026) states the rule they work under: "In most cases, outsourcing facilities cannot compound drugs using bulk drug substances unless the substance appears on the 503B bulks list, or the compounded drug is on the FDA's drug shortage list at the time of compounding, distribution, and dispensing." With the shortages over, the bulks list was the remaining door.

On April 30, 2026 the FDA "announced it is proposing to exclude semaglutide, tirzepatide, and liraglutide on the 503B bulks list, finding no clinical need for outsourcing facilities to compound these drugs from bulk substances." Its reasoning: "After evaluating the nominations for these three substances, the FDA did not identify a clinical need for outsourcing facilities to compound semaglutide, tirzepatide, and liraglutide from bulk drug substances." Commissioner Makary is quoted: "When FDA-approved drugs are available, outsourcing facilities cannot lawfully compound using bulk drug substances unless there is a clear clinical need."

When is it final? The press release says comments were invited "through the docket by June 29, 2026" and that "The agency will consider submitted comments before making a final determination." The page links to Federal Register document 2026-08552 (published May 1, 2026 per its title). Search-result titles also show a Federal Register notice dated June 26, 2026 described as a comment-period extension; we could not read it, so the extended deadline is unverified. As of Nov 18, 2026 the 503B Bulk Drug Substances List page (content current as of May 16, 2024) has no row for semaglutide, tirzepatide or liraglutide, and no final determination appears on fda.gov. That is an absence in our search, not a confirmation that nothing has happened, and this page does not predict a date.

The 503B route is a proposal under review. The FDA's April 1, 2026 status line: "Tirzepatide and semaglutide do not currently appear on the 503B bulks list or on FDA's drug shortage list." For what the two pharmacy types mean for your vial, see 503A vs 503B pharmacies and the 28-day rule.

The dates the shortages ended, from the compounding-policy page: tirzepatide "[12/19/2024] FDA re-evaluated its determination from October 2, 2024 ... determining the tirzepatide injection shortage is resolved"; semaglutide "[2/21/2025] FDA has determined the shortage of semaglutide injection products ... is resolved." Source: Treatments Hub GLP-1 price index; the Medvi, bmiMD and SHED sites could not be opened on Nov 18, 2026, so their rows carry the index date. All products in this table are compounded and not FDA-approved. For the record, the FDA's warning-letter database shows letters dated June 8, 2026 to Eden and altRx; both concern website claims (the FDA calls the representations "false or misleading" and objects to the brand's name on labels "suggesting" it is the compounder). Neither uses the "essentially copies" wording or cites production volumes, so they are a different kind of letter from Empower's. Our provider comparison carries both.

Ask any provider:

  • Which pharmacy, by name, and is it 503A or 503B? embody names four 503A pharmacies on its page; HealthRx says 503A without a name; DirectMeds says "certified U.S. pharmacy." The FDA's page for telehealth companies (content current as of June 15, 2026) warns against "claiming a compounded drug is sourced from an FDA-approved or FDA-licensed pharmacy or outsourcing facility. FDA does not approve or license any facility."
  • What is the dose in mg and the concentration in mg/mL on the label? The Empower letter writes every product as mg/mL and mL. Instructions given only in "units" are the pattern behind the FDA's dosing-error reports (content current as of October 1, 2026): "multiple reports of adverse events, some requiring hospitalization, that may be related to dosing errors associated with compounded injectable semaglutide products."
  • Is the prescriber's "significant difference" statement individual? That is the exact point the Empower letter turns on. A reader cannot audit the pharmacy's records, but can ask whether the prescriber wrote a reason specific to them.
  • What happens to my plan if the pharmacy stops this product? None of the three pages read on Nov 18, 2026 answers it. The next section is what the refund terms do say.

sections.heading: What happens to your plan if your pharmacy stops?
sections.body:
No provider page we read commits to anything if its pharmacy stops compounding semaglutide. What the pages do state is their ordinary refund and renewal terms, and those decide how exposed you are. embody: payments already made are non-refundable, and a cancellation must land 72 hours before the next billing date, so on a 4-week plan the most you have at risk is one cycle, while on a 52-week plan paid upfront the page gives no refund path. HealthRx: a full refund only "if a provider does not approve you," then automatic renewal "at the price shown at checkout until you cancel." DirectMeds: "no subscriptions," a full refund if the doctor does not approve the treatment, and bulk 6- or 12-month pricing that is not published.

What a year costs at the prices displayed on Nov 18, 2026, before any unpublished bulk discount (all compounded, not FDA-approved):

PlanArithmetic12-month totalAverage per month
embody, GLP-1 injections$49 × 12$588$49
embody, GLP-1/GIP injections$99 × 12$1,188$99
HealthRx, semaglutide$39 + (11 × $125)$1,414$117.83
HealthRx, tirzepatide$39 + (11 × $199)$2,228$185.67
DirectMeds, sublingual semaglutide$249 × 12$2,988$249
DirectMeds, injection$297 × 12$3,564$297

Source: provider pages read Nov 18, 2026; arithmetic shown. Billing cadence (monthly vs upfront) is as each page states and is not the same across the three.

The brand-name comparators our providers publish on their own brand shelves, from the price index verified Nov 3, 2026: Ozempic $1,149 to $1,399 a month, Wegovy $1,579 to $1,799, Zepbound $1,249 to $1,599. The Wegovy pill was listed at $149 for the first month then $299 when we last checked it (Oct 9, 2026; not re-verified on Nov 18 because the manufacturer's sites were unreachable from our network). Wegovy is the FDA-approved semaglutide product for weight management (Wegovy label, revised 6/2026); Ozempic is approved for type 2 diabetes, not weight management (Ozempic label, revised 5/2026). Our Zepbound price page covers the approved tirzepatide injection.

A month-to-month plan carries one cycle of risk if a pharmacy stops; a prepaid year carries the whole year unless the terms say otherwise, and on the pages we read they do not. That is the question our guide before you prepay for a GLP-1 plan is built around, and the sale prices on our Black Friday GLP-1 deals page are mostly tied to longer terms. If you are weighing a move to a brand product because of this, the page on what to do when coverage for Zepbound or Wegovy ends lists the cash routes; a change of medication is a prescriber's decision.

sections.heading: Is compounded tirzepatide going away too?
sections.body:
The same documents cover it. Two of the three products named in the Empower letter are TIRZEPATIDE/NIACINAMIDE (2.5 mL at 8/2 mg/mL and 4 mL at 17/2 mg/mL), and the FDA's "essentially copies" and "inordinate amounts" language applies to them as it does to the semaglutide product. The 503B proposal of April 30, 2026 names tirzepatide alongside semaglutide and liraglutide. The tirzepatide shortage was declared resolved on December 19, 2024, the 503A grace period ended when the court denied the injunction on March 5, 2025, and the 503B period ran "until March 19, 2025." Tirzepatide does not appear in the shortage database as read on Nov 18, 2026.

Compounded tirzepatide is not FDA-approved. Today's prices on the pages read Nov 18, 2026: embody's GLP-1/GIP injections at $99/month, HealthRx at $39 for the first month then $199/month; the rest of the field is in the index table above. Zepbound (tirzepatide) injection is the FDA-approved product for chronic weight management; see our Zepbound price page.

sections.heading: The FDA record, dated: what each document changed
sections.body:
Each row is a document read at fda.gov on Nov 18, 2026.

DocumentDateWhat it changedStatus as read Nov 18, 2026
Tirzepatide shortage resolved (policy page entry)12/19/2024Shortage basis for compounding tirzepatide ends; 503A grace to Feb 18, 2025 or the court decision; 503B to Mar 19, 2025Court denied injunction Mar 5, 2025; 503A grace "has ended"; 503B ended Mar 19, 2025
Semaglutide shortage resolved (policy page entry)02/21/2025Same for semaglutide; 503A to Apr 22, 2025 or the court decision; 503B to May 22, 2025Court denied injunction Apr 24, 2025; 503A grace "has ended"; 503B ended May 22, 2025
30 warning letters to telehealth companies03/03/2026Marketing claims: "implying sameness with FDA-approved products" and branding products with the telehealth firm's name "implying they are the compounder"Press release read; individual letters not counted here
Policy page update04/01/2026Defines "essentially a copy," gives the B12 example and the "within 10%" strength test, states the "four or fewer prescriptions" lineCurrent
503B bulks-list proposal04/30/2026 (Federal Register 05/01/2026)Would keep semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide off the 503B bulks listComments to June 29, 2026 per the FDA page; a June 26, 2026 extension notice exists (deadline unread); no final determination found
Eden and altRx letters06/08/2026Website claims only; no "essentially copies" findingPosted 06/16/2026
Empower Warning Letter 73823809/18/2026 (posted 09/22/2026)First letter in this record naming semaglutide/B12 and tirzepatide/niacinamide vials as "essentially copies," compounded "regularly and in inordinate amounts," under 503ANo response or close-out letter posted
Drug shortage databaseLiveSemaglutide injection and tirzepatide: not listed; liraglutide injection: "Currently in Shortage"; semaglutide tablet: Rybelsus "Discontinuation"As read Nov 18, 2026

Source: fda.gov and accessdata.fda.gov pages linked in each row, all read Nov 18, 2026. Dates are the FDA's own; where the FDA writes February 18, 2025 for the tirzepatide 503A date we keep its date rather than our arithmetic.

sections.heading: Is compounded semaglutide being discontinued?
sections.body: No document we read announces a discontinuation of compounded semaglutide. The only "Discontinuation" entry in the FDA shortage database under semaglutide is Novo Nordisk's Rybelsus tablets (3 mg, 7 mg, 14 mg), posted June 4, 2026, "replaced by Ozempic (semaglutide) tablets." That is a brand-name tablet, not a compounded product. What has changed is the legal basis for compounding in volume, covered above. Whether a particular provider continues is that provider's decision and its pharmacy's; none of the three pages we read on Nov 18, 2026 says it is stopping.

sections.heading: Is compounded semaglutide still legal?
sections.body: Compounding under section 503A remains lawful when its conditions are met, and the FDA's own April 1, 2026 text preserves the exception: a product is not "essentially a copy" where "a prescriber determines and documents the compounded drug product contains a change that produces a significant difference from the commercially available drug product for an identified individual patient." The Empower letter is about products the FDA says did not meet those conditions, compounded "regularly and in inordinate amounts." Legal and FDA-approved are different things: the FDA's policy page says plainly, "Compounded drugs are not approved by FDA. FDA-approved drugs go through FDA's rigorous review for safety, effectiveness, and quality as part of the premarket approval process." The FDA's concerns page (content current as of October 1, 2026) adds that salt forms "including semaglutide sodium and semaglutide acetate, are different active ingredients than are used in the approved drugs." Nothing on this page is legal or medical advice.

sections.heading: How do you switch from compounded semaglutide to Wegovy or Zepbound?
sections.body: Through your prescriber. A change of product is a prescribing decision, and this page gives no dose or timing instructions. The approved semaglutide product for weight management is Wegovy (label revised 6/2026, read Nov 18, 2026), indicated "in combination with a reduced calorie diet and increased physical activity" to reduce excess body weight and, in adults with established cardiovascular disease and obesity or overweight, to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events. Ozempic (label revised 5/2026) is indicated for glycemic control in type 2 diabetes, not weight management. The approved tirzepatide injection for weight management is Zepbound. Cash prices for the brands on our providers' shelves ran $1,149 to $1,799 a month at the Nov 3, 2026 index check; the Wegovy pill's $149 first month then $299 figure dates from Oct 9, 2026 and was not re-verified. The money side of a switch is covered on semaglutide cost per month and the complete guide to GLP-1 weight loss online.

sections.heading: What this page could not verify
sections.body:
• The Federal Register text of the 503B proposal (document 2026-08552, May 1, 2026) and the June 26, 2026 extension notice (2026-12937): federalregister.gov, govinfo.gov and regulations.gov were unreachable from our network. The docket number and any extended comment deadline are unverified; we use the FDA press release's June 29, 2026.
  • Any final 503B determination on semaglutide, tirzepatide or liraglutide: none found on fda.gov through Nov 18, 2026. Absence, not confirmation.
  • The appeal in OFA v. FDA: secondary sources describe an outcome; the court's site was unreachable, so it is left out.
  • How many telehealth warning letters were issued in 2026 beyond the 30 announced on March 3, 2026: the database view we could read showed a further batch dated June 8, 2026 with no total.
  • Whether Empower responded within 15 working days, or whether the FDA has closed the letter out: nothing posted as of Nov 18, 2026. The order volumes in the letter are redacted.
  • Prices at Medvi, bmiMD, SHED and Hims on Nov 18, 2026 (sites unreachable or blocked); Wegovy pill and Zepbound vial prices from the manufacturers (sites unreachable). Index figures carry their own dates above.
  • A stated formulation in mg/mL on any of the three provider pages read: none. Black Friday end dates on those pages: none stated.

sections.heading: Where the compounded providers fit in this picture
sections.body: Every provider in the tables above sells a compounded product that is not FDA-approved, and every one of the three we read on Nov 18, 2026 says so on its own page. The differences that matter after the Empower letter are the ones the pages make checkable: whether the pharmacy is named with its type stated (embody does both; HealthRx states 503A without a name; DirectMeds states neither) and what the refund terms say when a shipment does not come. Prices change; the GLP-1 price tracker logs every verified move with its date, and the cheapest GLP-1 page ranks the current index. The weight-loss hub links every review. This page will be updated when the FDA posts a final 503B determination or a response to the Empower letter, with the date it was read. Nothing here is medical advice; your prescriber decides your treatment.

articles.title: How to Cancel a GLP-1 Telehealth Subscription: 7 Providers
articles.description: Cancel steps, charge cutoffs (72 hours down to 12) and refund rules taken from seven GLP-1 telehealth providers' own terms, read Nov 22, 2026.
articles.author: Treatments Hub Research Team
keyTakeaways: Three different windows in seven sets of terms, all read Nov 22, 2026: 72 hours before the next billing date (altRx, embody), 48 hours or 2 days (DirectMeds, welludr's terms) and 12 hours (REX MD). HealthRx and Collective state no hour count for month-to-month billing.

welludr's two documents disagree. Its terms (updated Oct 16, 2026) require cancelling at least 2 days before the renewal date. Its refund policy (no date shown) says cancellation is effective when received and states no cutoff. Neither says it overrides the other.

No provider here promises a refund for medication you have already received. altRx and embody refund the unused part of a term only if their provider finds you not clinically eligible. HealthRx still bills the rest of a 3, 6 or 12-month minimum if you cancel early.
We could not read the cancel terms for TrimRx, Medvi, Eden, SHED, Sprout, bmiMD or Hims, so this page does not cover them.

sections.heading: How do you cancel a telehealth GLP-1 subscription?
sections.body:
The short answerUse the channel in the provider's own terms and cancel before its cutoff: 72 hours before the next billing date at altRx and embody, 48 hours at DirectMeds, 2 days at welludr (its terms), 12 hours at REX MD. None of the seven states a right to a refund for medication you already received. Keep the confirmation. Cancelling billing does not tell your prescriber to stop treatment.

This table comes from the providers' own documents, not from reviews or forum posts. Every cell is quoted or closely paraphrased in the sections below the table, with the document's URL and date. "Not stated" means the documents we read do not say. All documents were read on Nov 22, 2026.

ProviderHow to cancelCutoff before the next chargeBilling cadenceRefund after shipmentPause option
welludrAccount or portal message, email, or phoneTerms: 2 days before the renewal date. Refund policy: none, effective when received21-Day plan every 21 days; 3, 6 and 12-month plans prepaid in full; "Monthly Plan" cadence not statedNone once the pharmacy has started the order, except the unearned part of a prepaid plan"May" be offered; only valid once confirmed in writing
altRxEmail, phone or patient portal72 hours before the next billing date"Recurring intervals disclosed" at checkoutAll payments final; partial refund of the unused term only if the provider finds you not clinically eligibleHomepage FAQ says "pause or cancel"; how it works not stated

HealthRxEmailMonth-to-month: none stated. Paid-up-front plans: "before your next renewal date"Monthly; 3, 6 and 12-month plans bill monthly with a minimum; paid-in-full plans renew every 3, 6 or 12 monthsUnshipped dose refunded; once handed to carriers, sales are finalNot stated
DirectMedsTurn off auto-refill in the account portal48 hours before the next processing dateEvery 30 days, with notice 5 to 7 days before each chargeNone for medication received; returns only for listed casesNot stated

Source: each provider's own terms, refund policy or FAQ, read Nov 22, 2026. Document dates and quotes are in the sections below.

Most of these providers sell compounded semaglutide or tirzepatide. The FDA states that "compounded drugs are not FDA approved" and that it does not review them "for safety, effectiveness or quality before they are marketed" (FDA, content current as of 10/01/2026, read Nov 22, 2026). This page is general information, not medical advice. For what each plan costs, see the verified price index; for whether each provider is what it says it is, see is welludr (welludr) legit, is altRx legit, is embody legit, is HealthRx legit and is DirectMeds legit.

sections.heading: How do I cancel welludr (formerly wellmedr)?
sections.body:
welludr (formerly wellmedr) has two documents that cover cancelling, and they give different rules.

DocumentDate shownCutoffWhen cancellation takes effect
Terms and ConditionsLast updated Oct 16, 2026At least 2 days before the scheduled renewal date, "measured from the originally scheduled date even if a charge or shipment is processed early""at the end of your current billing period"
Refund, Cancellation and Subscription PolicyNo date shown on the pageNone stated: "You may cancel automatic renewal at any time""at the timestamp our system receives the online request, email, telephone request, or voicemail"

Source: both pages read Nov 22, 2026. Neither document says it overrides the other, so we do not pick one. A request sent more than 2 days before your renewal date satisfies both. Keep the confirmation.

How to cancel. The terms say: "Cancel any time in your account, by emailing [the support address on the terms page], or by calling 1-888-397-6905 (8 AM to 8 PM ET)." The refund policy adds a portal message ("Cancel my subscription") and says "A voicemail clearly requesting cancellation will be treated as a cancellation request." It also says "No retention conversation or administrative approval is required."

If the charge is already submitted. The refund policy: "A request received before a scheduled charge is actually submitted will stop that charge. If the charge was already submitted before cancellation became effective, cancellation stops later renewals and the current payment is reviewed under the refund rules below."

Reminders. The refund policy says welludr sends a reminder "at least seven days before each 21-Day or 3-Month Plan charge and at least 15 days before each 6-Month Plan charge," and for a 12-Month Plan "notice 30 days before the Billing Date and a courtesy reminder seven days before it."

The same documents say what cancelling does not do. See does cancelling stop my treatment below, and our welludr legitimacy check and welludr cost page. Read our full welludr review.

sections.heading: How do I cancel altRx, embody, HealthRx, DirectMeds, REX MD or Collective?
sections.body:
altRx

Documents: refund and cancellation policy (Last Updated: August 25, 2026) and terms (Last Updated: May 6, 2026).

  • How: "To cancel, contact patient support at care@altrx.com or +1 607-601-6969 and request cancellation, or cancel through your online account/patient portal."
  • Cutoff: "Cancellation requests must be received at least 72 hours prior to your next billing date in order to stop the next charge. If your request is received inside that 72-hour window, your Subscription Service will be charged in accordance with the then-current billing cycle, that charge is non-refundable, and the cancellation will take effect at the start of the subsequent billing cycle."
  • Cadence: "your selected payment method will be automatically charged at the recurring intervals disclosed for that product during the checkout process unless and until you cancel." The interval is not in the terms.
  • Pause: the homepage FAQ says "You may pause or cancel your membership at any time." Neither the terms nor the refund policy explains pausing. The homepage also says "Cancel anytime"; the 72-hour cutoff above is in the policy.

embody

Documents: refund policy (Last Updated: August 25, 2026) and terms (Last updated: April 24th, 2026). The cancellation and refund text matches altRx's word for word.

  • How: "contact patient support at support@joinem.co or +1 (347) 269-4270 and request cancellation, or cancel through your online account/patient portal." The terms add "by replying to any email communications sent from embody."
  • Cutoff: the same 72-hour sentence as altRx, including that a late request is charged, non-refundable, and takes effect at the start of the next billing cycle.
  • Cadence: the terms say charges "will continue until you cancel your subscription." The interval is not stated. Pause: not found.

HealthRx

Documents: terms (Last updated November 7, 2026), returns and refund policy (no date shown) and FAQ. Read our full HealthRx review.

  • How: "You can cancel future renewals anytime by emailing support@healthrx.com." The FAQ adds: "No phone call needed."
  • Cutoff: none stated for month-to-month plans. For paid-up-front plans the terms say "To cancel, email support@healthrx.com before your next renewal date," with no hours or days given.
  • Cadence: the refund policy says "Subscribe & Save renews automatically at the price and interval shown at checkout until canceled." The 3, 6 and 12-month plans carry "a minimum of 3, 6 or 12 monthly payments" and bill monthly; paid-in-full plans "renew at the same price every 3, 6 or 12 months."
  • The minimum: "On a 3, 6 or 12-month plan, the monthly payments in your minimum are still due if you cancel early." The terms add "Payments still due in your minimum are charged on their normal dates, and your medication keeps shipping." After the minimum the plan "continues month to month at the same price until you cancel." Month-to-month plans "have no minimum."
  • Price changes: "If we propose a change to your renewal price or billing period, we will notify you at the email address on your account before it takes effect. You may cancel before the change." Pause: not found.

DirectMeds

Document: terms (Last updated: April 16, 2026), sections 5 and 7. Read our full DirectMeds review.

  • How and cutoff: "You may cancel any time up to 48 hours before the next processing date by turning off auto-refill in your account portal. Contact help@directmeds.com for assistance."
  • Cadence: "You will be charged the total subscription price (which may include pharmacy, medical group, and platform fees) every 30 days. You will receive advance notification 5-7 days prior to each charge." The statement descriptor is "DM2*DirectMeds".
  • A gap on its own site: the weight-loss page says "no subscriptions, no surprise charges, and no pressure," while the terms say "Certain products are sold on a subscription basis" with a charge every 30 days. Both statements are on DirectMeds' own site. Pause: not found.

REX MD

Documents: terms (Last Updated: May 22, 2026) and FAQ.

  • How: the terms say "you may do so at any time by calling us at: (866) 294-3772." For California and New York customers, and select Vermont customers with an initial subscription of one year or longer, the terms add the member portal or email. The FAQ is broader: "Simply reach out to our customer Care Team at 1-866-294-3772, [email], or through your patient portal." The two sections differ, so use the phone number if in doubt.
  • Cutoff: "all automatic renewal program subscription orders must be cancelled within (12) hours of the renewal subscription date to avoid the order being shipped and you incurring charges for same." This is the shortest window we found.
  • Cadence: "Recurring Fees will be charged in advance." The interval is not stated in the terms. The statement descriptor is "REX MD 866-294-3772" or "REX Wellness."
  • Pause: the FAQ says "We offer the flexibility to pause or cancel your subscription at any time." Mechanics are not stated.

Collective

Document: terms of use, "Version 2026-11-19 ... last updated: 19 November 2026," and the homepage FAQ. Read our full Collective review.

  • How: "You can cancel anytime, right from your account - no phone calls, no retention games." The terms say the membership renews "unless you cancel your membership before the end of the then-current membership period by canceling online through our Platform."
  • Cutoff: the 21-day free trial "will automatically convert to a paid annual membership ... unless you cancel before the Trial Period expires." No hour count is stated for the membership period or for medication orders.
  • Cadence: membership "$199/year, billed annually-not monthly." Medication is billed separately: "we obtain a pre-authorization on your payment card at checkout and charge your card only when the pharmacy ships your order." Pause: not found.

sections.heading: What is the cutoff to avoid the next charge?
sections.body:
Cutoffs from longest notice to shortest, as the documents word them:

ProviderCutoffIf you miss it
altRx, embody72 hours before the next billing dateThe charge goes through, is non-refundable, and the cancellation starts with the following billing cycle
welludr (terms)2 days before the scheduled renewal date, measured from the original date"Otherwise your subscription renews for another period"
DirectMeds48 hours before the next processing dateNot stated
REX MDWithin 12 hours of the renewal subscription dateThe order ships and you incur the charges

Source: the documents listed in the sections above, read Nov 22, 2026. "2 days" is welludr's wording; it equals 48 hours. REX MD's 12 hours is counted from the renewal date as its terms word it. welludr says early processing can happen: its first renewal "may be charged early to avoid a gap in treatment," and later renewals and shipments "may be processed up to two (2) days early for holidays or operational reasons."

A cutoff is a deadline set by the provider's own contract. We have not tested any of these by cancelling.

sections.heading: Can I get a refund after the medication ships?
sections.body:
Not on the terms we read, apart from the exceptions listed. The wording, provider by provider:

  • welludr: the refund policy says "Documented clinical services already performed and patient-specific medication for which Medication Fulfillment Start occurred are nonrefundable, except where law requires otherwise. Every objectively unearned or unfulfilled portion will be refunded, and future renewals will stop." "Medication Fulfillment Start" means "the dispensing pharmacy has documented that it began preparing, compounding, filling, or dispensing the patient-specific prescription." The terms are shorter: "Medication is not refundable once shipped." If the initial clinician does not approve treatment, the policy says the "full initial checkout payment will be refunded automatically within seven business days."
  • altRx and embody: "ALL PAYMENTS FOR THE SUBSCRIPTION SERVICES ARE FINAL AND NON-REFUNDABLE AT THE TIME OF PURCHASE." "Cancellation of your Subscription Service stops future billing only. It does not refund amounts already paid." Medications are "non-returnable and non-refundable under all circumstances." Multi-month and bundled plans "ARE NON-REFUNDABLE IN WHOLE AND IN PART." The exception: if their provider finds you "not clinically eligible," you get "a refund for any unused portion of the amount paid for the then-current term," less the consultation, review, prescriptions, shipped medication and labs already used. The policy gives no prices for those, so the refund cannot be worked out in advance.
  • HealthRx: "State and Federal regulations do not allow the return of prescription medications after being dispensed by the pharmacy. Once charged and handed to carriers, all sales become final." If the provider declines you, "HealthRX.com will issue a full refund of the related charge to the original payment method." The FAQ says it will "refund any unshipped dose."
  • DirectMeds: "Subscriptions can be canceled anytime, but no refunds for medication already received." Returns are accepted only for "incorrect medication, damaged products, products not meeting safety standards, unshipped products, or medication denied by a DirectMeds doctor," and "Returned medication incurs a $35 disposal fee." A prescription order can be cancelled "within 24 hours of placing it (if not yet received by the provider network)"; after that, orders "generally cannot be canceled."
  • REX MD: "UNLESS OTHERWISE INDICATED, ALL SALES ARE FINAL AND NON-REFUNDABLE." "Medications are not eligible for return or refund." The FAQ says a provider who finds you ineligible leads to "a full refund," and mentions refunds "on a case-by-case basis."
  • Collective: "all membership fees are non-refundable, and partial-period refunds are not provided" except as law or checkout states. Products "may not be returned and are nonrefundable except as otherwise determined by CollectiveOS in its sole discretion." If the doctor declines: "you get a full refund - you're never charged for medication you don't receive."

Source: the refund and terms documents named above, read Nov 22, 2026. welludr also asks you to "Contact patient portal support within seven calendar days after delivery if an item is missing, damaged, leaking, incorrect, or otherwise unusable." The other providers' damaged-item rules we did not compare beyond DirectMeds' return list above.

sections.heading: What if I am still charged after cancelling?
sections.body:
Only welludr's and altRx's documents describe this case, so this is what they state and nothing more.

  • welludr: the refund policy lists "Charge submitted after an effective cancellation: Full refund of the post-cancellation charge." Its FAQ asks you to call with "the charge date and amount, the date of your cancellation request, and any confirmation or message reference." Refunds go back to "the original payment method," approved refunds are submitted "within seven business days," and "Your bank or card issuer determines when the credit appears on your statement." This is why the confirmation matters: the policy ties the refund to when the request was received.
  • altRx: "If you believe a charge was made in error, contact patient support at care@altrx.com or +1 607-601-6969 before initiating a dispute with your card issuer or bank so that we can review the charge. Initiating a payment dispute does not alter the non-refundable nature of the Subscription Services under this policy." That is altRx's request in its own policy, not a rule from a regulator.

We did not find a process for a charge after cancelling in the other five providers' documents. A late request is a different case: altRx, embody and REX MD say a charge inside their window goes through (see the cutoff table). This page does not cover consumer-protection rules or card disputes, because we did not read a primary source on either.

sections.heading: Does cancelling stop my treatment?
sections.body:
No, not by itself, and the providers say so. welludr's refund policy: "Canceling automatic renewal does not automatically: Refund a payment already processed; Cancel a prescription or order that has received Medication Fulfillment Start; End the Current Term of a prepaid plan; or Tell your clinician to discontinue treatment." It then says: "Do not discontinue prescribed treatment solely because you canceled billing without first obtaining appropriate medical guidance." Its terms add: "Cancelling your membership also cancels your Medication Plan." HealthRx's refund policy says "Canceling a subscription does not return medication already dispensed."

Whether to stop, taper or switch is a question for your prescriber. altRx's FAQ makes the same point: "If you and your provider decide to discontinue GLP-1 treatment, your provider may recommend a tapering schedule." For what the research says about stopping, read what happens when you stop a GLP-1. For how plans can change if compounding rules change, read is compounded semaglutide going away.

sections.heading: What could we not verify?
sections.body:
We could not read the cancellation terms for TrimRx, Medvi, Eden, SHED, Sprout, bmiMD or Hims. Their sites or terms pages did not load for us on Nov 22, 2026 (or loaded without any text), so this page says nothing about their cutoffs, refunds or pause options. TrimRx's homepage shows the line "Cancel Before Your Next Billing Cycle," which is marketing text with no steps or deadline behind it. Check their own terms before you rely on a rule from another company's page. Our is TrimRx legit and is Eden legit pages cover what we could read of each company's own documents.

Three more limits. First, welludr's "Monthly Plan" shows "Cancel or change anytime" on its plan page, but none of the documents we read says how often that plan is charged; ask for the billing date in writing. Second, we did not test any cancellation flow, and the documents above can change; the dates shown are the dates on the documents, and Nov 22, 2026 is the date we read them. Third, a provider's terms are its side of a contract. They are not a ruling on what you can recover in every state.

Compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide are not FDA-approved. Nothing here is medical advice. Questions about your own treatment go to your prescriber.
